questions.stem: The aspect ratio of a letter refers to the ratio of its:
questions.solution:
**Height to width.**

In engineering lettering the **aspect ratio is stated height-first**, matching the convention that lettering is **specified by its HEIGHT**.

> For **vertical capital letters the proportion is h : w = 7 : 5**.

**Why height leads.** Height is what determines **legibility at a given reduction** — a drawing printed at half size halves the lettering height, and it is that height which decides whether the text can still be read. The width simply follows from the height by a fixed proportion.

**The lettering standards (IS 9609 / ISO 3098):**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Standard heights** | **2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm** |
| **Ratio between successive heights** | **√2** — matching the A-series paper progression |
| **Stroke thickness** (type B) | **h/10** |
| Character spacing | about 2/10 h |
| Minimum line spacing | 14/10 h |
| **Vertical style** | **90°** |
| **Inclined (italic) style** | **75°** to the horizontal, sloping right |

> The **√2 progression** is why a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 keeps its lettering exactly **one standard size smaller** and remains legible. It is the same reasoning that governs the paper sizes themselves — **A0 is exactly 1 m²**, and each size halves the longer dimension.

**Other proportions worth carrying:**

| Character | h : w |
|---|---|
| **Most capitals** | **7 : 5** |
| **W** | Wider — 7 : 7 |
| **I** | A single stroke |
| Numerals | 7 : 5 |

**And the rule that is tested as often as the ratio itself:**

> **Only ONE lettering style may be used on a single drawing.** Mixing vertical and inclined lettering is a drafting fault, however neat each is on its own.

examTip.trick: Lettering is **specified by HEIGHT**, so the aspect ratio is quoted **height-first**: **h : w = 7 : 5** for vertical capitals. The convention is consistent throughout the standard.
examTip.trap: Options (b) and (d) are the same ratio inverted, and (c) swaps in "length", which is not a lettering dimension at all. Only one option states it in the standard order.
examTip.mnemonic: **Heights 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 — each √2 times the last**, matching the A-series paper progression. That is why a reduced drawing keeps legible lettering exactly one size down.

questions.stem: The soil of the Kathmandu valley is:
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — the valley fill contains all three.

**What the Kathmandu valley is geologically:**

> A **LACUSTRINE DEPOSIT** — the bed of a former lake, filled over hundreds of thousands of years with fine sediment washed in from the surrounding hills.

> That single fact explains everything about the soil. A lake bed accumulates **fine-grained material in quiet water**: silts and clays, interbedded with **organic layers** from vegetation, and locally very dark (**"black cotton"-like**) horizons rich in organic matter.

**The engineering consequences, which are the reason this is examined:**

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Fine grained, low permeability** | **Consolidation settlement over years**, not months |
| **High compressibility** | Large settlements under load |
| **Organic content** | **Very high compressibility and creep**; unreliable strength |
| **Soft to medium consistency** at depth | Low bearing capacity |
| **High water table** | Reduces effective stress further |
| **Saturated fine sand and silt lenses** | **LIQUEFACTION potential** in an earthquake |

> **The black "kalimati"** layers found across the valley are the classic problem stratum — soft, organic, highly compressible clay, and the reason so many Kathmandu buildings need piled foundations rather than pads.

**Why the seismic behaviour matters so much:**

> A deep, soft sedimentary basin **AMPLIFIES ground motion** — seismic waves slow down and grow in amplitude as they enter softer material, and the basin geometry traps and reverberates them.

> That amplification is a large part of why the 2015 Gorkha earthquake caused the damage it did in the valley, while the shaking on nearby rock sites was much less severe.

**The design responses:**

| Response | Note |
|---|---|
| **Site-specific investigation** | Presumptive bearing values are unsafe here |
| **Piles** through the soft layers | To a competent stratum |
| **Raft** foundations | Where piling is impractical — ties the structure to settle uniformly |
| **Liquefaction assessment** | For saturated loose sand and silt lenses |
| **Ground improvement** | Preloading, stone columns |

> **The most important single point** is that **presumptive bearing capacity tables do not apply** to a lacustrine fill. IS 1904 gives no value at all for peat, fill or made ground, and the same caution belongs here.

examTip.trick: Anchor on the one geological fact: the valley is a **LACUSTRINE (former lake bed) deposit**. Everything else — fine grained, organic layers, black kalimati, soft and compressible — follows from quiet-water deposition.
examTip.trap: Each option on its own is defensible, which is exactly why "all of the above" is correct. A lake fill is heterogeneous, not one uniform material.
examTip.mnemonic: **A deep soft basin AMPLIFIES earthquake shaking** — a large part of why 2015 hit the valley harder than nearby rock sites. And **presumptive bearing tables do not apply**: a lacustrine fill needs site-specific investigation.

questions.stem: For a given discharge, the efficiency of a sedimentation tank can be increased by:
questions.solution:
**Increasing the surface area of the basin.**

**The governing relation.** A particle is removed if its **settling velocity exceeds the OVERFLOW RATE** (surface loading rate):

> **V_s = Q/(B × L) = Q/A_surface**

> **Increasing the surface area REDUCES the overflow rate**, so **slower-settling particles are also captured** and the efficiency rises.

**The result that surprises everyone:**

> **Removal efficiency depends on the SURFACE AREA ALONE — not on the depth, and not on the detention time.**

> Two tanks of the same plan area remove the same particles whether one is 2 m deep or 4 m deep, even though the deeper one holds twice the water and gives twice the detention time.

**Why depth does not help.** A particle entering at the surface must fall the full depth to be captured — but it also has proportionally longer to do it. **The two effects cancel exactly.** The particle's fate is decided by the ratio of its settling velocity to the overflow rate, in which depth does not appear.

> This is **Hazen's law**, and it is the single most important idea in sedimentation design.

**What the ideal settling basin theory assumes** and where reality departs:

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| Uniform horizontal flow | **Short-circuiting** and dead zones |
| Quiescent settling | Turbulence, wind, density currents |
| Particles do not re-suspend | **Scour** at high velocity |

> Depth **does** matter in practice — for **sludge storage**, to avoid **scouring** already-settled material, and to give room for the inlet and outlet zones. But it does not change which particles are removed.

**The design consequence — TUBE and PLATE SETTLERS:**

> If efficiency depends only on surface area, then **stacking inclined plates or tubes inside a tank multiplies its effective settling area** without enlarging its footprint.

> A tank fitted with plate settlers can achieve **several times** the throughput of the same empty tank. It is a direct, and very profitable, application of the theory.

**The other efficiency factors** (from the source's own note): efficiency rises if the **flow velocity falls**, if the **viscosity falls** (warmer water settles faster), and if the **particle size increases** — which is precisely what **COAGULATION** achieves, by aggregating colloids into large flocs.

**Typical design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Overflow rate** | **20 – 40 m³/m²/day** (plain sedimentation) |
| Detention time | 2 – 4 hours |
| **Horizontal velocity** | **≤ 0.3 m/min** — above it, scour |
| Weir loading | ≤ 300 m³/m/day |

examTip.trick: **V_s = Q/A_surface** — efficiency is set by the **overflow rate**, which contains the surface area and nothing else. Bigger area, lower overflow rate, more particles captured.
examTip.trap: **Depth does NOT affect which particles are removed.** A deeper tank gives longer detention, but the particle also has further to fall — the two cancel exactly. Depth matters only for sludge storage and to avoid scour.
examTip.mnemonic: **Because only AREA counts, stacking inclined PLATE or TUBE settlers multiplies capacity without enlarging the tank** — several times the throughput from the same footprint. That is Hazen's law paying for itself.

questions.stem: Web crippling in a steel beam occurs due to:
options: Failure of web under concentrated load
questions.solution:
**Failure (local buckling and yielding) of the web under a concentrated load.**

**What happens.** A concentrated load — a reaction at a support, or a beam framing in from above — is delivered through the **flange into the thin web**. The load spreads out through the flange at a **1 : 2.5 dispersion**, but over that short length the web must carry a **very high local bearing stress**.

> If the web is too thin, it **crumples locally** just below the flange. That is web crippling.

**The two related but distinct web failures**, which are constantly confused:

| Failure | Mechanism | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **WEB CRIPPLING (bearing)** | **Local YIELDING/crumpling** of the web where the load enters | **At the web-to-flange junction** — the root |
| **WEB BUCKLING** | The web acts as a **slender COLUMN** and buckles over its full depth | **Mid-depth** of the web |

> **Crippling is a LOCAL crushing at the root; buckling is a COLUMN failure over the whole depth.** Both are checked at every concentrated load and every support, and both are cured the same way.

**The remedies:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **BEARING STIFFENERS** | The standard solution — vertical plates welded each side of the web at the load point |
| **Thicker web** | Effective but wasteful over the whole span |
| **Longer bearing length** | Spreads the load further; a wider bearing plate at a support |

> **Bearing stiffeners are cheap and they solve both failures at once** — which is why they are provided at every support and every major point load in a plate girder.

**Why the distractors describe other things entirely:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| Excessive bending moment | **Flexural failure** — a strength check on the section |
| Secondary bending moment | Effects from joint eccentricity or P-Δ |
| **Column action of the compression flange** | **LATERAL TORSIONAL BUCKLING** — the flange buckling sideways |

**Lateral torsional buckling** deserves a note because it is the governing failure of most unrestrained steel beams:

> The **compression flange, unrestrained laterally, buckles sideways** and drags the section into twist. The beam fails at a moment far below its full plastic capacity.

> **The cure is LATERAL RESTRAINT**, not a bigger section — a floor slab, decking, or purlins connected to the compression flange. **A beam fully restrained along its compression flange cannot fail this way at all**, which is why composite floor beams develop their full capacity while the same beam bare does not.

**The full checklist for a steel beam:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bending strength** | Section classification governs whether the plastic modulus may be used |
| **Lateral torsional buckling** | Unless fully restrained |
| **Shear** | Web area |
| **Web buckling and crippling** | At loads and supports |
| **Deflection** | Serviceability — often governs a long span |

> **For a long-span steel beam DEFLECTION frequently governs**, not strength — which is why depth, not grade, is the usual answer to an inadequate beam.

examTip.trap: **Crippling versus buckling** is the pair to keep apart: crippling is **local crushing at the web-flange root**; web **buckling** is a **column failure over the full depth**. Both are cured by bearing stiffeners.
examTip.trick: Option (d), "column action of the compression flange", describes **LATERAL TORSIONAL BUCKLING** — a different failure entirely, and one cured by lateral restraint rather than by stiffeners.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load enters through the flange and crumples the thin web — so stiffen where the load lands.** Bearing stiffeners are cheap and fix crippling and web buckling together.

questions.stem: The condition for a well-conditioned triangle in triangulation is that no angle should be less than:
questions.solution:
**30 degrees.**

**The definitions:**

| Triangle | Condition |
|---|---|
| **WELL-conditioned** | **No angle smaller than 30°** and **none greater than 120°** |
| **ILL-conditioned** | An angle **below 30°** or **above 120°** |
| **IDEAL (equilateral)** | **All three angles 60°** — the theoretical best |

> Note the two figures the question separates: **60° is the IDEAL**; **30° is the LIMIT**. The question asks for the limiting condition, not the ideal — and 60° is offered precisely because it is the more memorable number.

**Why a small angle is dangerous.** In triangulation, the unknown sides are computed by the **sine rule**:

> **a/sin A = b/sin B**

> The error in a computed side depends on **how fast the sine changes with the angle** — that is, on **cos A**. Near **0° or 180° the cosine is largest**, so a small angular error produces the **largest** error in the computed length.

> Near **60°** the sine is changing moderately and the geometry is at its most robust, which is why the equilateral triangle is ideal.

**Put simply:**

> **A long thin triangle locates its far vertex badly.** Two rays that intersect at a shallow angle define their crossing point poorly — move either ray by a few seconds of arc and the intersection slides a long way.

> **The same principle governs the strength of fix in any intersection problem**, which is why it recurs in resection, in GPS satellite geometry (as **DOP**, dilution of precision) and in setting out.

**Triangulation figures**, in ascending order of strength:

| Figure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Chain of triangles** | Simple, rapid, fewest conditions — **weakest** |
| **Braced quadrilateral** | **The strongest simple figure** — four stations, both diagonals observed, many redundant checks |
| **Centred polygon** | Good for covering an area |

> **The braced quadrilateral is the workhorse of precise triangulation** precisely because its redundancy lets the observations check each other.

**Triangulation versus traversing:**

| | **Triangulation** | **Traversing** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | **ANGLES**, with a few measured base lines | **Angles AND distances** for every leg |
| Suits | Open, hilly country with long sights | Built-up areas, routes, corridors |
| Error control | Strong — abundant redundancy | Depends on the closure |

> Modern **EDM and GPS** have largely displaced classical triangulation, since measuring a distance is now as easy as measuring an angle — but the **well-conditioned geometry principle survives unchanged** in every kind of fix.

examTip.trap: **60° is the IDEAL (equilateral); 30° is the LIMIT.** The question asks for the limiting condition, and 60° is offered because it is the number most people remember first.
examTip.trick: Reason from geometry: **two rays crossing at a shallow angle locate their intersection badly.** A few seconds of angular error slides the point a long way — which is why thin triangles are barred.
examTip.mnemonic: **Well-conditioned: nothing below 30°, nothing above 120°.** The same "strength of fix" principle appears again as **DOP** in satellite positioning — good geometry beats good instruments.

questions.stem: The professional code of conduct issued by the Nepal Engineering Council has:
questions.solution:
**8 articles**, as keyed at the time of this sitting.

> **The source itself records that the number has since been increased to 11.** The paper's key reflects the earlier figure of 8, and it is transcribed as printed — but a candidate should know both, because a later paper may well ask for the current count.

**What the code of conduct covers.** The articles set out the professional obligations of a registered engineer:

| Obligation | Substance |
|---|---|
| **Competence** | Practise only within the field and level for which one is qualified |
| **Public safety** | **Hold the safety, health and welfare of the public paramount** |
| **Honesty and integrity** | No misrepresentation of qualifications or of work |
| **Confidentiality** | Protect the client's information |
| **Conflict of interest** | Disclose any interest that could affect judgement |
| **No secret commissions** | Neither offer nor accept |
| **Respect for colleagues** | No malicious injury to another engineer's reputation |
| **Continuing development** | Maintain and update competence |
| **Compliance with law and codes** | Including the building code |
| **Proper documentation** | Sign only work actually done or supervised |

**The obligation that overrides the rest:**

> **Public safety comes before the client's instructions and before the engineer's own interest.** Every professional code in the world places it first, and it is the provision that gives an engineer both the duty and the standing to refuse unsafe work.

**Enforcement:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| Warning or reprimand | For minor breaches |
| **Suspension** of registration | For a period |
| **REMOVAL from the register** | The ultimate sanction — the engineer may no longer practise |

> **Because registration is a legal requirement to practise, removal from the register ends the career.** That is what gives the Council's disciplinary power real force.

**A common misunderstanding worth correcting:**

> **Signing drawings one did not prepare or supervise is a disciplinary offence**, not a formality. It is among the most frequent breaches, and it is treated seriously because the signature is the public's only assurance that a competent person took responsibility.

**The standing institutional distinction:**

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION (NEA) represents.** Registration with the NEC is a **legal requirement**; NEA membership is voluntary.

verification.notes: The paper keys (a), 8 articles, and the source explanation itself records that the code of conduct has since been expanded to 11 articles. The keyed answer is retained because it reflects the position at the date of this sitting, but the discrepancy is flagged so that a candidate meeting a later paper is not misled. Nothing about the option text or the answer position was altered.

examTip.trick: This is pure recall with a moving target — the paper keys **8**, and the source itself notes the number has since risen to **11**. Know both, and answer with whichever the paper's era implies.
examTip.trap: The substance matters more than the count: **public safety overrides the client's instructions and the engineer's own interest.** That is the provision most likely to be tested in a scenario question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Signing drawings you did not prepare or supervise is a disciplinary offence** — one of the commonest real breaches. And the ultimate sanction, **removal from the register**, ends the right to practise entirely.

questions.stem: The relation between E, G and μ is:
questions.solution:
**μ = E/(2G) − 1**, which is simply **E = 2G(1 + μ)** rearranged.

**The elastic constant relations, all four:**

| Relation | Links |
|---|---|
| **E = 2G(1 + μ)** | **E, G, μ** |
| **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** | **E, K, μ** |
| **E = 9KG/(G + 3K)** | E, K, G |
| **μ = (3K − 2G)/(6K + 2G)** | μ, K, G |

> **Only TWO elastic constants are independent** for an isotropic material. Given any two, the other two follow — which is why these four relations exist and why they are all equivalent.

**Checking the answer by substitution:**

> **E = 2G(1 + μ)** → **E/(2G) = 1 + μ** → **μ = E/(2G) − 1** ✓

**A sanity check with real numbers.** For steel, **E = 200 GPa** and **G ≈ 80 GPa**:

> **μ = 200/(2 × 80) − 1 = 1.25 − 1 = 0.25** ✓ — the accepted value for steel.

> That check takes five seconds and eliminates every wrong option: (b) gives 200/80 − 1 = 1.5, (c) gives 0.25 − 1 = −0.75, (d) gives 0.75. **All are physically impossible.**

**The physical limits on Poisson's ratio**, which is what makes the sanity check decisive:

> **0 ≤ μ ≤ 0.5** for any ordinary material.

| Limit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **μ = 0** | No lateral contraction at all — **cork** is close |
| **μ = 0.5** | **INCOMPRESSIBLE** — volume unchanged; **rubber** is close |
| μ > 0.5 | Would mean the material **expands** in volume under compression — impossible |

> Setting **μ = 0.5** in **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** gives **E = 0**, i.e. **K → ∞** — infinite bulk modulus, which is exactly what incompressibility means. The formula encodes its own limit.

**Typical values:**

| Material | μ |
|---|---|
| **Steel** | **0.25 – 0.30** |
| **Concrete** | **0.15 – 0.20** |
| Aluminium | 0.33 |
| **Rubber** | **~0.50** |
| Cork | ~0 |

**Where Poisson's ratio matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Confined concrete** | Lateral expansion is what **spiral or closely-spaced ties** resist — which is why a spirally-reinforced column is so much more ductile |
| **Earth pressure at rest** | **K₀ = μ/(1 − μ)** in elastic terms |
| Thick cylinders, plates | Two-dimensional stress states |
| Strain gauge rosettes | Converting strain to stress |

> The **confinement effect** is the practically important one: concrete under axial load tries to expand sideways, and **preventing that expansion raises both its strength and its ductility dramatically** — the whole basis of confined concrete design.

examTip.trick: **Substitute steel: E = 200, G = 80.** Only option (a) gives μ = 1.25 − 1 = **0.25**, the right answer. The others give 1.5, −0.75 and 0.75 — all physically impossible.
examTip.trap: **0 ≤ μ ≤ 0.5** always. Any option producing a negative value or one above 0.5 can be discarded without algebra, which makes the numerical check decisive rather than merely confirmatory.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only TWO elastic constants are independent** — E = 2G(1+μ) and E = 3K(1−2μ) generate the rest. And **μ = 0.5 means incompressible**: put it in the second relation and K goes to infinity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an indeterminate structure?
questions.solution:
**The two-hinged arch** — indeterminate to the **first degree**.

**Counting the redundancy.** A two-hinged arch has a **pin at each abutment**, giving **two reaction components at each — four in total**. Statics provides only **three** equations, so:

> **D_s = 4 − 3 = 1** — one redundant.

> The redundant is conventionally taken as the **horizontal thrust H**, found from **strain energy** (Castigliano's theorem):

> **H = ∫(M y ds/EI) ÷ ∫(y² ds/EI)**

**The three arch types compared:**

| Arch | Reactions | D_s | H found from |
|---|---|---|---|
| **THREE-hinged** | 4, plus **M = 0 at the crown** | **0 — DETERMINATE** | **Statics: H = M_beam,crown/rise** |
| **TWO-hinged** | 4 | **1** | **Strain energy** |
| **FIXED** | 6 | **3** | Full indeterminate analysis |

> **The third hinge is what makes the three-hinged arch determinate** — it supplies the fourth equation (ΣM = 0 about the crown from one side).

**Why the other options are determinate:**

| Structure | Reactions | D_s |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported beam** | Pin (2) + roller (1) = **3** | **0** |
| **Cantilever** | Fixed end = **3** | **0** |

> Both have exactly three reactions against three equations — **determinate**, which is why they are the first structures taught.

**Why the third hinge is worth its cost:**

> A **three-hinged** arch is **completely unaffected by**:

| Effect | Two-hinged | Three-hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **Temperature change** | H **changes** | **No effect** |
| **Rib shortening** | H changes | **No effect** |
| **Abutment yielding (spread)** | H **falls substantially** | **No effect** |
| Support settlement | Induces stresses | **No stresses** |

> **That immunity — not the easier arithmetic — is the real reason for the third hinge.** A determinate structure develops **no stresses at all** from imposed deformations, because it can simply move to accommodate them.

> Conversely, **an indeterminate structure resists imposed deformation, and resisting it means stress.** A fixed arch on yielding abutments can be severely overstressed by a movement that a three-hinged arch would absorb without notice.

**The trade-off**, since indeterminacy is not simply a defect:

| Indeterminate structures | |
|---|---|
| **Advantage** | **Redundancy** — an alternative load path if one member fails; smaller deflections; smaller moments through continuity |
| **Disadvantage** | Sensitive to settlement, temperature and fabrication errors; harder to analyse |

> **A continuous beam uses less material than a series of simple spans** for exactly this reason — continuity redistributes the moment. The price is sensitivity to support settlement.

**The arch's structural virtue**, common to all three types:

> **M_arch = M_beam − H y** — the horizontal thrust **subtracts** from the beam moment. For the **funicular** shape (a **parabola** under UDL, a **catenary** under self weight) the subtraction is exact and **M = 0 everywhere**, which is why masonry spans so far as an arch and not at all as a beam.

examTip.trick: Count reactions against the three equations of statics. **Two-hinged arch: 4 reactions − 3 = 1 redundant.** The three-hinged arch's extra hinge supplies a fourth equation (M = 0 at the crown), making it determinate.
examTip.trap: "Three-hinged" sounds more complex than "two-hinged", so it looks like the more indeterminate one. It is the **opposite** — the third hinge **removes** the redundancy.
examTip.mnemonic: **A determinate structure develops NO stress from temperature, settlement or abutment spread** — it simply moves. That immunity, not the easier arithmetic, is why the third hinge is worth building.

questions.stem: Bitumen content is determined by which test?
questions.solution:
**The Marshall test** — the standard method of designing a bituminous mix and fixing its **optimum binder content**.

**What the Marshall method does.** Specimens are prepared at a **range of bitumen contents**, compacted with **75 blows per face** for heavy traffic, and tested for **stability and flow**. Five properties are then plotted against binder content:

| Property | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **Marshall STABILITY** | Maximum load the specimen carries — **minimum 9 kN** for heavy traffic |
| **FLOW value** | Deformation at maximum load — **2 to 4 mm** |
| **Air voids (Vv)** | **3 – 5%** |
| **Voids filled with bitumen (VFB)** | 65 – 75% |
| **Unit weight** | Density |

> **The OPTIMUM binder content is the average of the contents giving maximum stability, maximum density and 4% air voids** — then checked against every other criterion.

**Why both too little and too much bitumen fail:**

| Binder content | Failure |
|---|---|
| **Too LITTLE** | **RAVELLING** — the mix lacks cohesion and loses aggregate; water enters and strips the binder |
| **Too MUCH** | **BLEEDING and RUTTING** — the excess binder acts as a lubricant, the mix loses stability and shoves under traffic |

> **The optimum is a genuine optimum, not a maximum.** Adding more binder past the peak makes the pavement worse, which is a point candidates frequently get backwards.

**Why the other tests are wrong:**

| Test | What it actually measures |
|---|---|
| **Penetration** | The **hardness/grade of the BINDER alone** — in tenths of a millimetre |
| **Vee-bee** | The **WORKABILITY of CONCRETE** — not a bitumen test at all |
| **Ductility** | The binder's ability to stretch — **minimum 50 cm** |

> **The Vee-bee test is the odd one out on category** — it belongs to concrete workability (alongside slump and compacting factor), not to bituminous materials. Spotting that eliminates it immediately.

> Penetration and ductility both test the **BINDER ON ITS OWN**; only Marshall tests the **MIX** — and bitumen content is a property of the mix.

**The air voids requirement** deserves emphasis, because it explains the whole design:

> **3–5% air voids is a deliberate target, not a tolerance.** Below 3% the mix has no room for the binder to expand in hot weather and it **bleeds**; above 5% it is **permeable**, admitting water and air, which oxidises the binder and causes **stripping and ravelling**.

**Other mix design methods:** **Hveem** (used in parts of the USA) and **Superpave**, which uses a gyratory compactor and is now the international standard — but **Marshall remains the method specified in IRC and in Nepali practice**.

examTip.trick: **Penetration and ductility test the BINDER alone; Marshall tests the MIX.** Bitumen content is a property of the mix, so only Marshall can determine it.
examTip.trap: **Vee-bee is a CONCRETE workability test** — it does not belong to bituminous materials at all. Spotting the category error removes it instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Too little binder → RAVELLING; too much → BLEEDING and RUTTING.** The optimum is a genuine optimum, not a maximum — and **3–5% air voids** is a target, not a tolerance.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a hollow circular section of outer radius R and inner radius r is:
questions.solution:
**I = (π/4)(R⁴ − r⁴).**

**Reconciling the two forms.** The formula is more often met in terms of **diameters**:

> **I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64**

> Substituting **D = 2R** and **d = 2r**:
> **I = π(16R⁴ − 16r⁴)/64 = π(R⁴ − r⁴)/4** ✓

> **The 64 becomes a 4 because each diameter is twice its radius, and 2⁴ = 16.** That factor of 16 is exactly what converts one form into the other, and it is the whole content of the question.

**Checking by the solid case.** Setting r = 0:

> **I = πR⁴/4** — the standard solid circular value ✓ (equivalently πD⁴/64)

**The radius and diameter forms side by side:**

| Quantity | In terms of D | In terms of R |
|---|---|---|
| **I (second moment)** | **πD⁴/64** | **πR⁴/4** |
| **J (polar)** | **πD⁴/32** | **πR⁴/2** |
| Section modulus Z | πD³/32 | πR³/4 |

> Note that **J = 2I** in every form, which is the **perpendicular axis theorem** (J = I_xx + I_yy) applied to a shape with two equal principal second moments.

**Why hollow sections are efficient** — the substance behind the arithmetic:

> Since **I ∝ R⁴**, material near the centre contributes almost nothing. Removing a core of **half the outer radius** loses only **(1/2)⁴ = 1/16** of the second moment while removing **1/4 of the area**.

> **A very favourable exchange** — and the reason tubes, hollow piers and box sections dominate wherever weight matters.

**And for a column the advantage is greater still:**

> Buckling depends on the **radius of gyration r_g = √(I/A)**. A tube has a **large r_g for its area in EVERY direction**, so it has no weak axis — which is why it is the natural shape for a strut, and why a solid bar of equal area buckles at a fraction of the load.

**A caution on which value to use where:**

| Application | Use |
|---|---|
| **Bending stress σ = My/I** | **I** |
| **Torsional shear τ = Tr/J** | **J** |
| **Buckling P_cr = π²EI/L_e²** | **The MINIMUM I** |
| Deflection | I |

> **For buckling always take the LEAST second moment** — a column buckles about its **weak axis**, and using the strong-axis value is a serious error. For a circular or square section the two are equal, which is part of why they are so efficient as struts.

examTip.trick: The familiar form is **πD⁴/64**. Since **D = 2R** and **2⁴ = 16**, the 64 becomes **4** — giving **πR⁴/4**. That single substitution is the whole question.
examTip.trap: Option (d) keeps the **64** from the diameter form while writing radii. Mixing the two conventions is the commonest error here, and it understates I by a factor of sixteen.
examTip.mnemonic: **J = 2I for a circle** (perpendicular axis theorem). And since **I ∝ R⁴**, hollowing out half the radius costs only **1/16 of I** while shedding **1/4 of the area** — the whole case for tubes.

questions.stem: The maximum density of water occurs at ……… degree Celsius.
questions.solution:
**4 °C** — where water reaches its maximum density of **1000 kg/m³**.

**Why this is anomalous.** Almost every substance becomes **denser as it cools**, right down to freezing. Water does the opposite below 4 °C: it **EXPANDS on cooling from 4 °C to 0 °C**, and expands again on freezing.

> **Ice is about 9% less dense than water**, which is why it floats — and why a frozen pipe bursts.

**The reason is hydrogen bonding:**

> As water cools toward freezing, its molecules arrange into an increasingly **open, ordered hexagonal lattice** held by hydrogen bonds. That lattice occupies **more** space than the disordered liquid. Below 4 °C the ordering effect overtakes the ordinary thermal contraction, and the density falls.

**The consequence that makes life possible:**

> A lake cools from the surface. Water at 4 °C is **densest, so it sinks to the bottom**, while colder water stays on top and freezes there.

> **A lake therefore freezes from the TOP DOWN, and the bottom stays at 4 °C.** Aquatic life survives the winter beneath the ice.

> Had water behaved normally, lakes would freeze **solid from the bottom up** and never fully thaw.

**Engineering consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Frozen pipes BURST** | Water expands ~9% on freezing; the pipe cannot contain it |
| **FROST damage to concrete and masonry** | Water in pores freezes and spalls the surface — the reason for **air entrainment** |
| **Frost heave** | Ice lenses grow in **SILT**, lifting pavements |
| **Reservoir turnover** | Seasonal density stratification and overturn |
| Density stratification | Affects intake design and water quality |

> **AIR ENTRAINMENT** is the practical remedy for freeze–thaw damage: 4–6% of deliberately introduced microscopic air bubbles give the freezing water **somewhere to expand into**, relieving the pressure that would otherwise spall the concrete.

**Other water reference values** worth carrying:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Density at 4 °C** | **1000 kg/m³** |
| **Unit weight** | **9.81 kN/m³** |
| Density at 20 °C | 998 kg/m³ |
| **Specific heat** | **4.18 kJ/kg·K** — unusually high |
| **Latent heat of fusion** | 334 kJ/kg |
| **Surface tension at 20 °C** | **0.073 N/m** |
| Dynamic viscosity at 20 °C | 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s |
| **Bulk modulus** | **2.1 GPa** — nearly incompressible |

> **Water's very high specific heat** is the other anomaly with engineering consequences — it makes water an excellent coolant, and it is why large water bodies moderate the climate around them.

examTip.trick: **4 °C, density 1000 kg/m³** — the anomaly. Water expands on cooling below 4 °C and expands again on freezing, which is why **ice floats** and frozen pipes burst.
examTip.trap: 0 °C is the freezing point, not the density maximum. The two are different temperatures, and offering 0° exploits the assumption that they coincide.
examTip.mnemonic: **A lake freezes TOP DOWN and its bottom stays at 4 °C** — which is how aquatic life survives winter. In concrete the same expansion causes freeze-thaw spalling, cured by **4–6% AIR ENTRAINMENT** giving the ice room to grow.

questions.stem: The right of way (ROW) for a feeder road is:
questions.solution:
**30 m.**

**The Nepal Road Standard right-of-way table:**

| Road class | Right of way |
|---|---|
| **National highway** | **50 m** (25 m each side of the centre line) |
| **FEEDER road** | **30 m** |
| **District road** | **20 m** |
| **Village road** | **15 m** |

> The sequence **50 / 30 / 20 / 15** descends with the road's importance, and it is worth learning as a block — these four numbers are asked repeatedly.

**What the right of way IS**, and why it is so much wider than the road:

> The ROW is the **total width of land legally acquired and reserved** for the road — not the width of the carriageway.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CARRIAGEWAY** | The **travelled way** — where vehicles run |
| **ROADWAY** | Carriageway **plus shoulders** |
| **FORMATION WIDTH** | Roadway plus side drains — the **earthwork width** |
| **RIGHT OF WAY** | **All the land acquired** — formation, slopes, drains, and reserve |

> **The four are nested**, each containing the one before, and they are constantly confused. A national highway's 50 m ROW might carry a 7 m carriageway.

**Why the reserve is provided:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **FUTURE WIDENING** | The decisive reason — acquiring land later, after development, is enormously more expensive |
| Cut and fill **slopes** | A hill road's earthworks can be very wide |
| **Drainage** and services | Side drains, utilities, poles |
| **Sight distance** at curves | Clearing the inside of a bend |
| Safety clearance | Away from the travelled way |

> **Encroachment on the right of way is the single greatest obstacle to later road improvement in Nepal.** Once buildings occupy the reserve, widening requires demolition and compensation — often costing more than the road itself.

> **The reserve is cheap to protect and ruinous to recover**, which is why the ROW is defined in law rather than left to the designer.

**The sight distance point** is worth noting because it is often missed:

> On a horizontal curve, the **set-back distance** required to see round the bend can be considerable — and the obstruction is usually on the **inside** of the curve, within the ROW. Vegetation, embankments and structures there must be cleared and kept clear.

**Related road classification** (Nepal): **National Highways (H)**, **Feeder Roads (F)**, **District Roads (D)** and **Village Roads (V)** — with the **Strategic Road Network (SRN)** comprising the highways and feeder roads, managed by the Department of Roads, and the **Local Road Network** managed by local government.

examTip.trick: Learn the descending block: **National 50, Feeder 30, District 20, Village 15 m.** Four numbers, asked repeatedly and never derivable.
examTip.trap: **Carriageway ⊂ roadway ⊂ formation width ⊂ right of way** — four nested terms, constantly swapped. A 50 m ROW may carry only a 7 m carriageway.
examTip.mnemonic: **The reserve is for FUTURE WIDENING** — cheap to protect, ruinous to recover once built on. Encroachment on the ROW is the biggest single obstacle to road improvement in Nepal.

questions.stem: If one end of a column is kept free and the other end fixed, then the ratio of L_eff to L is:
questions.solution:
**2** — the effective length is **twice** the actual length.

**The effective length table** (theoretical values):

| End conditions | **L_e** | **P_cr** | Relative capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Both ends FIXED** | **0.5 L** | 4π²EI/L² | **4 ×** |
| **One fixed, one pinned** | **0.707 L** | 2.045π²EI/L² | 2 × |
| **Both ends PINNED** | **1.0 L** | π²EI/L² | **1 ×** (reference) |
| **One FIXED, one FREE** | **2.0 L** | **π²EI/(4L²)** | **1/4 ×** |
| One fixed, one fixed-but-sway | 1.0 L | π²EI/L² | 1 × |

> **The whole range spans a factor of SIXTEEN in buckling load** — from 4× down to ¼×. Nothing else in structural design is so sensitive to a detail as small as how the ends are held.

**Why the free end is so damaging.** Consider the buckled shape:

> A **cantilever column** buckles into **half** the shape that a pin-ended column of length 2L would form. Its effective length — the distance between points of contraflexure on the equivalent pin-ended member — is therefore **2L**.

> Since **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²** and L_e is **squared**, doubling L_e **quarters** the capacity.

**This is the case to fear in practice:**

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **A column unbraced during construction** | The floor that would restrain its top is not yet built |
| **Temporary props and shores** | Often free at the top |
| Scaffold standards with a missing tie | The tie **is** the restraint |
| **A cantilever pier or pole** | Free by design |

> **A column free at the top carries a QUARTER of what it would pinned, and a SIXTEENTH of what it would fixed–fixed.** Construction-stage stability failures very often come down to exactly this.

**Codes are more conservative than the theory:**

> **IS 456** and **IS 800** give **higher** effective lengths than the theoretical values — for instance **0.65 L** rather than 0.5 L for fixed–fixed, and **2.0 L or more** for a cantilever — because **a real "fixed" end always rotates a little**.

> **Never use the theoretical value in design.** Assuming a fixity the detail does not deliver is unconservative in the one direction where the penalty is a sudden collapse.

**Slenderness and the limits of Euler:**

> **λ = L_e/r**, with **r** taken about the **MINIMUM** axis — a column buckles the **weak** way.

| Slenderness | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **λ < 12** (concrete) | **SHORT** — fails by **crushing** |
| Moderate | **Inelastic** buckling — **Euler OVERESTIMATES**; use **Rankine** or code curves |
| **λ > ~100** (steel) | Euler's elastic formula applies |

> **Rankine's formula — 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler — bridges both ends** and is the safer general expression, because Euler alone is unsafe for intermediate slenderness where yielding intervenes.

**And the cheapest remedy:** **bracing at midheight halves L and QUADRUPLES the buckling capacity** — almost always cheaper than enlarging the section.

examTip.trick: A cantilever column buckles into **half** the shape of a pin-ended column of length 2L — hence **L_e = 2L**. Since P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², that is a **quarter** of the pinned capacity.
examTip.trap: **Codes use larger values than the theory** (2.0 L or more for a cantilever, 0.65 L rather than 0.5 L for fixed-fixed), because a real fixed end always rotates. The theoretical value is unconservative in design.
examTip.mnemonic: **The free end is the one to fear** — a quarter of pinned capacity, a sixteenth of fixed-fixed. Construction-stage failures very often come down to a column temporarily free at the top.

questions.stem: Culmann's graphical construction is used in:
questions.solution:
**Culmann's wedge theory** — the graphical construction for earth pressure on a retaining wall.

> The source prints the option as "Column wedge theory", which is a typographical slip for **CULMANN's wedge theory**. It is the keyed answer and the correct one.

**What Culmann's method does.** It is a **graphical solution of COULOMB's wedge theory** — a way of finding the **critical failure wedge** and the earth pressure it exerts, by construction rather than by trial calculation.

> A series of trial wedges is drawn, the weight of each is set out to scale along a reference line, and the **pressure locus** through the resulting points is drawn. **The maximum ordinate of that locus gives the active earth pressure**, and the wedge producing it is the critical one.

**Why a graphical method was worth having:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Handles ANY backfill surface** | Irregular, sloping, stepped — no formula required |
| **Handles surcharge loads**, including **line and point loads** | Simply added to the wedge weight |
| **Handles a broken or battered wall face** | — |
| Handles **wall friction** naturally | Coulomb's assumption |

> **That generality is the point.** Rankine's and Coulomb's closed-form expressions require a **plane backfill surface and simple geometry**; Culmann's construction works for cases no formula covers.

**COULOMB versus RANKINE** — the distinction the question sits on:

| | **RANKINE** | **COULOMB** |
|---|---|---|
| Based on | **Plastic equilibrium of the SOIL MASS** | **Equilibrium of a rigid WEDGE** |
| **Wall friction δ** | **NEGLECTED** (assumed zero) | **INCLUDED** |
| Wall face | Assumed **smooth, vertical** | Any inclination |
| Backfill surface | Plane | Any (with a graphical method) |
| Result | **More conservative** for active pressure | Less conservative |

> **Rankine ignores wall friction, so it OVERESTIMATES the active pressure** — which is safe, and why it remains the everyday design method despite being less realistic.

> For **PASSIVE** pressure the position reverses and is dangerous: **Coulomb's theory OVERESTIMATES passive resistance badly at high friction angles**, because the real failure surface is curved rather than plane. Passive resistance is where the assumption matters most, and it is where designers are warned to use curved-surface solutions or a reduced value.

**The Rankine coefficients**, for reference:

> **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2)** and **K_p = 1/K_a**

> For **φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3** — a **ninefold** ratio between the two, which is why a small wall movement toward the fill mobilises so much resistance.

**And the movement required**, which explains why the active case is the design case:

| State | Wall movement needed |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **Very small — about 0.001 H** |
| **PASSIVE** | **Large — 0.02 to 0.05 H** |

> **The active state is reached almost immediately**, so it is what a wall actually experiences. **Full passive resistance needs movement so large that the structure may be unserviceable before it develops** — which is why passive resistance is usually taken at a reduced value, or ignored entirely.

examTip.trick: Culmann's construction is a **graphical solution of COULOMB's wedge theory**. Its value is generality — it handles **irregular backfill, surcharges and battered walls** that no closed-form expression covers.
examTip.trap: **Rankine NEGLECTS wall friction; Coulomb INCLUDES it.** Rankine therefore overestimates active pressure (safe), but Coulomb badly **overestimates PASSIVE** resistance at high φ, because the real failure surface curves.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active needs only 0.001H of movement; passive needs 0.02–0.05H.** So the active state always develops, while full passive resistance may never be reached — which is why it is discounted or ignored.

questions.stem: Capital budgeting is:
questions.solution:
**Irreversible** — or very nearly so.

**What capital budgeting is.** The process of evaluating and selecting **long-term investments** — new plant, a new facility, a major project — whose returns accrue over many years.

**Why it is irreversible:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Large sums are committed** | Often the largest single commitment an organisation makes |
| **Assets are SPECIALISED** | A purpose-built plant has little value to anyone else |
| **Long time horizon** | The commitment binds the organisation for decades |
| **Sunk costs** | Money spent cannot be recovered by abandoning the project |
| Strategic direction is set | The decision shapes what the organisation can do next |

> **Selling a wrong investment recovers only a fraction of its cost**, because specialised assets have a thin second-hand market. That asymmetry — easy to enter, expensive to exit — is what makes the decision irreversible in practice even when it is reversible in principle.

**And the consequence:**

> **Because it cannot be undone, capital budgeting must be got right BEFORE committing.** That is why so much analysis is justified at the appraisal stage, where the spending is trivial and the influence is total.

> It is the same principle as the project life cycle: **the phase that spends the least decides the most.**

**The appraisal techniques:**

| Method | Basis | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **NPV — Net Present Value** | **Discounted** | **The theoretically correct method.** Accept if **NPV ≥ 0** |
| **IRR — Internal Rate of Return** | Discounted | The rate at which **NPV = 0**. Accept if **IRR > MARR** |
| **B/C ratio** | Discounted | Accept if **≥ 1**. Standard for public projects |
| **Payback period** | **NOT discounted** | Simple; **ignores everything after payback** |
| **ARR / accounting rate of return** | Not discounted | Uses accounting profit, not cash flow |

> **NPV is the correct method** because it measures the **absolute value added** in today's money, and because it can be added across projects.

**IRR's two well-known failures:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Multiple IRRs** | If the cash flow **changes sign more than once** (a project with a large end-of-life cost, like a mine closure or a decommissioning), several rates give NPV = 0 |
| **Mutually exclusive projects** | IRR can **rank them wrongly** — it favours a high percentage return on a small sum over a lower return on a large one |

> **When NPV and IRR disagree on mutually exclusive projects, NPV is right.** A 50% return on Rs 1 lakh adds less value than a 20% return on Rs 1 crore.

**Payback's limitation** is worth stating plainly:

> It answers **"how soon do I get my money back?"** — a **liquidity** question, not a profitability one. **It ignores everything that happens after the payback point**, so it systematically penalises long-lived infrastructure, which is exactly the kind of project it is often applied to.

> It survives because it is simple and because it does measure something real: **exposure to risk over time**.

**And for public projects:** the **discount rate itself** is the most consequential and most arguable assumption. A high rate makes long-lived infrastructure look poor, because benefits fifty years out are discounted almost to nothing.

examTip.trick: The reason is **asymmetry**: entering is easy, exiting recovers only a fraction, because specialised assets have no market. That is what makes the decision irreversible in practice.
examTip.trap: **When NPV and IRR disagree on mutually exclusive projects, NPV is right.** IRR favours a high percentage on a small sum over a lower return on a large one — and it can produce **multiple values** when cash flows change sign twice.
examTip.mnemonic: **Payback answers a LIQUIDITY question, not a profitability one** — it ignores everything after the payback point, which systematically penalises long-lived infrastructure.

questions.stem: The permissible pH value for a public water supply ranges between:
questions.solution:
**6.5 to 8.5.**

**Why the range is set where it is — both ends matter:**

| Below 6.5 (acidic) | Above 8.5 (alkaline) |
|---|---|
| **CORRODES pipes** — dissolves iron, **lead and copper** into the supply | **Reduces disinfection efficiency** |
| Metallic taste | Bitter or soapy taste |
| Damages fittings and fixtures | **Scale formation** in pipes and boilers |
| **Health risk from dissolved metals** | Precipitation of hardness |

> **Corrosion at low pH is a genuine health issue, not merely a maintenance one** — acidic water leaches lead from old pipework and solder, and lead has no safe level of exposure.

**The disinfection consequence at high pH:**

> Chlorine in water exists as **HOCl** and **OCl⁻**, in a balance governed by pH:

> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

| Species | Disinfecting power |
|---|---|
| **HOCl** | **Strong — about 80× more effective** |
| **OCl⁻** | Much weaker |

> **Raising the pH shifts the balance toward the weak OCl⁻**, so far more chlorine is needed for the same kill. Hence the operating rule: **chlorinate below pH 7.5 where possible.**

> Note the tension this creates: **corrosion control wants a slightly HIGH pH; disinfection wants a slightly LOW one.** Real operation settles near neutral, around **7.0 to 7.5**, which satisfies both.

**The LANGELIER SATURATION INDEX** is how the corrosion side is managed quantitatively:

| LSI | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negative** | **CORROSIVE** — water dissolves calcium carbonate |
| **Zero** | Balanced |
| **Positive** | **SCALE-FORMING** — deposits calcium carbonate |

> A **slightly positive LSI** is deliberately targeted in distribution, because a **thin CaCO₃ film lines the pipe and protects it** from corrosion. Too positive and the pipe scales up and loses capacity.

**Key Nepali drinking water standard values:**

| Parameter | Limit |
|---|---|
| **pH** | **6.5 – 8.5** |
| **Turbidity** | **5 NTU** |
| Total hardness | 500 mg/l as CaCO₃ |
| Iron | 0.3 mg/l |
| Chloride | 250 mg/l |
| **Nitrate** | **50 mg/l** |
| **Fluoride** | **0.5 – 1.5 mg/l** |
| **Arsenic** | **0.05 mg/l** (WHO 0.01) |
| **E. coli** | **0 per 100 ml** |
| Residual chlorine | 0.1 – 0.2 mg/l |

> **pH and fluoride are the two parameters with a RANGE rather than a maximum** — for both, too little is as much a defect as too much.

**And a caution about what pH measures:**

> **pH is a measure of intensity, not capacity.** Two waters at the same pH can have completely different **ALKALINITY** — the capacity to neutralise acid. A water with low alkalinity has little buffering, so its pH swings sharply with a small chemical addition, which makes treatment unstable and corrosion hard to control.

examTip.trick: The range straddles neutral (7) because **both ends cause problems**: acidic water **corrodes pipes and leaches lead**; alkaline water **weakens disinfection and forms scale**.
examTip.trap: Corrosion control wants a **slightly high** pH while disinfection wants a **slightly low** one. Real operation settles near **7.0–7.5**, satisfying both — the two objectives genuinely pull opposite ways.
examTip.mnemonic: **pH and FLUORIDE are the two parameters with a RANGE, not a maximum** — too little is a defect too. And pH measures **intensity, not capacity**: low **alkalinity** means no buffering and wild pH swings.

questions.stem: The minimum size of a sewer is:
questions.solution:
**150 mm (15 cm).**

> Available sizes then run **15, 20, 30, 35, 40 cm** and upward to about **1.6 m** in Nepali practice.

**Why there is a minimum at all**, and why it is so much larger than the flow requires:

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **BLOCKAGE by solids** | Sewage carries rags, grit, paper and objects that never should have entered. A small pipe blocks |
| **Cleaning and rodding access** | A smaller pipe cannot be cleared |
| Root intrusion | Roots enter at joints and block small pipes readily |
| Grease accumulation | Narrows the bore over time |

> **The minimum is set by what a sewer must SURVIVE, not by the flow it must carry.** A 150 mm sewer running at its self-cleansing velocity carries far more than a small community produces — but a smaller pipe would block.

**The two velocity limits** that govern the gradient:

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum (SELF-CLEANSING)** | **0.6 – 0.75 m/s AT MINIMUM FLOW** | Below it, **grit and solids deposit** and the sewer silts up |
| **Maximum** | **3.0 m/s** | **Erosion** of the invert by grit |

> **The self-cleansing requirement is checked at MINIMUM flow, and that is what makes sewer design harder than water main design.**

> A new development's early flows are a small fraction of the ultimate design flow. The gradient must be steep enough to scour the pipe **on day one**, when only a few houses are connected — while not exceeding 3 m/s at full development.

> **Satisfying both ends of that range simultaneously is the real design problem**, and it is why sewers in flat terrain need pumping stations rather than merely gentler gradients.

**Why sewers are designed to run PART FULL:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | Sewer gases must escape; a full sewer cannot ventilate |
| Reserve capacity | For peak and infiltration |
| **Gravity (free surface) flow** maintained | Pressurising a gravity sewer surcharges the manholes |
| **Corrosion control** | H₂S in a sealed sewer becomes sulphuric acid on the crown |

**Design practice (CPHEEO):** small sewers **half full**, medium **two-thirds**, large **three-quarters** at peak flow.

**CROWN CORROSION** is the failure the ventilation guards against, and it is worth understanding:

> Septic sewage releases **H₂S**. Bacteria on the **moist crown** oxidise it to **SULPHURIC ACID**, which destroys concrete sewers from the top down — often within a few decades.

> The defences are **ventilation**, **maintaining self-cleansing velocity** (so sewage does not go septic), and where necessary a **protective lining**.

**Design flow for a foul sewer:**

> **Peak dry weather flow (about 3 × average) plus INFILTRATION**

> Sewage flow is normally taken as **80% of the water supply**, the remainder being consumed, evaporated or used for irrigation.

> **Infiltration through joints and defects is not a minor allowance** — in an old or poorly-built system it can exceed the sewage flow itself, overloading the treatment works with clean groundwater.

examTip.trick: The minimum is set by **what a sewer must survive — blockage and cleaning access — not by the flow it carries.** 150 mm is far larger than a small community's flow needs.
examTip.trap: **Self-cleansing velocity (0.6–0.75 m/s) is checked at MINIMUM flow, not design flow.** A new scheme's early flows are tiny, and the gradient must still scour the pipe on day one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Part full for VENTILATION** — a sealed sewer breeds H₂S, which bacteria turn into **sulphuric acid on the crown** and destroy the pipe from the top down. And infiltration can exceed the sewage flow itself.

questions.stem: For 1 m³ volume of 1:1.5:3 PCC, how many bags of cement are required?
questions.solution:
**About 8 bags.**

**Working.**

> **Mix ratio 1 : 1.5 : 3**, so the **sum of the ratio = 1 + 1.5 + 3 = 5.5**
>
> **Wet volume = 1 m³**
> **Dry volume = 1 × 1.54 = 1.54 m³** — wet volume increased by **54%**
>
> **Cement volume = (1/5.5) × 1.54 = 0.28 m³**
> **Cement bags = 0.28 × 28.8 bags/m³ ≈ 8 bags** ✓

**The two constants that carry this calculation:**

| Constant | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Bulking factor (dry/wet)** | **1.54** (sometimes 1.52–1.57) | The **dry materials contain VOIDS** which disappear when mixed and compacted |
| **Bags per cubic metre** | **28.8** | A bag is **50 kg**, and cement's bulk density is **1440 kg/m³**: 1440/50 = 28.8 |

> **The 1.54 factor is the step candidates most often omit**, and omitting it understates the cement by a third. Dry sand and aggregate are full of air; once mixed with cement paste and compacted, that air is displaced.

> **The 28.8 is not arbitrary either** — it is simply **1440 ÷ 50**. Knowing where it comes from means never mis-remembering it.

**Checking by weight**, which is the more reliable route:

> **Cement = 0.28 m³ × 1440 kg/m³ = 403 kg = 8.06 bags** ✓

**The nominal mixes (IS 456) and their grades:**

| Mix | Grade | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **1 : 3 : 6** | **M10** | Lean concrete, levelling course |
| **1 : 2 : 4** | **M15** | Plain concrete, foundations |
| **1 : 1.5 : 3** | **M20** | **The commonest structural nominal mix** |
| **1 : 1 : 2** | **M25** | — |
| Above M25 | — | **DESIGN mix only** |

> **IS 456 permits nominal mixes only up to M20**, and requires **design mixes** above it. The reason is that a nominal mix is a rule of thumb which cannot account for the actual aggregate grading, shape, moisture and cement strength — and above M20 those variables matter too much to guess.

**The complete quantity set for this mix:**

| Material | Quantity per m³ |
|---|---|
| **Cement** | **0.28 m³ ≈ 8 bags ≈ 403 kg** |
| **Sand** | 1.5/5.5 × 1.54 = **0.42 m³** |
| **Coarse aggregate** | 3/5.5 × 1.54 = **0.84 m³** |
| **Water** (w/c = 0.5) | ~200 litres |

**A caution about volume batching on site:**

> **BULKING OF SAND** is the trap. **Damp sand occupies up to 20–30% more volume than dry sand**, because surface moisture films push the grains apart.

> **Batching damp sand by volume therefore delivers substantially LESS sand than intended**, making the mix richer in cement and harsher than designed. The remedy is either a **bulking test and correction**, or — far better — **batching by WEIGHT**, which is immune to the effect.

> Note the paradox worth remembering: **bulking peaks at about 4–6% moisture and vanishes when the sand is fully saturated** — so completely wet sand and bone-dry sand occupy nearly the same volume, and only damp sand misleads.

examTip.trick: Two constants do the work: **dry volume = 1.54 × wet**, and **28.8 bags per m³** (which is just 1440 kg/m³ ÷ 50 kg). Then cement = (1/5.5) × 1.54 × 28.8 ≈ **8 bags**.
examTip.trap: **Omitting the 1.54 factor** is the standard error — it understates the cement by a third. Dry aggregates are full of voids that disappear on mixing and compaction.
examTip.mnemonic: **BULKING OF SAND is the site trap**: damp sand occupies 20–30% more volume, so volume-batching delivers **less** sand than intended. It peaks at 4–6% moisture and **vanishes when fully saturated** — only damp sand misleads.

questions.stem: A canal fall is provided if:
options: Ground slope exceeds designed bed slope
Design bed slope exceeds ground slope
Ground slope is same as designed bed slope
questions.solution:
**When the natural ground slope exceeds the canal's designed bed slope.**

**Why.** A canal's **bed slope is fixed by hydraulics** — it must be flat enough to keep the velocity within non-scouring limits, and steep enough to avoid silting. Typically it is a few centimetres per kilometre.

> The **natural ground**, by contrast, falls at whatever rate the terrain dictates — often much more steeply.

> If the ground falls **faster** than the canal bed, the canal would emerge **higher and higher above the ground**, requiring an ever-deeper embankment.

> **A FALL takes the canal bed down a step**, bringing it back to a workable depth below ground, and **dissipates the surplus energy** in the process.

**What a fall achieves:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lower the bed** to match the ground | The primary purpose |
| **Dissipate surplus energy** safely | So the drop does not scour the downstream bed |
| Reduce **earthwork** | Avoids excessive embankment |
| Often combined with a **regulator, bridge or metering flume** | A fall is a natural place to put other works |

> **Combining a fall with a regulator or a metering device is standard practice** — the structure is being built anyway, and the drop provides a convenient control section for measuring discharge.

**Types of canal fall:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Ogee fall** | Smooth transition; minimal energy dissipation |
| **Vertical drop (Sarda) fall** | Raised crest, vertical impact; a **cistern** dissipates the energy |
| **Glacis fall** | Sloping glacis with a **hydraulic jump** for dissipation |
| **Baffle fall** | Baffle blocks force the jump |
| Well type / cylinder fall | For a large drop in a small channel |

> **Sarda type falls** (from the Sarda canal in Uttar Pradesh) use a **rectangular crest for discharges up to 14 cumecs**, and a **trapezoidal** section above that.

**The distinction from other canal structures**, which is what the question really tests:

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **FALL** | Take the **BED** down where the **ground falls faster than the canal** |
| **CROSS REGULATOR** | **Raise the water level** so an offtake can draw |
| **HEAD REGULATOR** | Control flow **into the distributary** |
| **ESCAPE** | Discharge **surplus water OUT** of the canal |
| **Cross-drainage works** | Carry the canal past a natural drain |

**Choosing where to put falls** is an economic optimisation:

> **Fewer, larger falls** cost less in structures but more in earthwork; **more, smaller falls** the reverse. The optimum balances the cost of the fall structures against the cost of the earthwork saved — and it is settled on the **longitudinal section**, where the ground line and the designed bed line are plotted together.

> **The falls go wherever those two lines diverge too far.** That is the whole design method, and it is a good example of a decision that is obvious once the right drawing is made.

examTip.trick: The canal's bed slope is **fixed by hydraulics**; the ground's is fixed by terrain. Where the **ground falls faster**, the canal would ride up out of the ground — so a fall steps the bed back down.
examTip.trap: Keep the canal structures apart: a **FALL lowers the bed**; a **cross regulator raises the water level**; an **escape discharges surplus out**. All three appear together as distractors.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plot the ground line and the designed bed line on the longitudinal section — falls go where they diverge.** Fewer large falls cost less in structures, more small ones less in earthwork; the optimum balances the two.

questions.stem: The condition for supercritical flow is:
questions.solution:
**Fr > 1.**

**The three flow states:**

| Froude number | State | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Fr < 1** | **SUBCRITICAL (tranquil, streaming)** | **Deep and slow**; control from **DOWNSTREAM** |
| **Fr = 1** | **CRITICAL** | Minimum specific energy |
| **Fr > 1** | **SUPERCRITICAL (rapid, shooting)** | **Shallow and fast**; control from **UPSTREAM** |

> **Fr = V/√(gD)** where D is the hydraulic depth (A/T), reducing to **V/√(gy)** for a rectangular channel.

**What the Froude number physically means** — and this is the idea worth carrying:

> **√(gy) is the speed of a small surface wave** in shallow water. So the Froude number is:

> **Fr = flow velocity ÷ wave speed**

| Fr | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **< 1** | Waves **CAN travel upstream** — so downstream conditions influence the flow upstream. **Control is DOWNSTREAM** |
| **> 1** | The flow **outruns its own waves** — nothing can propagate upstream. **Control is UPSTREAM** |

> **That is why a disturbance in a fast, shallow channel is swept away without affecting anything above it**, while in a slow deep channel a downstream obstruction backs water up for a long distance.

> It is the **exact hydraulic analogue of subsonic and supersonic flow**, with the wave speed playing the role of the speed of sound — and the **hydraulic jump is the analogue of a shock wave**.

**The practical consequence for computation:**

> A **backwater profile** in subcritical flow is computed **starting at the downstream control and working UPSTREAM**; a **supercritical** profile is computed **from the upstream control DOWNSTREAM**.

> **Getting that direction wrong makes the computation diverge**, and it is the commonest error in gradually varied flow analysis.

**Critical flow relations** (rectangular channel):

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Critical depth** | **y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}** |
| **Minimum specific energy** | **E_min = 1.5 y_c** |
| **Critical velocity** | **V_c = √(g y_c)** |
| At critical | **y_c = (2/3)E_min** |

> **E_min = 1.5 y_c** is the single most useful critical-flow result, and it is what makes a **broad-crested weir or a flume** into a **discharge measuring device**: force the flow through critical, measure the upstream head, and the discharge follows uniquely.

**Where each state occurs:**

| State | Typical location |
|---|---|
| **Subcritical** | Most **natural rivers and canals** |
| **Critical** | At a **free overfall**, over a **broad-crested weir**, at a channel constriction |
| **Supercritical** | **Steep chutes and spillways**, below a sluice gate |

> The transition **supercritical → subcritical** is a **HYDRAULIC JUMP** — abrupt, turbulent, and dissipating a great deal of energy. The reverse transition, **subcritical → supercritical**, is **smooth and gradual**, and needs no jump.

> **The asymmetry is thermodynamic**: a jump destroys energy, which is possible; the reverse would create it, which is not.

**A caution about "critical":**

> Flow **at or very near critical is UNSTABLE** — small changes in energy produce large changes in depth, and the surface becomes wavy and unpredictable. **Channels are therefore deliberately designed AWAY from critical**, which is why a long reach at Fr ≈ 1 is avoided in design.

examTip.trick: **√(gy) is the speed of a surface wave**, so **Fr = flow speed ÷ wave speed**. Supercritical flow **outruns its own waves** — nothing can travel upstream, so the control is upstream.
examTip.trap: **Compute subcritical profiles from DOWNSTREAM upward, supercritical from UPSTREAM downward.** Getting the direction wrong makes gradually-varied-flow computation diverge — the commonest error in the topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **E_min = 1.5 y_c** — which is what turns a broad-crested weir or flume into a discharge meter. And flow **near critical is UNSTABLE**, so channels are designed deliberately away from Fr = 1.

questions.stem: A reversible turbine is used in which plant?
questions.solution:
**A pumped storage plant.**

**What a reversible machine does.** A **pump-turbine** runs in **both directions**:

| Mode | Operation |
|---|---|
| **GENERATING** | Water falls from the upper reservoir; the machine acts as a **turbine** driving a generator |
| **PUMPING** | The machine acts as a **pump**, driven as a motor, lifting water back to the upper reservoir |

> The **same machine, the same shaft, the same waterway** — only the direction of rotation changes. That is what makes pumped storage economically viable: one set of plant does both jobs.

**Why pumped storage exists.** It is **NOT a net energy producer** — it consumes more energy pumping than it returns generating, at a **round-trip efficiency of about 70–80%**.

> **It is a STORAGE device, and its value is in TIME-SHIFTING energy**, not creating it.

| When | Action |
|---|---|
| **Off-peak** (night, or a solar/wind surplus) | **PUMP** using cheap surplus electricity |
| **Peak demand** | **GENERATE**, selling into a high-price period |

> It profits from the **price difference** between off-peak and peak power — buying cheap and selling dear. Losing 20–30% in the round trip is worth it when the price ratio is larger than that.

**Why it matters increasingly:**

| Service | Note |
|---|---|
| **Grid-scale energy storage** | Still **by far the largest form of storage in the world** — more than all batteries combined |
| **Balancing intermittent renewables** | Absorbs a midday solar surplus, releases it in the evening peak |
| **Very fast response** | Seconds to change output — invaluable for frequency control |
| **Spinning reserve** | Available almost instantly |
| Black start capability | Can restart a collapsed grid |

> **Its speed of response is as valuable as its energy storage.** A pumped storage unit can go from standstill to full output in a couple of minutes, and can swing between pumping and generating — a range of twice its rating.

**For Nepal specifically:**

> The country's structural problem is **seasonal and daily mismatch**: run-of-river plants generate most in the monsoon and least in the dry season, and generate steadily through the day while demand peaks in the evening.

> **Pumped storage addresses the DAILY mismatch directly**, and the mountainous terrain provides exactly what it needs — **large head differences over short horizontal distances**, which is what makes a scheme cheap to build.

**Why the other options do not use reversible machines:**

| Plant | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir (storage) plant** | Stores **water**, but only generates — it does not pump back |
| **Run-of-river** | Generates from natural flow; no storage at all |
| **Tidal** | Some tidal schemes do generate on both ebb and flood, but they use **bi-directional turbines rather than pump-turbines**, and they do not pump |

> The **tidal** option is the closest near-miss, because two-way generation sounds like reversibility. But generating in both flow directions is not the same as **reversing between pumping and generating**.

**The machine itself:** usually a **Francis-type pump-turbine**, since the Francis geometry works acceptably in both directions. A Pelton cannot pump at all, and Kaplan pump-turbines exist but are less common.

examTip.trick: Pumped storage is a **STORAGE device, not a generator** — round-trip efficiency 70–80%, so it consumes more than it returns. Its value is **time-shifting** energy from off-peak to peak.
examTip.trap: **Tidal** is the near-miss: some tidal plants generate on both ebb and flood, but that is **bi-directional generation**, not reversing between pumping and generating.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pump at night, generate at the evening peak.** It is still the world's largest form of grid storage — more than all batteries combined — and Nepal's terrain offers exactly what it needs: big head over short distance.

questions.stem: The Vicat apparatus is used in:
questions.solution:
**The consistency test** of cement — and, with different attachments, the setting time tests.

**What the Vicat apparatus measures:**

| Attachment | Test | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| **PLUNGER (10 mm)** | **Standard (normal) consistency** | Penetrates to **5–7 mm from the bottom** |
| **Needle (1 mm²)** | **Initial setting time** | Needle **fails to penetrate** to within 5–7 mm of the bottom |
| **Needle with annular attachment** | **Final setting time** | The **annulus leaves no impression** on the surface |

> **Standard consistency** is the water content — usually **26–33% by weight of cement** — at which the plunger penetrates to the specified depth.

**Why standard consistency matters at all:**

> It is not a property of interest in itself. It is the **reference water content at which the setting time and soundness tests are performed**, so that results from different cements are comparable.

> **Without a standard consistency, setting times would be meaningless** — a wetter paste always sets more slowly, so the water content must be fixed before the times can be compared.

**The setting time limits (IS 269):**

| Limit | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Initial setting time** | **NOT LESS THAN 30 minutes** |
| **Final setting time** | **NOT MORE THAN 600 minutes (10 hours)** |

> **The two limits run in OPPOSITE directions** — a minimum on the first, a maximum on the second. That asymmetry is the most-tested point in the topic: you need **time to place** (hence a minimum initial set) and you need to **get on with the work** (hence a maximum final set).

**The apparatus for each cement test** — the discrimination this question requires:

| Test | Apparatus |
|---|---|
| **Consistency and setting time** | **VICAT** |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **LE CHATELIER** apparatus (or the autoclave) |
| **Fineness** | **Blaine air permeability** apparatus, or the **90 μm sieve** |
| **Compressive strength** | **Compression testing machine** on 70.6 mm mortar cubes |

> **VICAT and LE CHATELIER are the pair that gets swapped**, and both appear as options here. **Vicat for setting; Le Chatelier for soundness.**

**SOUNDNESS deserves emphasis because it is the most dangerous defect:**

> Unsoundness is caused by **excess free lime or magnesia**, which hydrate **very slowly** and **expand** as they do.

> **The expansion appears MONTHS after construction**, cracking concrete that was perfectly sound when placed — and by then nothing can be done. The limits are **10 mm** (Le Chatelier) and **0.8%** (autoclave).

**The other cement requirements:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Fineness (Blaine)** | **≥ 225 m²/kg** |
| **Compressive strength (OPC 33)** | **16 / 22 / 33 MPa at 3 / 7 / 28 days** |
| Specific gravity | 3.15 |

> **Finer cement hydrates faster** — more surface area exposed to water — giving higher **early** strength, but also more **heat of hydration** and greater **shrinkage**. It is a trade-off, not a straightforward improvement.

**And the compound that controls setting:**

> **C₃A hydrates almost instantly and would cause a FLASH SET.** **Gypsum (2–3%) is interground with the clinker purely to retard it** — that is the entire reason gypsum is present in cement.

examTip.trap: **VICAT and LE CHATELIER** are the pair that gets swapped, and both are offered here. **Vicat = consistency and SETTING; Le Chatelier = SOUNDNESS.**
examTip.trick: Standard consistency exists only so that setting time and soundness can be measured on a **comparable paste** — a wetter mix always sets slower, so the water must be fixed first.
examTip.mnemonic: **Initial set has a MINIMUM (30 min), final set a MAXIMUM (600 min)** — opposite directions. And **unsoundness is the worst defect** because free lime expands **months later**, cracking concrete that was fine when placed.

questions.stem: The strength of timber is maximum in the direction:
questions.solution:
**Parallel to the grain.**

**Why.** Timber is a **natural fibre composite**. Its **cellulose fibres run along the grain**, bound by lignin. Loading along the fibres engages their full tensile and compressive strength; loading across them merely pulls apart the much weaker bond between fibres.

> **Timber is strongly ANISOTROPIC** — its properties depend entirely on direction, and this is the single most important fact about it as a structural material.

**The strength ratios:**

| Loading | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| **Compression PARALLEL to grain** | **Strong — the reference** |
| **Tension parallel to grain** | **Strongest of all** |
| **Compression PERPENDICULAR** | About **1/4 to 1/5** of parallel |
| **Tension perpendicular** | **Very weak — about 1/20** |
| **SHEAR parallel to grain** | Weak — about **1/10** |

> **Tension perpendicular to the grain is timber's greatest weakness**, and good detailing avoids it entirely. The fibres simply separate — the material splits.

**The two practical consequences that follow:**

> **1. BEARING perpendicular to the grain often governs a connection.** A beam resting on a wall plate crushes into it long before the beam itself fails in bending. Bearing area, not beam size, is the constraint.

> **2. Notches and holes are far more damaging in timber than in steel**, because they create local tension across the grain and start a split that runs along the fibres. **A notch on the tension face of a timber beam is particularly dangerous** — codes restrict notch depth and position tightly.

**Factors affecting timber strength:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **MOISTURE CONTENT** | The dominant factor — strength rises sharply as timber dries **down to the fibre saturation point (~30%)**, then changes little |
| **DEFECTS** — knots, shakes, splits | Knots **deflect the grain** around them, creating local cross-grain stress |
| **Duration of load** | Timber under **sustained** load carries **less** than under short-term load — the opposite of most materials' fatigue behaviour |
| Density | Denser species are stronger |
| Temperature | Minor within normal ranges |

> **The FIBRE SATURATION POINT (~30% moisture)** is the key threshold: **above it, water sits free in the cell cavities and affects nothing**; **below it, water leaves the cell WALLS**, which shrink and strengthen.

> So **seasoning below 30% both shrinks and strengthens the timber** — and above 30% neither happens. That single threshold explains both the shrinkage and the strength behaviour.

**SEASONING** is therefore essential, not optional:

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Air seasoning** | Slow (months to years), cheap, low risk |
| **KILN seasoning** | Fast (days), controlled, more expensive; **risk of case-hardening if hurried** |

> **Unseasoned timber shrinks in place**, opening joints, loosening fasteners and distorting the structure. Shrinkage is also **anisotropic** — roughly **tangential 2× radial, and almost nil along the grain** — which is why boards **cup** away from the heart as they dry.

**Preservation** against decay and insects: decay needs **moisture above about 20%** and oxygen, so **keeping timber DRY is the primary defence**. Where that cannot be assured, preservatives (creosote, CCA, boron) are applied — most effectively by **pressure impregnation**.
