> **Heartwood is naturally more durable than sapwood** but also far harder to impregnate — so treated sapwood can outlast untreated heartwood.

examTip.trick: Timber is a **fibre composite** — load along the fibres and you engage their full strength; load across and you only separate them. That one picture gives every strength ratio.
examTip.trap: **Tension PERPENDICULAR to grain is the great weakness (~1/20)**, which is why **notches and holes** are far more damaging in timber than in steel — they start a split that runs along the fibres.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fibre saturation point ≈ 30%**: above it water is free in the cavities and nothing happens; below it water leaves the cell **walls**, and the timber both **shrinks and strengthens**. That threshold explains both behaviours at once.

questions.stem: The ordinate of a unit hydrograph is obtained by dividing the ordinate of the DRH by:
questions.solution:
**The effective runoff depth** (the depth of direct runoff, in cm or mm).

**What a unit hydrograph is:**

> The **direct runoff hydrograph resulting from ONE UNIT DEPTH of effective rainfall** (1 cm in Indian practice, 1 mm in SI) falling **uniformly over the catchment** in a **specified duration**.

**Deriving it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Take the observed **flood hydrograph** |
| **2** | **Separate the BASE FLOW** to leave the **direct runoff hydrograph (DRH)** |
| **3** | Compute the **volume** under the DRH; divide by catchment **area** to get the **effective runoff DEPTH** |
| **4** | **Divide every DRH ordinate by that depth** → the unit hydrograph |

> **Base flow separation comes FIRST (step 2), and division by the depth LAST (step 4).** Option (c) names the right quantity for the wrong step — base flow is **subtracted**, never divided by.

**And option (a) is used in step 3, not step 4:**

> The **catchment area** converts a volume into a depth. It is part of computing the depth, not the divisor itself.

> **Both wrong options name real quantities used at real steps of the procedure** — which is what makes this a genuine test of whether the method is understood rather than half-remembered.

**The three assumptions of unit hydrograph theory:**

| Assumption | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **TIME INVARIANCE** | The same rainfall always produces the same hydrograph shape — the catchment does not change |
| **LINEARITY (proportionality)** | **2 cm of rain gives ordinates 2× those of 1 cm**, with the **same time base** |
| **SUPERPOSITION** | Hydrographs from successive rainfall blocks simply **add**, offset in time |

> **Linearity is the assumption doing all the work**, and it is the one that is only approximately true. Real catchments respond **non-linearly** — a very large storm produces a proportionally **faster and peakier** response than a small one, because overland flow depths and velocities increase.

> **So a unit hydrograph derived from moderate storms UNDERESTIMATES the peak of an extreme event** — which matters greatly, since extreme events are exactly what design is concerned with.

**Key properties:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Duration** | A unit hydrograph is always **for a stated duration** — a 6-hour UH differs from a 12-hour UH |
| **Area under it** | Always equals **1 unit depth × catchment area** |
| **Time base** | **Same for all storms of that duration**, whatever the intensity |
| **Shorter duration** | Gives a **higher, sharper peak** |

> **Quoting a unit hydrograph without its duration is meaningless**, and it is a common slip.

**Changing the duration:**

| Method | Use |
|---|---|
| **S-CURVE** | Convert to **any** duration — the general method |
| **Superposition** | Convert to an **integer multiple** of the original duration |

**For an ungauged catchment** — the common Nepali case — a **SYNTHETIC unit hydrograph** (Snyder's, SCS dimensionless) is derived from catchment characteristics: area, length, slope, and the length to the centroid.

**And the practical limits:**

| Limit | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Catchment area** | Best for **a few hundred to a few thousand km²**. Too small and the storm duration assumption fails; too large and rainfall is never uniform |
| Uniform rainfall | The larger the catchment, the less true |
| Constant catchment condition | Urbanisation, deforestation and reservoirs all invalidate an old UH |

> **A unit hydrograph derived twenty years ago may no longer describe a catchment that has since been urbanised** — the time invariance assumption quietly fails, and the peak arrives sooner and higher than it predicts.

examTip.trap: **Base flow is SUBTRACTED (step 2), not divided by**; the **catchment area** converts volume to depth (step 3). Both wrong options name real quantities from real steps — the question tests whether you know the order.
examTip.trick: Work the procedure: separate base flow → get the DRH → volume ÷ area = **effective depth** → divide every ordinate by that depth. The divisor is always the last quantity computed.
examTip.mnemonic: **LINEARITY is the assumption doing all the work, and it is only approximate.** Real catchments respond more sharply to big storms — so a UH from moderate events **underestimates** an extreme peak.

questions.stem: Which of the following is right?
questions.solution:
**P_abs = P_atm + P_gauge.**

**The three pressures and their reference points:**

| Pressure | Measured from | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **ABSOLUTE** | **Absolute vacuum (true zero)** | **Can never be negative** |
| **GAUGE** | **Atmospheric pressure** | **Can be negative** (a vacuum) |
| **VACUUM** | Atmospheric, downward | **P_vac = P_atm − P_abs** |

> **The whole topic is a question of WHERE ZERO IS SET.** A gauge reads zero when open to the atmosphere, because it measures the **difference** from atmospheric. Absolute pressure measures from true vacuum.

> So to convert a gauge reading to absolute, **add the atmospheric pressure back on** ✓

**Note that option (d) is the correct expression for VACUUM pressure**, not gauge pressure — a well-made distractor, since it is a real and correct formula in its own right.

**Reference values:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Standard atmospheric pressure** | **101.325 kPa** |
| In head of water | **10.33 m** |
| In head of mercury | **760 mm** |
| In bar | 1.013 bar |

> **10.33 m of water is the number that matters most in practice**, because it sets an absolute physical limit.

**The limit it sets — why a suction pump cannot lift water more than about 7 metres:**

> A pump does not "pull" water up. It **reduces the pressure at its inlet**, and **atmospheric pressure pushes the water up** the suction pipe.

> The theoretical maximum lift is therefore **10.33 m** — the height atmospheric pressure can support. In practice it is limited to about **6–7 m** by:

| Loss | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Friction** in the suction pipe | Reduces the available head |
| **Velocity head** | — |
| **VAPOUR PRESSURE** of the water | The water **boils** before a perfect vacuum is reached |
| Safety margin against **cavitation** | The binding constraint |

> **A perfect vacuum is impossible because the water vaporises first** — and long before that, **cavitation** damages the pump. This is why **NPSH available must exceed NPSH required**, and why pumps are set **low** with **short, large, straight suction pipes free of high points**.

> **And vapour pressure RISES with temperature**, so a pump handling hot water needs far more submergence than the same pump on cold water — often it must have a **flooded suction** instead of a lift at all.

**Where each pressure is used:**

| Use | Pressure |
|---|---|
| **Structural design** — pipes, tanks, gates | **GAUGE** (the atmosphere acts on both sides and cancels) |
| **Cavitation and NPSH** calculations | **ABSOLUTE** |
| Gas laws, thermodynamics | **ABSOLUTE** |
| Everyday engineering | Gauge, usually without saying so |

> **Unless stated otherwise, an engineering pressure is a GAUGE pressure.** But **cavitation is always an absolute-pressure question**, because it depends on how close the pressure is to the vapour pressure — an absolute quantity.

> **Using gauge pressure in a cavitation check is a real and serious error**, and it is exactly the situation where the distinction stops being academic.

examTip.trick: It is entirely a question of **where zero is set**. A gauge reads zero in air because it measures the **difference** from atmospheric — so add atmospheric back to get absolute.
examTip.trap: Option (d) is the correct formula for **VACUUM** pressure, not gauge pressure. It is a genuine expression placed where it does not belong.
examTip.mnemonic: **10.33 m of water = 1 atmosphere**, which is why a suction pump cannot lift more than about **6–7 m** in practice — vapour pressure and cavitation intervene first. **Cavitation is always an ABSOLUTE pressure question.**

questions.stem: Which is not a component of river training works?
questions.solution:
**The catchment area** — which is a **geographical feature of the basin**, not a structure built to train a river.

> The other three are all **constructed works**. Recognising that category difference settles the question without knowing any detail about the structures themselves.

**What river training means:**

> Guiding and confining a river to a **stable, defined course** so that it does not attack banks, outflank structures, or wander across its floodplain.

**The river training works:**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **SPUR (groyne)** | Projects **from the bank into the river**; deflects the current away and induces **silting** in its lee |
| **GUIDE BANK (Bell's bund)** | Confines the river to the **waterway of a bridge or barrage** and prevents **outflanking** |
| **MARGINAL BUND** | An **embankment along the bank** confining floodwater to the channel |
| **LAUNCHING APRON** | Loose stone laid at the toe which **"launches" itself down the developing scour hole** as it forms, armouring the slope |
| **Revetment / pitching** | Armours the bank face directly |
| Cut-off | Shortens an excessive meander |

**The launching apron is the most ingenious of these and worth understanding:**

> Stone is laid **horizontally** at the toe of the bank. As the river **scours a hole** beside it, the stone at the edge **falls (launches) into the hole**, progressively armouring the newly exposed slope.

> **It is designed to be destroyed in a controlled way** — the apron consumes itself to protect the structure. The quantity of stone is calculated so that there is enough to cover the **anticipated scour slope** (usually taken as **2:1**) down to the **deepest expected scour level**.

> That anticipated scour depth comes from **Lacey's relation R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a location factor — **2.0 at a bridge pier nose, 2.75 at a severe bend**.

**Spur types**, which are frequently examined:

| Type | Orientation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Attracting** | Pointing **downstream** | Draws the current toward the bank |
| **Repelling** | Pointing **upstream** | **Pushes the current away** — the usual choice |
| **Deflecting** | Perpendicular | Local change of direction |
| **Denehy's T-headed** | With a head | Protects the nose of the spur itself |

> **A repelling spur points UPSTREAM**, which is counter-intuitive — the instinct is that pointing downstream would deflect flow away. In fact an upstream-pointing spur throws the current off, while a downstream-pointing one draws it in.

**Why the catchment nevertheless matters** — the honest qualification:

> The **catchment area** determines the **discharge and the sediment load** the river carries, and therefore what training works are needed. **Catchment management** (afforestation, check dams) is a genuine long-term measure that reduces sediment at source.

> But it is a **basin characteristic and a watershed practice, not a river training structure**, which is what the question asks for.

examTip.trick: Three options are **constructed works**; one is a **geographical feature**. The category difference settles it without knowing anything about spurs or aprons.
examTip.trap: **A REPELLING spur points UPSTREAM** — counter-intuitive, but an upstream-pointing spur throws the current off the bank while a downstream-pointing one attracts it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A launching apron is DESIGNED to be destroyed** — its stone falls into the scour hole as it forms, armouring the new slope. Size it from **Lacey's scour depth × a location factor** (2.0 at a pier nose).

questions.stem: In PERT analysis, the time estimates of activities and probability of their occurrence follow:
questions.solution:
**The Beta distribution** — for **individual activities**.

**The distinction that this question turns on:**

| Level | Distribution |
|---|---|
| **INDIVIDUAL activity durations** | **BETA distribution** |
| **TOTAL PROJECT duration** | **NORMAL distribution** |

> Both are correct — **at different levels** — and the option list offers both. The question asks about **activities**, so the answer is beta.

**Why beta for an activity:**

| Property | Why it fits |
|---|---|
| **Bounded at both ends** | An activity has a genuine minimum (optimistic) and maximum (pessimistic) duration |
| **Can be SKEWED** | Delays stretch further than early finishes — the distribution has a **long right tail** |
| Flexible shape | Fits many real activity patterns |

> **The skew is the realistic part.** An activity estimated at 10 days might finish in 8 at best, but could take 30 if things go wrong. **The downside is far longer than the upside**, and a symmetric distribution cannot represent that.

**Why normal for the project total:**

> By the **CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM**, the sum of many independent random variables tends to a **normal distribution**, whatever the individual distributions are.

> A project path contains many activities, so **their total approaches normal** even though each is skewed. That is what allows the probability calculations PERT is used for.

**The PERT formulae:**

> **Expected time t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6**
> **Standard deviation σ = (t_p − t_o)/6**
> **Variance = σ²**

> where **t_o** optimistic, **t_m** most likely, **t_p** pessimistic.

> **The weight of 4 on the most likely time** is what makes t_e a weighted average rather than a simple mean — the most likely value dominates, but the extremes pull it.

> **The 6 in the standard deviation** comes from the assumption that the range t_o to t_p spans about **six standard deviations** (±3σ), which covers 99.7% of a normal distribution.

**Making a probability statement — what PERT is FOR:**

> **Project variance = SUM of the variances of the CRITICAL PATH activities only**
> **Z = (Target date − Expected date)/√(project variance)**
> Then read the probability from the standard normal table.

> **Variances ADD; standard deviations do NOT.** Adding standard deviations is the standard error in this calculation and it overstates the spread substantially.

**PERT versus CPM:**

| | **PERT** | **CPM** |
|---|---|---|
| Time estimates | **THREE — probabilistic** | **ONE — deterministic** |
| Orientation | **EVENT** oriented | **ACTIVITY** oriented |
| Suits | **R&D, novel work** with uncertain durations | **Construction, repetitive work** with known durations |
| Cost | Not usually included | **Time–cost trade-off (crashing)** |

> **Modern practice merges them**, and most software offers both — three-point estimates with activity-on-node networks and cost analysis.

**The trap that PERT's own arithmetic hides:**

> Computing the project variance from the **critical path only** ignores the possibility that a **near-critical path with high variance** overruns and becomes critical.

> **PERT therefore tends to be OPTIMISTIC** about completion probability. A path with a slightly shorter expected duration but much greater uncertainty can easily end up governing — and only a **simulation (Monte Carlo)** across all paths captures that.

examTip.trap: **Both "beta" and "normal" are correct — at different levels.** Individual **activities** follow beta; the **project total** follows normal, by the central limit theorem. Read which one the question asks for.
examTip.trick: Beta fits an activity because it is **bounded at both ends and SKEWED** — delays stretch much further than early finishes, which a symmetric distribution cannot represent.
examTip.mnemonic: **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6, σ = (t_p − t_o)/6, and VARIANCES add — never standard deviations.** And PERT is optimistic: it ignores near-critical paths with high variance that may overrun and take over.

questions.stem: Lacey's silt factor for 0.35 mm diameter particles is:
questions.solution:
**About 1.**

**Working.**

> **f = 1.76 √d**, with **d in MILLIMETRES**
> **f = 1.76 × √0.35 = 1.76 × 0.5916 = 1.04 ≈ 1** ✓

**The anchor value worth carrying:**

> **f = 1.0 corresponds to "standard silt" of about 0.32 mm** — the reference against which Lacey calibrated the whole system. Since 0.35 mm is barely coarser than standard silt, f must be barely above 1.

> **That single anchor answers this question in two seconds without any arithmetic**, and it catches a units error immediately: if a fine sand gives f = 0.03, the diameter was entered in metres.

**Typical values:**

| Material | d (mm) | f |
|---|---|---|
| Fine silt | 0.05 | **0.4** |
| Medium silt | 0.16 | 0.7 |
| **Standard silt** | **0.32** | **1.0** |
| Coarse sand | 0.72 | 1.5 |
| **Fine gravel** | **2.0** | **2.5** |

**Lacey's regime equations:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Velocity** | V = 0.4382 (f R)^{1/2} |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Normal scour depth** | **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** |

**What "in regime" means** — a stricter criterion than hydraulic efficiency:

> A channel in regime carries **both its water AND its sediment load** without net scour or deposition. Its **width, depth and slope have all adjusted** to the discharge and the bed material.

> **Lacey's advance over KENNEDY** was recognising that a regime channel adjusts **all three dimensions**, not merely its velocity. Kennedy gave only a critical velocity relation; Lacey gave a complete self-consistent set.

**The modern successor** is the **TRACTIVE FORCE** method:

> Compare the **bed shear stress τ₀ = γRS** against the **critical shear** for the bed material, from **Shields: τ_c = 0.056(γ_s − γ)d**.

> **This is physically better founded**, because it is the **shear stress at the bed, not the mean velocity, that actually moves a grain**. Two channels with the same mean velocity can have very different bed shear.

> And on the **SIDE slopes** the permissible shear is about **25% lower** than on the bed, because the grain's own weight has a component down the slope helping the flow move it — a refinement the velocity methods cannot express at all.

**The scour application** is where f is most consequential:

> **R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a location factor — **2.0 at a bridge pier nose**, **2.75 at a severe bend** — fixes the **foundation depth** of piers, abutments and guide banks.

> **That scour depth usually governs foundation depth near a watercourse, far more than bearing capacity does.** A pier founded above the scour level will be undermined in a flood however adequate its bearing pressure.

> **Scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide**, which is why this apparently minor empirical relation carries so much weight.

examTip.trick: Anchor on **f = 1.0 at 0.32 mm ("standard silt")**. Since 0.35 mm is barely coarser, f is barely above 1 — no arithmetic needed.
examTip.trap: **d must be in MILLIMETRES.** Entering metres gives an answer about 32 times too small, and the anchor value catches it instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Scour, not bearing capacity, usually fixes foundation depth near a river** — R = 1.35(q²/f)⅓ × a location factor (2.0 at a pier nose). Scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.

questions.stem: Terracotta is used in buildings for:
questions.solution:
**Ornamental work** — decorative elements, facade panels and roofing tiles.

**What terracotta is:**

> **"Baked earth"** — a **fine-grained, refined clay** moulded into shape and **fired at a high temperature**, harder and denser than ordinary brick clay.

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Porous terracotta** | Made from clay with sawdust or ground cork; **lighter, better insulating** |
| **Polished (glazed) terracotta** | Fired twice with a glaze; **weather resistant, washable, coloured** |

**Why it is used decoratively:**

| Property | Advantage |
|---|---|
| **Moulded before firing** | Takes **fine, intricate detail** — cornices, brackets, string courses, tracery |
| **Repeatable from a mould** | Identical units at low unit cost once the mould exists |
| **Durable** | Resists weathering far better than carved stone in a polluted atmosphere |
| **Lighter than stone** | Reduces the load on the structure |
| Fire resistant | Non-combustible |
| **Colour-fast** | The colour is in the fired body, not applied |

> **It is a substitute for CARVED STONE** — achieving by moulding and firing what would otherwise need a mason's chisel on every unit. That is the whole economic argument for it.

**Note the honest qualification about "insulation":**

> **Porous terracotta genuinely does have insulating value**, and the source's own explanation lists insulation among its properties. But its **primary building use is ornamental**, which is what the question asks — and the keyed answer reflects that.

> Option (a) is therefore not absurd; it is a **secondary property offered as if it were the principal use**, which is a well-constructed distractor.

**Terracotta in Nepal:**

> The Kathmandu valley's traditional architecture uses terracotta extensively — **roofing tiles (jhingati)**, **decorative brick (dachi appa)** with its fine moulded face, and ornamental work on temples and palaces.

> **Dachi appa** deserves mention: a wedge-shaped facing brick with a **finely finished exposed face**, laid with an almost invisible joint. It is the reason Newari brickwork looks so precise, and it is a terracotta product in everything but name.

**Related clay products** for comparison:

| Product | Note |
|---|---|
| **Common brick** | Structural; coarser clay, lower firing |
| **TERRACOTTA** | **Refined clay, higher firing; ornamental and facing** |
| **Earthenware** | Porous, glazed; drainage pipes, sanitary ware |
| **Stoneware** | Vitrified, impervious; **sewer pipes, chemical vessels** |
| **Porcelain** | Fully vitrified, white; sanitary ware, insulators |
| **Faience** | Glazed terracotta |

> **The series runs from coarse and porous to fine and vitrified** as the clay is refined and the firing temperature raised. **Vitrification is what makes a product impervious**, which is why stoneware is used for sewers and common brick is not.

> That single progression — refinement and firing temperature determining porosity and strength — explains the whole family, and it is more useful than memorising the individual products.

examTip.trick: Terracotta is a **substitute for CARVED STONE** — moulded before firing, so it takes fine detail and repeats cheaply from a mould. That is its whole purpose.
examTip.trap: **Porous terracotta really does insulate**, so option (b) is a genuine secondary property presented as the principal use. The question asks what it is *used for*, and that is ornament.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brick → terracotta → earthenware → stoneware → porcelain**: finer clay and hotter firing all the way. **Vitrification is what makes a product impervious** — which is why stoneware serves as sewer pipe and brick does not.

questions.stem: In open channel flow, the alternate depths are:
options: Which have the same specific force
Which occur at the same specific energy
questions.solution:
**The two depths that occur at the same SPECIFIC ENERGY** for a given discharge.

**The pairing that must be kept straight:**

| Pair | Same quantity | Where it occurs |
|---|---|---|
| **ALTERNATE depths** | **Specific ENERGY** | Two possible states at the same E |
| **CONJUGATE (sequent) depths** | **Specific FORCE (momentum)** | **Across a HYDRAULIC JUMP** |

> **Option (a) defines CONJUGATE depths**, which is the near-miss and the most-picked wrong answer. The two pairs are constantly swapped.

**Specific energy:**

> **E = y + V²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²)**

> Plotting E against y for a fixed Q gives the **specific energy curve** — a curve with **two branches** and a **minimum**:

| Branch | State |
|---|---|
| **Upper** | **SUBCRITICAL** — deep and slow, energy mostly **potential** |
| **Lower** | **SUPERCRITICAL** — shallow and fast, energy mostly **kinetic** |
| **The nose (minimum E)** | **CRITICAL depth** — the two branches meet |

> **For any E above the minimum there are TWO depths — the alternate pair.** One deep and slow, one shallow and fast, both carrying the same discharge with the same specific energy.

> **At the minimum they coincide**, which is the critical depth — and this is why option (d) is wrong: at critical depth there is only **one** depth, not a pair.

**Key critical relations** (rectangular channel):

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Critical depth** | **y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}** |
| **Minimum specific energy** | **E_min = 1.5 y_c** |
| **Critical velocity** | **V_c = √(g y_c)**, so **Fr = 1** |

**Why the distinction matters practically — it decides which analysis to use:**

| Transition | Governed by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Smooth transition** (a step, a contraction, a gradual change) | **ENERGY** — alternate depths | Losses are small and **can be estimated** |
| **HYDRAULIC JUMP** | **MOMENTUM** — conjugate depths | The loss is **large and unknown in advance**, but the **external forces are small** |

> **That is the whole reason two different pairings exist.** Across a smooth transition, energy is nearly conserved and can be used; across a jump it is not, but momentum is — because the jump is short, so bed friction over its length is negligible.

> **Applying Bernoulli across a hydraulic jump is therefore a serious error**, and it is exactly the mistake the conjugate/alternate distinction exists to prevent.

**The specific energy curve explains channel transitions:**

| Situation | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **A step UP in the bed** (subcritical flow) | E available falls, so the **depth DECREASES** — the water surface **drops** over the step |
| A step up (supercritical flow) | The depth **increases** |
| **A step too high** | The flow **CHOKES** — it cannot pass, and the upstream level rises |

> **The subcritical result is counter-intuitive** — raising the bed lowers the water surface. It follows directly from moving leftward along the upper branch of the E–y curve.

> **CHOKING** occurs when the step exceeds **E₁ − E_min**: there is simply not enough specific energy to get the flow over it, so the upstream depth must rise until there is. That is the same mechanism by which a **broad-crested weir** works as a measuring device.

examTip.trap: **Option (a) defines CONJUGATE (sequent) depths** — same specific FORCE, across a hydraulic jump. Alternate depths share specific ENERGY. The two pairs are swapped constantly.
examTip.trick: Picture the E–y curve: **two branches (subcritical above, supercritical below) meeting at a nose (critical)**. Any E above the minimum cuts it twice — that pair is the alternate depths.
examTip.mnemonic: **Energy for smooth transitions, MOMENTUM for the jump** — because a jump's loss is large and unknown but its forces are small. Applying Bernoulli across a jump is exactly the error this distinction prevents.

questions.stem: The X and Y axes of Mohr's circle represent:
options: principal shear stress and principal normal stress
principal normal stress and principal shear stress
questions.solution:
**Normal stress on the X axis, shear stress on the Y axis.**

> The convention is universal: **σ horizontal, τ vertical**. Option (b) is the same pair inverted, and (a) and (c) confuse the axes with the **points on the circle**.

**What Mohr's circle is.** A graphical representation of the **state of stress at a point**. Every point on the circle gives the **(σ, τ) pair acting on one particular plane** through that point; rotating the plane moves you round the circle.

**The circle's geometry:**

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Centre** | **((σ_x + σ_y)/2, 0)** — always **on the σ axis** |
| **Radius** | **R = √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]** |
| **Principal stresses** | **Centre ± R** — where the circle **crosses the σ axis** |
| **Maximum shear stress** | **= R** — the **top and bottom** of the circle |

**Three results follow immediately from the picture:**

> **1. PRINCIPAL PLANES carry ZERO shear.** They are where the circle crosses the σ axis, and on that axis τ = 0 by definition.

> **2. τ_max = R = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2**, at the top of the circle.

> **3. The plane of maximum shear is at 45° to the principal planes** — because the top of the circle is **90° round from the σ axis**, and **angles on Mohr's circle are DOUBLE the real angles**.

**The doubling of angles is the one thing that must be remembered:**

> **A rotation of θ in the physical element corresponds to 2θ on the circle.** That is why principal planes, 90° apart in reality, appear 180° apart on the circle — at opposite ends of a diameter.

> **Forgetting the factor of two is the standard error** in every Mohr's circle problem.

**Why the plane of maximum shear also carries normal stress:**

> At the top of the circle, σ = the **centre value** = (σ_x + σ_y)/2, which is **not zero**. So **the plane of maximum shear is not free of normal stress** — a point that surprises many candidates.

> **Only the principal planes are free of shear.** No plane is generally free of normal stress.

**The failure theories the circle supports:**

| Theory | Criterion | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum principal stress** (Rankine) | σ₁ = σ_y | **BRITTLE** materials |
| **Maximum shear stress** (Tresca) | (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 = σ_y/2 | **DUCTILE**; conservative |
| **Distortion energy** (von Mises) | — | **DUCTILE**; the best fit to test data |
| **MOHR–COULOMB** | **τ = c + σ tan φ** | **SOIL, rock, concrete** |

> **Mohr–Coulomb is the soil mechanics application**, and it is the same circle used differently: a series of circles from triaxial tests at different confining pressures, with their **common tangent** giving **c and φ**.

> **That is exactly how shear strength parameters are extracted from a triaxial test**, and it is why Mohr's circle appears in both the structures and the geotechnics parts of the syllabus.

**A note on the undrained case:** for a saturated clay tested undrained, **every circle has the SAME diameter** whatever the cell pressure — because the extra pressure goes entirely into pore water and the effective stress is unchanged. Their common tangent is therefore **horizontal**, giving **φ_u = 0** and **τ = c_u**.

examTip.trick: **σ horizontal, τ vertical** — always. Then the geometry gives everything: **centre (σ_x+σ_y)/2, radius R = τ_max**, principal stresses where the circle crosses the σ axis.
examTip.trap: **Angles on Mohr's circle are DOUBLE the real angles.** Principal planes are 90° apart in reality but 180° apart on the circle. Forgetting the factor of two is the standard error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only PRINCIPAL planes are shear-free; the plane of MAXIMUM SHEAR still carries normal stress** (the centre value). And the same circle gives **c and φ** from a triaxial test — the Mohr–Coulomb envelope.

questions.stem: Early strength of cement is achieved by:
questions.solution:
**C₃S — tricalcium silicate.**

**The four Bogue compounds and what each does:**

| Compound | Name | Role | Heat of hydration |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C₃S** — 3CaO·SiO₂ | **Alite** | **EARLY STRENGTH — up to 7 days** | High (500 J/g) |
| **C₂S** — 2CaO·SiO₂ | **Belite** | **LATER strength — beyond 28 days** | **Low (260 J/g)** |
| **C₃A** — 3CaO·Al₂O₃ | Celite | **FLASH SET** — hydrates almost instantly | **VERY HIGH (865 J/g)** |
| **C₄AF** | Felite | Little strength; gives the **grey colour** | Moderate |

**The organising sentence:**

> **C₃A sets, C₃S gives early strength, C₂S gives late strength.**

> The source's own note puts it exactly that way, and it answers most questions in this topic.

**Typical proportions in OPC:** C₃S about **50%**, C₂S **25%**, C₃A **10%**, C₄AF **8%**.

**Why gypsum is present in cement:**

> **C₃A hydrates almost instantly and would cause a FLASH SET** — the cement would stiffen in the mixer, unusable. **Gypsum (2–3%) is interground with the clinker purely to retard it.**

> **That is the entire reason gypsum is in cement**, and it is worth knowing because it connects to the first question of every cement paper.

**How the special cements are made — by adjusting these proportions:**

| Cement | Adjustment | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **RAPID HARDENING** | **More C₃S**, ground **finer** | 3-day strength equals OPC's 7-day. **Setting time UNCHANGED** |
| **LOW HEAT** | **Less C₃A and C₃S, MORE C₂S** | Slow strength gain, **low heat** — for **mass concrete** |
| **SULPHATE RESISTING** | **C₃A limited to under 5%** | Resists sulphate attack |
| Portland pozzolana | OPC + fly ash | Lower heat, better durability, slower early strength |

> **Rapid hardening cement does NOT set faster** — its setting times are the same 30 minutes and 600 minutes as OPC. It gains **strength** faster. That distinction is examined constantly.

**Why C₃A is limited in sulphate-resisting cement:**

> **Sulphates react with hydrated C₃A to form ETTRINGITE**, which is **expansive**. The expansion cracks the concrete from within.

> **Removing the C₃A removes the vulnerability** — which is why sulphate-resisting cement is specified for foundations in sulphate-bearing soils and for marine work.

**Why heat of hydration matters:**

> In a **mass pour** — a dam, a thick raft, a large pile cap — the heat cannot escape. The **core heats up and expands** while the **surface cools and contracts**, and the differential causes **THERMAL CRACKING**.

| Control | Note |
|---|---|
| **Low heat cement** | Less C₃A and C₃S |
| **Pozzolana or fly ash replacement** | Reduces the cement content directly |
| **Chilled aggregate or ice** in the mix | Lowers the placing temperature |
| **Cooling pipes** embedded in the pour | Used in large dams |
| **Lift height limits** and placing sequence | Lets each lift shed heat |

> **The limit is usually a temperature DIFFERENTIAL of about 20 °C between core and surface**, not an absolute temperature — because it is the differential that causes the cracking.

examTip.trick: One sentence carries the topic: **C₃A SETS, C₃S gives EARLY strength, C₂S gives LATE strength.** C₄AF contributes little but the grey colour.
examTip.trap: **Rapid hardening cement does NOT set faster** — same 30 min / 600 min limits as OPC. It has more C₃S and finer grinding, so it gains **strength** faster.
examTip.mnemonic: **GYPSUM exists in cement solely to retard C₃A**, which would otherwise flash-set. And **sulphate-resisting cement limits C₃A below 5%**, because sulphates turn hydrated C₃A into expansive ettringite.

questions.stem: Which crop has the highest water use efficiency?
questions.solution:
**Millet.**

**What water use efficiency means:**

> **WUE = yield produced per unit of water consumed** — how much crop you get for each cubic metre of water.

> **A high WUE means the crop is EFFICIENT with water, not that it needs a lot.** The relation reads backwards to many candidates.

**Why millet leads:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adapted to semi-arid, drought-prone regions** | Evolved for exactly this |
| **Short growing season** | Less total transpiration |
| **Deep, efficient root system** | Extracts water other crops cannot reach |
| **Drought tolerant** | Survives and yields under water scarcity |
| **C4 photosynthesis** | Fundamentally more water-efficient than C3 crops like wheat and rice |

> **The C4 pathway is the underlying reason.** C4 plants (millet, maize, sorghum, sugarcane) fix carbon more efficiently and can keep their stomata closed longer, losing less water per unit of carbon fixed. **Wheat and rice are C3** and cannot match them.

**Rice is the opposite extreme:**

> Rice has the **highest water REQUIREMENT** of the three — it is grown in **standing water**, with a **delta of 1200–2000 mm**, and much of that water is lost to **percolation and evaporation** rather than transpiration.

> The source notes that **rice has the highest water RESISTANCE** — it tolerates waterlogging, which is why it can be grown in flooded fields. **Tolerating water is not the same as using it efficiently**, and confusing those two is exactly the trap here.

**Delta (total water depth) for common crops:**

| Crop | Delta |
|---|---|
| **Rice** | **1200 – 2000 mm** |
| Sugarcane | 1500 – 2000 mm |
| **Wheat** | **350 – 400 mm** |
| **Millet / maize** | **300 – 500 mm** |
| Cotton | 500 – 700 mm |

**The relation between the irrigation terms:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B/D** metres, with **B in days** and **D in hectares per cumec**

> The **8.64** is simply **86 400 s/day ÷ 10 000 m²/ha**.

> **Duty and delta are INVERSELY related**: a **high duty** means one cumec irrigates a large area, which means **less water per hectare** — an efficient crop or system.

**Why this matters for Nepal and for irrigation planning:**

> **Crop choice is a water management decision.** Growing rice where water is scarce commits the system to the highest delta of any crop; shifting to millet or maize serves several times the area with the same supply.

> **The System of Rice Intensification (SRI)** addresses the same problem from the other end — growing rice with **alternate wetting and drying** rather than continuous flooding, cutting water use substantially while often raising yield.

**And the efficiency chain that determines what must actually be supplied:**

> **η_overall = η_conveyance × η_application** — and efficiencies **MULTIPLY**. Two stages at 70% give **49%**, so the water delivered at the canal head can be **twice** what the crop consumes.

> **Improving conveyance efficiency by lining is often cheaper than developing new water**, which is why lining pays for itself so quickly in a water-short system.

examTip.trap: **Rice has the highest water RESISTANCE (tolerates flooding) but the LOWEST efficiency.** Tolerating water is not using it well — that confusion is the whole trap here.
examTip.trick: The underlying reason is photosynthesis: **millet and maize are C4**, fundamentally more water-efficient than **C3** wheat and rice. C4 plants fix more carbon per unit of water lost.
examTip.mnemonic: **High duty means LESS water per hectare** — duty and delta are inverse. **Δ = 8.64 B/D**, where 8.64 = 86 400 s/day ÷ 10 000 m²/ha. Rice needs 1200–2000 mm; millet 300–500.

questions.stem: The President of the NEA is an ex-officio member of which council?
questions.solution:
**The Nepal Engineering Council (NEC).**

> The **President of the Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** sits on the Council **ex officio** — that is, **by virtue of holding that office**, without any separate appointment or election to the Council.

**The Council's composition (21 members) under the NEC Act 2055:**

| Position | Number | How appointed |
|---|---|---|
| **Chairman** | 1 | **Nominated by GoN** — bachelor's + **15 years** |
| **Vice-Chairman** | 1 | **Nominated by GoN** — bachelor's + **10 years** |
| Members | 7 | Nominated by GoN — **one per province, at least three women** |
| **President of the NEA** | **1** | **EX OFFICIO** |
| Members | 5 | **ELECTED from the NEA** |
| Campus chief of an engineering campus | 1 | Nominated by GoN |
| Representative, Institute of Engineering (TU) | 1 | Nominated by GoN |
| Representative of universities teaching engineering | 1 | Nominated by GoN |
| **Members** | **2** | **NOMINATED BY THE COUNCIL ITSELF** |
| **Member Secretary (Registrar)** | 1 | Bachelor's + **10 years** |

**The four appointment routes** — the discriminator in every question of this kind:

| Route | Who |
|---|---|
| **Nominated by the Government** | Chairman, VP, 7 provincial members, 3 academic representatives |
| **ELECTED from the NEA** | 5 members |
| **EX OFFICIO** | **The NEA President** |
| **Nominated by the Council itself** | 2 members |

> Note that **the NEA is represented twice over** — once by its President ex officio, and again by five elected members. That is **six of the twenty-one**, a substantial voice for the profession's own association within its regulator.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Body | What it is |
|---|---|
| **SONA** | Society of Nepalese Architects — a separate professional body |
| **SCAFF** | Not an engineering regulatory council |
| **NPC** | **National Planning Commission** — the government's economic planning body, unrelated to professional regulation |

**The standing institutional distinction:**

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.**

| | **NEC (Council)** | **NEA (Association)** |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Statutory regulator** | **Voluntary professional body** |
| Membership | **Registration is a LEGAL REQUIREMENT to practise** | **Voluntary** |
| Function | Register, license, set education standards, **discipline** | Represent members' interests, professional development, advocacy |
| Created by | **NEC Act 2055** | Association, not statute |

> **Practising or signing engineering drawings without NEC registration is an offence under the Act.** NEA membership carries no such force — but the Act deliberately gives the Association seats on the Council, so that the profession has a voice in its own regulation.

**The Council facts most often examined**, as a block: **Act 2055 (1998 AD)**, **Regulations 2057**, **21 members**, **chairman 15 years / VP 10 years / Registrar 10 years**, **2 nominated by the Council**, **5 elected from the NEA**, **70% for institutional affiliation**, first Registrar **Er. Bindeshwar Yadav**.

examTip.trick: **Ex officio** means "by virtue of the office" — no separate election or appointment. The NEA President sits on the NEC automatically on becoming NEA President.
examTip.trap: Note the **NEA is represented twice**: its President ex officio **plus five elected members** — six of twenty-one seats. That is a deliberate design, giving the profession a voice in its own regulator.
examTip.mnemonic: **Council REGULATES, Association REPRESENTS.** NEC registration is a **legal requirement** to practise and to sign drawings; NEA membership is voluntary. That one line answers most institutional questions.

questions.stem: If the depth of foundation is D, the bearing capacity of soil does not depend upon the water table corrections R_w1 and R_w2 when the water table is at:
questions.solution:
**At a depth D below the foundation** — beyond that, the water table has no influence.

**The two water table correction factors (IS 6403):**

| Factor | Applies to | Formula | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R_w1** | The **SURCHARGE term qN_q** | **0.5[1 + Z_w1/D]** | **0.5 to 1.0** |
| **R_w2** | The **WIDTH term 0.5γBN_γ** | **0.5[1 + Z_w2/B]** | **0.5 to 1.0** |

> where **Z_w1** is measured from the **ground level** and **Z_w2** from the **base of the foundation**.

**Reading the limits off the formulae:**

| Water table position | R_w1 | R_w2 |
|---|---|---|
| At **ground level** (Z_w1 = 0) | **0.5** | 0.5 |
| At the **foundation base** (Z_w1 = D, Z_w2 = 0) | **1.0** | **0.5** |
| At depth **B below the base** (Z_w2 ≥ B) | 1.0 | **1.0** |
| **Deeper still** | **1.0 — no further influence** | **1.0** |

> **Once both factors reach 1.0, the water table has no effect at all** — which is the condition the question asks about, and it is reached once the water table lies far enough below the foundation.

**Why the water table matters so much:**

> Submergence replaces the **bulk unit weight γ** with the **submerged unit weight γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w**, which is roughly **HALF**.

> **A high water table can therefore HALVE the bearing capacity of a sand.** That is not a refinement — it is one of the largest single corrections in foundation design, and omitting it is a serious error.

> **The effect is much smaller in clay**, because for **φ = 0** the term **N_γ = 0** and the width term vanishes entirely — so submergence affects only the surcharge term.

**The full Terzaghi/IS 6403 expression with corrections:**

> **q_u = c N_c s_c d_c i_c + q N_q s_q d_q i_q R_w1 + 0.5 γ B N_γ s_γ d_γ i_γ R_w2**

| Factor set | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **s** | **Shape** — strip/square/circular/rectangular |
| **d** | **Depth** of embedment |
| **i** | **Inclination** of the load |
| **R_w** | **Water table** |

**And the shape factors** for the base equation:

| Shape | Cohesion term | Width term |
|---|---|---|
| **Strip** | **1.0** | **0.5** |
| **Square** | **1.3** | **0.4** |
| **Circular** | **1.3** | **0.3** |

> The two move in **opposite directions** — cohesion up because the wedge is confined on all sides, width down because the wedge is smaller relative to B.

**The final step that decides the design pressure:**

> **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F** with **F = 2.5 to 3**, applied to the **NET** value — then take the **LESSER** of that and the **settlement-limited** pressure.

> **Settlement usually governs**, not bearing failure. A soil can safely carry the pressure and still settle more than the structure tolerates — and it is **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement (limit about **1 in 300** angular distortion) that does the damage, not uniform settlement.

examTip.trick: Read the limits straight off the formulae: **R = 0.5[1 + Z/D]** runs from **0.5 (water at the top) to 1.0 (water far below)**. At 1.0 there is no correction left — that is the answer.
examTip.trap: **A high water table can HALVE a sand's bearing capacity**, because γ is replaced by γ′ ≈ γ/2. It is one of the biggest corrections in foundation design, not a refinement — and in **clay it barely matters**, since N_γ = 0.
examTip.mnemonic: **R_w1 measures from GROUND LEVEL and corrects the surcharge term; R_w2 measures from the FOUNDATION BASE and corrects the width term.** Getting the datum wrong swaps the two corrections.

questions.stem: The simultaneous equations of the slope deflection method can be solved by iteration in:
questions.solution:
**The moment distribution method.**

**The relationship between the two methods.** Both are **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness) methods** — both take the joint rotations as unknowns.

| | **SLOPE DEFLECTION** | **MOMENT DISTRIBUTION** |
|---|---|---|
| Unknowns | **Joint rotations θ** | The same, implicitly |
| Solution | **Solve the simultaneous equations directly** | **ITERATE** — relax one joint at a time |
| Hand suitability | Poor beyond 2–3 unknowns | **Excellent** — no simultaneous equations at all |

> **Moment distribution is slope deflection solved by successive approximation.** Hardy Cross's insight was that the simultaneous equations need never be written down: **release one joint at a time, distribute the unbalanced moment, carry over, and repeat until the corrections become negligible.**

**The slope deflection equation:**

> **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM_AB**

**The moment distribution procedure:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Compute **fixed end moments (FEM)** with all joints locked |
| **2** | Compute **distribution factors: DF = K/ΣK** at each joint |
| **3** | **Release a joint**; distribute the out-of-balance moment in proportion to DF |
| **4** | **CARRY OVER half** of each distributed moment to the far end |
| **5** | Repeat until the carried-over moments are negligible |

**The two constants that make it work:**

| Constant | Value | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| **Carry-over factor** | **½** | Far end **FIXED** |
| **Carry-over factor** | **0** | Far end **PINNED** |
| **Stiffness K** | **4EI/L** | Far end fixed |
| **Stiffness K** | **3EI/L** | Far end **PINNED** |

> **Using the modified stiffness 3EI/L for a pin-ended member saves enormous effort** — it removes the need to carry over to that end at all, which for an end span cuts the work substantially.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Method | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Conjugate beam** | A device for finding **deflections and slopes** of a beam — not an indeterminate analysis method |
| **Consistent deformation** | A **FORCE (flexibility)** method — the opposite family, taking redundant **forces** as unknowns |
| **Williot–Mohr** | A **graphical** construction for **truss joint displacements** |

> **Consistent deformation is the near-miss**, and the distinction is fundamental:

| | **FORCE (flexibility) methods** | **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness) methods** |
|---|---|---|
| Unknowns | **Redundant FORCES** | **Joint DISPLACEMENTS** |
| Number of unknowns | **Static** indeterminacy D_s | **Kinematic** indeterminacy D_k |
| Examples | Consistent deformation, **Castigliano**, three-moment, column analogy | **Slope deflection, moment distribution, MATRIX STIFFNESS** |

> **Choose whichever has fewer unknowns** for hand analysis. A **continuous beam** usually has fewer redundant forces; a **multi-storey frame** usually has fewer joint rotations — which is why frames are analysed by displacement methods.

> **And all modern software uses the STIFFNESS method**, because it is systematic, assembles automatically from element matrices, and needs no judgement about which redundants to choose. Moment distribution is its hand ancestor.

examTip.trick: **Moment distribution IS slope deflection solved by iteration** — Hardy Cross's insight was that the simultaneous equations need never be written: release one joint, distribute, carry over, repeat.
examTip.trap: **Consistent deformation is a FORCE method** (unknowns are redundant forces); slope deflection and moment distribution are **DISPLACEMENT methods** (unknowns are rotations). Opposite families.
examTip.mnemonic: **Carry-over ½ to a fixed end, 0 to a pinned one; stiffness 4EI/L fixed, 3EI/L pinned.** Using the modified 3EI/L for end spans removes the carry-over entirely and saves large amounts of work.

questions.stem: The middle one-third rule is used in:
questions.solution:
**To prevent TENSION developing in the section.**

**The rule.** For a rectangular section of width b, the base pressure under combined direct load and moment is:

> **p = (P/b)(1 ± 6e/b)**

> For **no tension**, the minimum must be **≥ 0**: **1 − 6e/b ≥ 0**, so **e ≤ b/6**.

> Since the load may be eccentric either way, the resultant must lie within the **middle third** — a band of width **b/3** centred on the section.

**Why it is a TENSION criterion, not a compression one:**

> The materials this rule governs — **masonry, plain concrete, soil beneath a footing** — carry **compression well and tension not at all**.

> **The rule exists precisely because these materials cannot pull.** Compression is never the concern; it is checked separately as a stress limit, and it is rarely critical.

**The stress states:**

| Eccentricity | Distribution | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **e = 0** | Uniform P/A | Full |
| **0 < e < b/6** | **Trapezoidal**, all compression | Full |
| **e = b/6** | **Triangular**, zero at one edge | Full, just |
| **e > b/6** | **TENSION develops; the section LIFTS OFF** | **Partial** |

> Beyond the limit the contact width reduces to **x = 3(b/2 − e)** and the maximum stress becomes **2P/(3bx)** per unit length.

**Why the limit is enforced absolutely rather than treated as a stress check:**

> Once part of the base lifts off, the **contact area shrinks**, so the **resultant moves further toward the edge**, which **reduces the contact further**.

> **The process is PROGRESSIVE and self-accelerating** — and progressive instability is a different matter from a section merely being overstressed.

**The consequence in a gravity dam is the clearest case:**

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1** | Tension opens a **crack at the heel** |
| **2** | **Full reservoir pressure enters the crack** |
| **3** | **UPLIFT increases** dramatically |
| **4** | The resultant moves further downstream |
| **5** | The crack **propagates** |

> **The crack makes the conditions that opened it worse.** That feedback is why no tension is permitted at all, rather than a small tension being allowed against the material's modest tensile strength.

**The KERN — the general concept:**

| Section | Kern | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | A **rhombus**, diagonals **b/3 and d/3** | **e ≤ b/6** |
| **Circle diameter D** | A **circle** of diameter **D/4** | **e ≤ D/8** |
| Hollow sections | **Larger** kern | More tolerant |

> **The "middle third" belongs to the RECTANGLE.** A circle's limit is the middle **quarter** — so the rule as commonly stated is section-specific, and generalising it is wrong.

> **Hollow sections have a larger kern** relative to their size, because their material is further from the centroid — genuinely useful for chimneys and hollow piers.

**Where it governs:** masonry walls and columns, **gravity dams**, retaining wall bases, footings on soil, and chimney bases. **It does NOT apply to reinforced sections**, where the steel carries the tension by design.

examTip.trick: The rule exists because **masonry, plain concrete and soil cannot carry TENSION**. Compression is never the concern — it is checked separately and rarely governs.
examTip.trap: **"Middle third" is specific to the RECTANGLE.** For a **circle** the limit is the middle **quarter (e ≤ D/8)**. The general concept is the **KERN**, whose shape depends on the section.
examTip.mnemonic: **A crack at the heel admits full reservoir pressure, raising uplift, moving the resultant further out, extending the crack.** Self-accelerating — which is why no tension is allowed at all, not merely limited.

questions.stem: The maximum compressive strain in concrete in axial compression is taken as:
questions.solution:
**0.002 in AXIAL compression** (IS 456).

**The two limiting strains, and the distinction the question turns on:**

| Loading | Limiting compressive strain |
|---|---|
| **AXIAL compression** (pure, uniform) | **0.002** |
| **BENDING (flexure)** | **0.0035** |

> **Option (c), 0.0035, is the bending value** and it is the more familiar of the two — which is exactly why it is offered here. **Read whether the question says axial or flexural.**

**Why bending permits a higher strain than axial compression:**

> In **axial** compression the **whole section reaches the peak strain simultaneously**. Once the most-stressed material fails, there is nothing to redistribute to — the failure is immediate and complete.

> In **bending** the strain **varies linearly across the depth**. Only the extreme fibre reaches the limit; the material below it is less strained and can still take load. **The less-strained fibres restrain the extreme fibre**, allowing it to strain further before the section fails.

> **That restraint is why the flexural limit is 75% higher.** It is the same reason a section in bending is more forgiving than one in pure compression — and it is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it explains the intermediate cases too.

**The combined case** (a column with moment), which is where both values appear together:

> **IS 456 cl. 39.1(b):** for a section under combined axial load and bending where the neutral axis lies **outside** the section, the **maximum strain is 0.0035 minus 0.75 times the strain at the least compressed extreme fibre**.

> That expression **interpolates between the two limits** — reducing to **0.002 for pure axial** load (uniform strain) and **0.0035 for pure bending**. The code encodes exactly the reasoning above.

**The design stress values that go with them:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Concrete design strength** | **0.67 f_ck/1.5 = 0.447 f_ck** |
| **Steel design strength** | **0.87 f_y** |
| **Stress block: compressive force** | **0.36 f_ck b x_u** |
| **Centroid of the stress block** | **0.42 x_u** from the extreme fibre |

**The stress block shape:**

> **Parabolic up to a strain of 0.002, then RECTANGULAR (constant stress) to 0.0035.**

> **Notice that 0.002 is where the parabola ends** — it is the strain at which concrete reaches its peak stress. Beyond that the stress stays constant while the strain grows, which is the plastic plateau the flexural limit exploits.

> **So the two numbers are not independent: 0.002 is peak stress, 0.0035 is the useful limit of the plateau in bending.** That connection makes both easy to remember.

**The limiting neutral axis depths, which follow:**

| Steel | x_u,max/d | M_u,lim |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** | 0.148 f_ck b d² |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** | **0.138 f_ck b d²** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** | 0.133 f_ck b d² |

> Derived from **x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + ε_y)** — the concrete's flexural limit against the steel's yield strain. **Higher grade steel yields at a higher strain, so the neutral axis must be shallower** for it to yield before the concrete crushes.

> That is the whole basis of the **under-reinforced** requirement: **steel must yield first**, giving warning through large deflections and wide cracks, rather than the concrete crushing suddenly.

examTip.trap: **0.0035 is the BENDING value and 0.002 the AXIAL one.** The flexural figure is far more familiar, so it is the natural wrong answer — read which loading the question specifies.
examTip.trick: In bending the strain **varies across the depth**, so less-strained fibres restrain the extreme one and it can go further. In axial compression the **whole section peaks at once**, with nothing to redistribute to.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.002 is where the parabolic stress block ENDS; 0.0035 is the end of the rectangular plateau.** The two numbers are the same curve read at two points — which is why both are easy to hold together.

questions.stem: For radial shear in a two-hinged arch, where the tangent to the arch makes an angle θ with the horizontal, the radial shear is:
options: H cos θ + V sin θ
V cos θ + H sin θ
H cos θ − V sin θ
V cos θ − H sin θ
questions.solution:
**Radial shear Q = V cos θ − H sin θ.**

**The companion pair**, which must be learned together:

> **NORMAL THRUST N = V sin θ + H cos θ**
> **RADIAL SHEAR Q = V cos θ − H sin θ**

**Where they come from.** At any section of an arch the tangent makes an angle θ with the horizontal. The vertical shear **V** and horizontal thrust **H** are resolved into components **along** and **perpendicular** to that tangent:

| Direction | Component |
|---|---|
| **Along the tangent** (normal thrust — the axial force) | **V sin θ + H cos θ** |
| **Perpendicular to the tangent** (radial shear) | **V cos θ − H sin θ** |

> **The two expressions are the same pair of terms with the sine and cosine exchanged, and one sign reversed** — which is exactly what makes them easy to confuse and why all four permutations are offered.

**The check that settles it — take θ = 0** (at the crown, where the tangent is horizontal):

| Quantity | At θ = 0 |
|---|---|
| **Normal thrust** | **V(0) + H(1) = H** ✓ — at the crown the axial force **is** the horizontal thrust |
| **Radial shear** | **V(1) − H(0) = V** ✓ — at the crown the radial shear **is** the vertical shear |

> **Both reduce to exactly what they must at the crown.** Substituting θ = 0 takes five seconds and eliminates every wrong option, because the incorrect permutations give H where V belongs and vice versa.

**Why the arch is designed for normal thrust rather than shear:**

> An arch works predominantly in **AXIAL COMPRESSION**. The normal thrust is the dominant action; the radial shear and the bending moment are secondary, and in a well-shaped arch they are small.

> **The arch equation** shows why:

> **M_arch = M_beam − H y**

> The horizontal thrust **subtracts** from what the bending moment would otherwise be — and that subtraction is the entire structural virtue of an arch.

**For the FUNICULAR shape the subtraction is exact:**

| Loading | Ideal shape | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **UDL on the horizontal projection** | **PARABOLA** | **M = 0 everywhere** |
| **Self weight along the arch** | **CATENARY** | M = 0 everywhere |

> Which is why **masonry — unable to carry tension — spans so far as an arch and not at all as a beam.**

**The three arch types:**

| Arch | D_s | H found from |
|---|---|---|
| **Three-hinged** | **0 — determinate** | **Statics: H = M_crown/rise** |
| **Two-hinged** | **1** | **Strain energy** |
| **Fixed** | **3** | Full indeterminate analysis |

**And the two-hinged arch's sensitivities**, which the third hinge removes entirely:

| Effect | Two-hinged |
|---|---|
| **Temperature RISE** | **Increases** H |
| **Rib shortening** | Decreases H |
| **Abutment yielding (spread)** | **Decreases H substantially** |

> **A three-hinged arch is immune to all of them**, being determinate — which is the real reason for the third hinge, not the easier arithmetic.

examTip.trick: **Substitute θ = 0** (the crown, tangent horizontal). Radial shear must reduce to **V** and normal thrust to **H**. Only one option does each — five seconds, no recall.
examTip.trap: The two formulae are **the same terms with sin and cos exchanged and one sign flipped**, which is why all four permutations are offered. Learn them as a pair: **N = Vsinθ + Hcosθ, Q = Vcosθ − Hsinθ**.
examTip.mnemonic: **M_arch = M_beam − Hy** — the thrust subtracts the beam moment away entirely for the **funicular** shape (parabola under UDL, catenary under self weight). That is why masonry arches span and masonry beams do not.

questions.stem: A revised estimate is prepared when the original sanctioned detailed estimate exceeds by:
questions.solution:
**5%.**

> When the actual expenditure is expected to exceed the **sanctioned detailed estimate by more than 5%**, a **REVISED ESTIMATE** must be prepared and sanctioned before the excess is incurred.

**Why the threshold exists:**

> The sanction is a **financial authorisation**, not a prediction. Spending materially beyond it means spending money that was never approved — so the approving authority must be given the opportunity to reconsider.

> **The revised estimate must state the REASONS for the excess**, item by item, comparing the revised figures with the original. That comparison is the point of the document: it is an account to the sanctioning authority, not merely a new total.

**The types of estimate, in the order they occur:**

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary / rough cost** | Feasibility; obtain administrative approval | ±15–20% |
| **Plinth area** | From plinth area × rate | Approximate |
| **Cube rate** | From volume × rate | Approximate |
| **DETAILED estimate** | **Item-by-item from drawings**; obtain technical sanction | **±5%** |
| **REVISED estimate** | When the sanctioned amount is exceeded by **>5%**, or the rates change materially | — |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY estimate** | For **ADDITIONAL work** not in the original scope | — |
| Annual repair / maintenance | Recurring upkeep | — |
| Complete estimate | The whole project including all ancillaries | — |

**The distinction that is most often examined:**

> **REVISED estimate = the SAME work costing more.**
> **SUPPLEMENTARY estimate = ADDITIONAL work not originally included.**

> The two are constantly swapped, and the discriminator is simple: **has the scope changed, or only the cost?**

**What a detailed estimate contains:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Detailed measurement sheet** | Quantities from the drawings |
| **Abstract of cost** | Quantity × rate for each item |
| **Analysis of rates** | Materials, labour, plant, overheads and profit for each item |
| **Contingencies** | Usually **3–5%** |
| Work-charged establishment | Usually 1.5–2% |
| Specifications and drawings | — |

> **The ANALYSIS OF RATES is the substance of an estimate.** A rate is built up from the actual quantities of material and labour per unit of work, plus a percentage for overheads and profit — typically **10% contractor's profit** and **15% overheads** in Nepali practice.

**The measurement conventions** that most often cause disputes:

| Item | Convention |
|---|---|
| **Earthwork** | **Mean area or prismoidal formula** — the two differ, and which is specified matters |
| **Brickwork / concrete** | Cubic metres; **deductions for openings** above a stated size |
| **Plastering** | Square metres; specific rules for jambs and soffits |
| Reinforcement | Weight, from the bar bending schedule |

> **The deduction rules for openings are a classic source of dispute**, because they differ between codes and between items — and an unstated convention is where money is lost.

**The sequence of approvals** worth knowing: **administrative approval** (from the department that will use the work, based on the preliminary estimate) → **technical sanction** (from the competent engineering authority, based on the detailed estimate) → **expenditure sanction** → tender → work.

> **Technical sanction certifies that the estimate is structurally and financially sound** — it is an engineer's responsibility, not an administrator's, and it is why the detailed estimate must be accurate to about 5%.

examTip.trick: 5% is also the accuracy expected of a **detailed estimate** — so the threshold is simply "beyond the accuracy the estimate was supposed to have". The two 5% figures are the same idea.
examTip.trap: **REVISED = same work, more money. SUPPLEMENTARY = additional work.** The two are swapped constantly; the discriminator is whether the **scope** changed or only the **cost**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Administrative approval → technical sanction → expenditure sanction → tender.** Technical sanction is the **engineer's** certification that the estimate is sound, which is why it needs ±5% accuracy.

questions.stem: The power generated by a turbine under unit head and unit discharge condition is:
questions.solution:
**Unit power.**

**The unit quantities.** These express a turbine's performance **reduced to a head of 1 metre**, so that a machine tested at one head can be compared with, or predicted at, another.

| Unit quantity | Definition | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **UNIT POWER** | Power under **unit head** | **P_u = P/H^{3/2}** |
| **UNIT SPEED** | Speed under unit head | **N_u = N/√H** |
| **UNIT DISCHARGE** | Discharge under unit head | **Q_u = Q/√H** |

> The exponents follow directly from the physics: **Q ∝ √H** (velocity goes as √H), **N ∝ √H**, and **P = ρgQHη ∝ H × √H = H^{3/2}**.

> **Knowing where the exponents come from means never mis-remembering them.**

**Their use:** given a turbine's performance at one head, the unit quantities predict it at another:

> **N₂ = N₁√(H₂/H₁)**, **Q₂ = Q₁√(H₂/H₁)**, **P₂ = P₁(H₂/H₁)^{3/2}**

**SPECIFIC SPEED is a different concept entirely**, and it is the near-miss here:

> **N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}**

> It is the speed of a **geometrically similar turbine** producing **unit power under unit head**. Its purpose is **not** to predict performance at another head but to **SELECT THE TYPE of machine**:

| Turbine | N_s | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **Pelton** (single jet) | **10 – 35** | **High — above ~250 m** |
| Pelton (multi-jet) | 35 – 60 | — |
| **Francis** | **60 – 300** | **Medium — 30 to 250 m** |
| **Kaplan** | **300 – 1000** | **Low — below ~30 m** |

> **Specific speed rises as head falls.** It is a **single number combining head, discharge and speed**, and it is what actually selects the machine — which is why it is the most important of these quantities and the one most likely to be confused with the others.

**The distinction in one line:**

> **Unit quantities scale ONE machine to another head. Specific speed selects WHICH TYPE of machine.**

**Why "horse power" is wrong:** it is simply a **unit of power** (1 hp = 746 W), not a defined turbine parameter at all. It is offered as an option because it contains the word "power".

**The power equation** the whole subject rests on:

> **P = ρ g Q H η**

> with **η ≈ 0.85 – 0.90** for a good turbine–generator set. **Q comes from the flow duration curve; H from the topography.**

**And the efficiency comparison** worth carrying:

| Turbine | Part-load behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Pelton** | **Excellent at part load** — individual jets can be shut off |
| **Kaplan** | **Excellent** — **double regulation** (guide vanes AND runner blades) |
| **Francis** | **Poor below about 40%** of full load — fixed runner blades |
| Propeller (fixed blade) | **Very poor** off design point |

> **Kaplan's double regulation is what gives it a flat efficiency curve**, and it is the reason a Kaplan is preferred to a fixed-blade propeller despite costing more — a low-head plant sees widely varying flows, and a machine that loses efficiency off design would waste most of them.

examTip.trick: Derive the exponents rather than memorising: **Q ∝ √H, N ∝ √H, and P = ρgQHη ∝ H^{3/2}.** So unit power divides by **H^{3/2}** and unit speed and discharge by **√H**.
examTip.trap: **Specific speed is the near-miss and a different concept.** Unit quantities **scale one machine to another head**; specific speed (**N√P/H^{5/4}**) **selects which TYPE** of machine to use.
examTip.mnemonic: **Specific speed rises as head falls: Pelton 10–35, Francis 60–300, Kaplan 300–1000.** And **Kaplan's double regulation** — guide vanes plus runner blades — is what keeps its efficiency flat at part load.

questions.stem: The length visible to a driver at any instance of time is called:
questions.solution:
**Sight distance** — the general term.

> The other options name **particular kinds** of sight distance, or a non-standard term. **Sight distance is the umbrella; the rest are cases of it.**

**The types of sight distance:**

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Stopping sight distance (SSD)** | The distance needed to **stop safely** before an obstruction. **The absolute minimum on every road** |
| **Overtaking sight distance (OSD)** | The distance needed to **overtake safely** on a two-lane two-way road |
| **Intermediate sight distance (ISD)** | **= 2 × SSD**, where full OSD cannot be provided |
| **Head light sight distance** | The distance lit by headlights at night — governs **VALLEY curves** |
| Intersection sight distance | Visibility at a junction |

**Stopping sight distance:**

> **SSD = v t + v²/(2 g f)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **v t** | **Reaction distance** — **t = 2.5 s** (IRC) |
| **v²/(2gf)** | **Braking distance** |
| **f** | Longitudinal friction, **0.35 to 0.40** |

> **On a gradient the friction term becomes f ± 0.01n** — **plus** for an upgrade (which helps stopping) and **minus** for a downgrade.

> **A downgrade lengthens the required SSD substantially**, which is a real design issue on hill roads, where steep descending gradients and sharp curves often coincide.

**Overtaking sight distance:**

> **OSD = d₁ + d₂ + d₃** — the distances travelled during **perception**, **the overtaking manoeuvre**, and **by the opposing vehicle**.

> **OSD is very much longer than SSD** — of the order of **five times**. For 80 km/h, SSD is about 120 m while OSD is about 470 m.

> **That is why overtaking zones cannot be provided continuously**, and why roads are marked with overtaking-prohibited sections rather than the reverse.

**What each curve type is governed by** — the pairing that is most often examined:

| Curve | Governed by |
|---|---|
| **SUMMIT (crest) curve** | **Stopping or overtaking sight distance** — the road surface itself obstructs the view |
| **VALLEY (sag) curve** | **HEADLIGHT sight distance** at night, and **comfort** (centrifugal acceleration) |

> **A summit curve is a daytime sight problem; a valley curve is a NIGHT-TIME headlight problem.** By day a valley curve has unobstructed visibility — the difficulty appears only after dark, when the headlight beam (**1.5° upward, from a height of 0.75 m**) limits how far ahead the driver can see.

> **Getting that pairing the wrong way round is a standard error**, and it matters because the two curves are designed by completely different criteria.

**The design object heights** (IRC):

| Height | Value |
|---|---|
| **Driver's eye** | **1.2 m** |
| **Object (for SSD)** | **0.15 m** |
| **Object (for OSD)** | **1.2 m** — another vehicle |
| Headlight | 0.75 m, beam 1° upward |

**And the practical point:**

> **Sight distance is obstructed on the INSIDE of a horizontal curve** — by cut slopes, walls, buildings and vegetation. The required **set-back distance** must be cleared and **kept clear**, which is a maintenance obligation as much as a design one.

> **Vegetation growing back into the set-back area is one of the commonest causes of degraded safety on an otherwise adequate road.**

examTip.trick: **Sight distance is the umbrella term**; the other options are particular kinds of it. When one option is the general category and the rest are its members, the category is usually the answer.
examTip.trap: **SUMMIT curves are governed by SIGHT distance (daytime); VALLEY curves by HEADLIGHT distance (night).** A sag curve looks unobstructed by day — its problem appears only after dark.
examTip.mnemonic: **SSD = vt + v²/2gf with t = 2.5 s, f = 0.35–0.40**, and on a downgrade use **f − 0.01n**, which lengthens it. **OSD is about FIVE times SSD** — which is why overtaking zones are the exception, not the rule.

questions.stem: The exhausted permutit is generally regenerated by percolating through it a solution of:
questions.solution:
**Sodium chloride** — a **10% brine solution**.

**How the permutit (zeolite) process works.** Permutit is a **sodium zeolite**, **Na₂Al₂Si₂O₈·xH₂O**, which exchanges its sodium for the calcium and magnesium that cause hardness:

> **Na₂Z + Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaZ + 2NaHCO₃**

> The hardness ions are **held on the zeolite** and sodium goes into the water. Eventually all the sodium is used up — the zeolite is **exhausted**, having become **CaZ**.

**Regeneration reverses the exchange:**

> **CaZ + 2NaCl → Na₂Z + CaCl₂**

> Flushing with **concentrated brine** drives the reaction backwards by sheer **mass action** — the huge excess of sodium displaces the calcium, which is washed to waste as calcium chloride.

> **Common salt is used because it is cheap and abundant**, and because sodium is the ion that must be restored. **Calcium, magnesium or barium chloride would be self-defeating** — they would deposit the very ions the process exists to remove.

> That reasoning eliminates the three wrong options without any recall.

**The process's characteristics:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hardness achieved** | **ZERO — complete removal** |
| Applies to | **Both carbonate and non-carbonate** hardness |
| Operation | Simple, compact, no sludge |
| **Limitation** | Water must be **low in turbidity** — suspended matter clogs the bed |
| **Limitation** | **Iron and manganese foul the zeolite** irreversibly |
| **Drawback** | **Raises the SODIUM content** of the water |

**Two consequences of that last point:**

> **Zero hardness water is CORROSIVE.** It has no calcium to deposit the protective CaCO₃ film that lines and protects a pipe. **Softened water is therefore usually BLENDED back with raw water** to leave a residual hardness of about **75–100 mg/l** — deliberately, not by omission.

> **And the added sodium matters for people on restricted-sodium diets** and for irrigation, where a high **sodium adsorption ratio (SAR)** damages soil structure.

**Comparison with the LIME–SODA process:**

| | **LIME–SODA** | **ZEOLITE (permutit)** |
|---|---|---|
| Achieves | **Residual 25–40 mg/l** | **ZERO hardness** |
| **Sludge** | **Large volumes** — a real disposal problem | **None** |
| Turbidity tolerance | **Handles turbid water** | Needs clear water |
| Chemicals | Lime and soda ash | **Salt only** |
| Suits | **Large works, high hardness** | Small works, clear water |

> **Lime–soda produces sludge; zeolite produces brine.** Both are disposal problems, but of quite different kinds — and the choice between the processes often turns on which waste is easier to handle at the site.

**Why hardness is removed at all:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCALE** in boilers and pipes | Wastes fuel; can cause boiler failure |
| **Wastes soap** | Forms scum instead of lather |
| Fabric damage in laundering | — |

> **Hardness is not a health hazard** — indeed some evidence suggests hard water is mildly beneficial. **It is an economic nuisance**, which is why the limit (500 mg/l) is so much more generous than the health-based parameters.

**The modern successor** is **ION EXCHANGE with synthetic resins**, which works on the same principle but can remove **all cations and anions** — producing **demineralised water** for boiler feed and industrial use.

examTip.trick: Reason it out: the process removes **calcium and magnesium** and must restore **sodium**. Regenerating with calcium or magnesium chloride would put back the very ions being removed — so only NaCl can be right.
examTip.trap: **Zero-hardness water is CORROSIVE** — no calcium means no protective CaCO₃ film. Softened water is deliberately **blended back** to leave 75–100 mg/l, which looks like incomplete treatment but is intentional.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lime–soda leaves 25–40 mg/l and makes SLUDGE; zeolite gives ZERO hardness and makes BRINE.** Both are disposal problems — the choice often turns on which waste the site can handle.

questions.stem: A vacuum filter is most suitable for:
questions.solution:
**None of these.**

**Why each offered option fails:**

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| **High viscosity** | **The opposite is true.** Vacuum filtration suits **LOW viscosity** liquids. Viscous or sticky material **clogs the filter medium** and the flow rate collapses |
| **High vapour pressure** | **Also the opposite.** A vacuum **lowers the pressure**, so a liquid of high vapour pressure would **BOIL** in the filter, breaking the vacuum and stopping the process |
| Removal of fines from liquid | Too loose a description — a vacuum filter's purpose in wastewater practice is **DEWATERING SLUDGE**, that is, removing water from solids rather than fines from a liquid |

> **The first two options fail for the same underlying reason, in opposite directions**: a vacuum filter needs a liquid that **flows easily** and **does not vaporise under reduced pressure**. High viscosity defeats the first requirement; high vapour pressure defeats the second.

**What a vacuum filter actually does in wastewater treatment:**

> **SLUDGE DEWATERING.** A rotating drum covered with a filter medium (cloth or coiled springs) dips into a sludge tank. **A vacuum inside the drum draws water through the medium**, leaving a **cake of solids** on the surface, which is then scraped off.

| Stage | Action |
|---|---|
| **Cake formation** | Drum submerged; vacuum draws water through |
| **Cake drying** | Drum emerges; vacuum continues to pull air through the cake |
| **Cake discharge** | Vacuum released; the cake is scraped or blown off |

> **Typical result: sludge at 5% solids becomes a cake at 20–30% solids** — a large reduction in volume and therefore in disposal cost.

**Why dewatering matters so much:**

> **Sludge handling is often the largest single cost in a wastewater treatment plant** — sometimes more than the liquid treatment itself.
