> **Water is heavy and expensive to transport.** Reducing sludge from 5% to 25% solids cuts its **volume by 80%**, and that is a direct saving on every tanker load hauled away.

**The sludge treatment sequence:**

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Thickening** | Gravity or flotation — raises solids from ~1% to ~5% |
| **Stabilisation** | **Anaerobic or aerobic digestion** — destroys volatile solids, reduces odour and pathogens |
| **CONDITIONING** | **Chemicals (polymer, lime, ferric) to make the sludge release its water** |
| **DEWATERING** | Vacuum filter, **belt press**, **centrifuge**, filter press, drying beds |
| Disposal | Land application, landfill, incineration |

> **CONDITIONING is the step that makes dewatering possible.** Raw sludge holds water tenaciously in fine flocs and bound within cells; a **polymer coagulates it into larger flocs that release water freely**. Attempting to dewater unconditioned sludge gives very poor results whatever machine is used.

**Modern practice has largely replaced vacuum filters:**

| Device | Note |
|---|---|
| **BELT FILTER PRESS** | Continuous; lower energy; widely used |
| **CENTRIFUGE** | Compact, enclosed (good for odour), high energy |
| **Filter press** | Batch; produces the **driest cake (35–45%)** |
| **DRYING BEDS** | **Cheapest**; needs land, sun and dry weather |

> **For Nepal, drying beds remain attractive for small works** — no energy, no machinery, no imported spares — but they need **land and a dry season**, and they perform badly through the monsoon, which is exactly when the plant is most loaded.

examTip.trick: The first two options fail for **opposite reasons from the same cause**: a vacuum filter needs liquid that **flows easily** (so not viscous) and **does not boil under reduced pressure** (so not high vapour pressure).
examTip.trap: "None of these" is a genuine answer here, not a fallback. Two options state the **exact reverse** of the requirement — recognising that is the whole question.
examTip.mnemonic: **CONDITIONING is what makes dewatering work** — polymer coagulates fine flocs so they release water. And dewatering from 5% to 25% solids cuts sludge **volume by 80%**, which is where the cost saving lies.

questions.stem: The irrigation requirement depends on which of the following parameters?
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — crop, soil and climate together determine the irrigation requirement.

**How each enters the calculation:**

| Parameter | Influence |
|---|---|
| **CROP** | Sets the **crop coefficient K_c**, the **root depth**, the **growing season length**, and the **critical (kor) period** |
| **SOIL** | Sets the **water holding capacity** — field capacity, wilting point, and therefore the **available water** and the **irrigation interval** |
| **CLIMATE** | Sets the **reference evapotranspiration PET** — temperature, humidity, wind, sunshine — and the **effective rainfall** |

**The calculation chain:**

> **ET_crop = K_c × PET**

| Step | Quantity |
|---|---|
| **1** | **PET** from climate (Penman–Monteith, Blaney–Criddle) |
| **2** | × **K_c** for the crop and its growth stage → **ET_crop** |
| **3** | **Less effective rainfall** |
| **4** | Plus **leaching requirement** if salinity is a concern |
| **5** | ÷ **application efficiency** → field irrigation requirement |
| **6** | ÷ **conveyance efficiency** → **canal head discharge** |

> **Efficiencies MULTIPLY, never average.** Two stages at 70% give **49%** overall, so the water delivered at the head can be **1.5 to 2 times** what the crop actually consumes.

**Where the SOIL determines the schedule:**

| Soil property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Field capacity (FC)** | Water held **after free drainage** — the upper limit of available water |
| **Permanent wilting point (PWP)** | Water the plant **cannot extract** |
| **AVAILABLE water = FC − PWP** | What the crop can actually use |
| **Readily available water** | Usually about **50%** of available, before stress begins |

> **Irrigation interval = readily available water in the root zone ÷ daily consumptive use.**

| Soil | Available water | Irrigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Sandy** | **LOW** | **Frequent, small applications** |
| **Clayey** | **HIGH** | Infrequent, large applications |

> **A sandy soil does not need MORE water in total — it needs the same water MORE OFTEN**, because it cannot store a large reserve. Confusing frequency with quantity is a common error.

**And the PEAK, not the seasonal average, sizes the canal:**

> The system must deliver the **maximum demand occurring at any one time** across all the crops in the command — the **kor depth over the kor period**.

> **Outlet discharge factor = 8.64B/Δ**, using the kor values, gives the peak capacity directly.

**The application methods and their efficiencies:**

| Method | Application efficiency |
|---|---|
| **Surface (flood, furrow, border)** | **40 – 60%** |
| **Sprinkler** | **70 – 80%** |
| **DRIP** | **90 – 95%** |

> **Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone**, eliminating evaporation from the soil surface and deep percolation. It roughly **doubles the area served by a given supply** compared with flood irrigation.

> Its cost and its need for **clean, filtered water** are the constraints — a drip system clogs readily on silty Himalayan water without proper filtration, which is a real practical obstacle in Nepal.

examTip.trick: Each factor enters at a different point: **climate gives PET, crop gives K_c, soil gives the storage and hence the INTERVAL.** All three are genuinely needed, which is why "all of the above" is correct.
examTip.trap: **A sandy soil needs the same water MORE OFTEN, not more water.** It has less storage, so the interval shortens — confusing frequency with quantity is a standard error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY** — two 70% stages give 49%, so head discharge is often double the crop's need. **Drip (90–95%) roughly doubles the area served** versus flood (40–60%), if the water can be filtered.

questions.stem: A clay is ……… if it has been subjected to a pressure in excess of its present pressure.
questions.solution:
**Over-consolidated.**

**The definitions, in terms of the preconsolidation pressure σ′_c** (the maximum effective stress the soil has ever experienced):

| State | Condition | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **NORMALLY consolidated (NC)** | **σ′_c = σ′₀** | The present stress **is** the greatest ever experienced |
| **OVER-consolidated (OC)** | **σ′_c > σ′₀** | The soil has been **more heavily loaded in the past** |
| Under-consolidated | σ′_c < σ′₀ | Still consolidating under its present load — a recent fill or hydraulic deposit |

> **OCR = σ′_c/σ′₀** — the over-consolidation ratio. OCR = 1 is normally consolidated; OCR > 1 is over-consolidated.

**What causes over-consolidation:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **EROSION** of overlying soil | The classic mechanism — the load was there and has gone |
| **Melting of an ICE SHEET** | Glacial loading removed |
| **Desiccation** — drying and shrinkage | Creates high suctions equivalent to a large load |
| **Fluctuating water table** | Lowering it raised σ′ temporarily |
| Ageing / secondary compression | Produces apparent over-consolidation |

> **The load need not still exist — only to have existed.** That is the essential idea: the soil **remembers** its greatest past stress, and its stiffness reflects that memory.

**Why it matters enormously in practice:**

| | **NC clay** | **OC clay** |
|---|---|---|
| Compressibility | **HIGH** — uses **C_c** | **LOW** — uses **C_r ≈ C_c/5 to C_c/10** |
| Settlement under new load | **Large** | **Small**, until σ′_c is exceeded |
| Strength | Lower | Higher |
| Behaviour in shear | **Contracts**; positive pore pressure | **DILATES**; negative pore pressure |

> **The recompression index C_r is five to ten times smaller than C_c.** So an over-consolidated clay settles far less — **provided the new stress stays below σ′_c**.

**The settlement calculation must therefore SPLIT at σ′_c:**

> **If σ′₀ + Δσ ≤ σ′_c**: use **C_r** throughout — small settlement.
> **If σ′₀ + Δσ > σ′_c**: use **C_r up to σ′_c** and **C_c beyond it** — the settlement jumps.

> **Using C_c throughout for an over-consolidated clay can OVERESTIMATE the settlement five-fold**, and buy a piled foundation that was never needed. Using C_r throughout when the load exceeds σ′_c does the reverse, and is dangerous.

> **Finding σ′_c is therefore among the most valuable outputs of a site investigation** — it is obtained from the **oedometer** e–log σ′ curve by **CASAGRANDE's construction**.

**The dilation point** is worth carrying too:

> A **heavily over-consolidated clay DILATES when sheared** — it tries to expand. Under **undrained** conditions that generates **NEGATIVE pore pressure**, which temporarily **raises** the effective stress and the strength.

> **As those negative pressures dissipate over time, the strength FALLS.** This is precisely why **a CUTTING in stiff clay is critical in the LONG term**, sometimes failing years after construction — while an **embankment** (loading, contracting) is critical in the **short term** and gains strength thereafter.

> **Getting that pairing backwards is a genuine design error**, and it is one of the most frequently examined points in soil mechanics.

examTip.trick: The soil **remembers its greatest past stress**. If it has carried more than it carries now — through erosion, ice, or desiccation — it is over-consolidated, and it is much stiffer for it.
examTip.trap: **Split the settlement calculation at σ′_c**: C_r below, C_c above. Using C_c throughout can **overestimate settlement five-fold** and buy piles you never needed; using C_r throughout is dangerous.
examTip.mnemonic: **Embankment → SHORT term critical (contracts, then gains strength). CUTTING in stiff clay → LONG term critical (dilates, negative pore pressures dissipate, strength falls).** Reversing that pairing is a real design error.

questions.stem: What is the function of a surge tank?
questions.solution:
**It relieves water hammer** — reducing the pressure surge in the conduit.

**What a surge tank is.** An **open vertical shaft or chamber** connected to the pressure conduit, **as close to the powerhouse as possible**, with a free water surface open to the atmosphere.

**Its functions:**

| Function | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **RELIEVES water hammer** | It **REFLECTS the pressure wave**, shortening the conduit length that must resist it |
| **Provides water on load increase** | The tank empties into the penstock while the tunnel flow accelerates |
| **Absorbs water on load rejection** | The decelerating tunnel flow discharges into the tank instead of surging the penstock |
| **Improves governing stability** | Reduces the water column that must be accelerated |
| Reduces water level fluctuations | After load changes |

**The key idea — why its POSITION matters so much:**

> **A surge tank does not absorb the water hammer wave; it REFLECTS it.**

> The pressure wave from a governor closure travels up the penstock, reaches the surge tank's **free surface**, and is reflected. **Only the length of conduit BELOW the tank experiences the full surge.**

> So **placing the tank as close to the powerhouse as possible minimises that length** — which is the whole basis of its siting. A surge tank far up the tunnel protects the tunnel but leaves the penstock exposed.

**The two phenomena, which must be kept apart:**

| | **WATER HAMMER** | **SURGE** |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Elastic pressure WAVE** | **Rigid column mass OSCILLATION** |
| Speed | **Very fast — c ≈ 1000 m/s** | Slow |
| Period | Milliseconds to seconds | **Minutes** |
| Where | **In the PENSTOCK** (below the tank) | **In the TUNNEL** and surge tank |
| Magnitude | **Δp = ρcΔV** — hundreds of metres of head | Water level rise and fall |

> **The surge tank converts a fast elastic wave problem into a slow mass oscillation problem** — and a slow oscillation is far easier to accommodate, because the tank simply has to be tall enough.

**The Joukowsky relation** and the timing criterion:

> **Δp = ρ c ΔV** for **sudden** closure — where "sudden" means faster than **2L/c**, the wave's round trip.

| Closure time | Result |
|---|---|
| **Faster than 2L/c** | **Full Joukowsky pressure**, however fast it actually is |
| **Slower than 2L/c** | **Greatly reduced** surge |

> **This is why the governor closure timing and the surge protection are designed together**, and why a Pelton uses a **deflector** — swinging across the jet instantly for fast load rejection while the **spear valve closes slowly**, giving fast response without the surge.

**Types of surge tank:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | A plain shaft |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE** | A throttle at the base — **damps the oscillation faster** |
| **Differential (Johnson)** | An inner riser plus an outer tank — rapid response **and** good damping |
| Expansion chamber | Extra volume at top and bottom for extreme levels |

> **The restricted orifice is the common choice** because it damps the oscillation without the complexity of a differential tank — the throttle dissipates energy each time water passes through it.

**Design requirements:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Height** | Must contain the **maximum upsurge** without overflowing, and the **minimum downsurge** without admitting air to the tunnel |
| **THOMA's criterion** | The cross-sectional area must **exceed a minimum** for the oscillation to be **STABLE and damped** |
| Location | **As close to the powerhouse as possible** |

> **Thoma's criterion is the one that must not be violated**: below the critical area, the surge oscillation is **UNSTABLE and grows** instead of decaying. An undersized surge tank is worse than none, because it can amplify what it was built to damp.

examTip.trick: A surge tank **REFLECTS the pressure wave at its free surface**, so only the conduit **below** it feels the full surge. That is why it is placed **as close to the powerhouse as possible**.
examTip.trap: **Water hammer and surge are different phenomena**: a fast **elastic wave** (Δp = ρcΔV, milliseconds, in the penstock) versus a slow **mass oscillation** (minutes, in the tunnel). The tank converts one into the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **Closure slower than 2L/c greatly reduces the surge; faster gives the full Joukowsky value however fast.** And **THOMA's criterion** sets a minimum tank area — below it the oscillation grows instead of damping.

questions.stem: What should be done to avoid the friction (sliding) failure of a dam?
questions.solution:
**Provide anchorage at the bottom** — anchoring the dam into its foundation.

**Why sliding occurs.** A gravity dam resists the horizontal water thrust by **friction and cohesion at its base**. Sliding failure occurs when:

> **Horizontal force P > friction available**

> **Factor of safety against sliding = μ(ΣV − U)/ΣH**

> where **μ** is the coefficient of friction, **ΣV** the vertical load, **U** the uplift, and **ΣH** the horizontal thrust.

> The more complete measure is the **SHEAR FRICTION FACTOR**, which includes the cohesion at the interface:

> **SFF = (μ(ΣV − U) + c·B)/ΣH ≥ 3 to 5**

**Why anchorage at the BOTTOM:**

> Sliding occurs **at the base** — on the dam–foundation contact, or on a weak plane within the foundation rock. **The resistance must therefore be added exactly there.**

> **Anchor bars or cables grouted into the foundation rock** tie the dam to the rock beneath, adding shear resistance directly across the potential sliding plane.

> **Anchorage at the TOP would do nothing** — there is no sliding plane at the top of a dam, and a tie there has no mechanism by which to resist a base failure. That is why option (b) is wrong, and it is a good check on whether the failure mode is understood.

**Why decreasing the base width is exactly wrong:**

> A **narrower base** means **less weight**, therefore **less friction**, and **less cohesive contact area** — sliding resistance falls on every count.

> Option (a) is the **precise reverse** of what helps. Option (d), increasing the base width, genuinely **does** improve sliding resistance and is a real measure — but the question asks for the anchorage answer, and the source keys (c).

**The full set of measures against sliding:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **ANCHOR bars/cables into the foundation** | Adds shear resistance at the plane |
| **KEY or shear key** in the foundation | A concrete plug cast into a trench cut in the rock |
| **STEPPING the base** | Presents a **series of horizontal surfaces**, raising the shear resistance |
| **Sloping the base upstream** | The thrust must then push the dam **uphill** |
| **Increasing the base width** | More weight, more friction |
| **DRAINAGE to reduce UPLIFT** | **Raises the effective ΣV directly** — often the most effective of all |
| Foundation treatment / grouting | Improves μ and c |

> **The stepped base is the measure this paper's own Q51 asks about** — it exists to **increase the shear strength at the base and at the joints**, and to improve the bond between dam and rock.

**Why DRAINAGE deserves particular emphasis:**

> Uplift **U subtracts from ΣV** in the sliding formula. **Reducing uplift therefore increases the sliding resistance directly**, with no additional concrete at all.

> **A drainage gallery with relief holes is typically more effective at reducing uplift than the grout curtain is** — grouting reduces **flow**, but drainage reduces **PRESSURE**, and it is pressure that threatens the dam.

> The scale of the effect: with uplift ignored, an elementary gravity profile needs a base of about **0.65H**; with full uplift, about **0.85H** — a **30% larger dam**. That difference measures what uplift costs, and what controlling it saves.

**The four stability checks for a gravity dam:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **No tension** (at the heel) | Resultant within the **middle third** |
| **Sliding (shear friction factor)** | **≥ 3 to 5** |
| **Overturning** | FoS ≥ 1.5 |
| **Compressive stress** | Within the allowable for concrete and rock |

> **In practice sliding usually governs before overturning** for a gravity dam — the section that satisfies sliding almost always satisfies overturning comfortably. That is why so much design attention goes to the base and its treatment.

examTip.trick: Sliding happens **at the base**, so the resistance must be added **there**. Anchorage at the **top** has no sliding plane to act on — which is what makes option (b) clearly wrong.
examTip.trap: Option (a) is the **exact reverse** of what helps — a narrower base gives less weight, less friction and less contact area. Both (a) and (d) are about base width, and only one direction helps.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reducing UPLIFT raises sliding resistance directly**, since U subtracts from ΣV. **Grouting cuts FLOW; drainage cuts PRESSURE** — and full uplift makes the section about 30% wider, which is what the drainage gallery saves.

questions.stem: Steel is preferred over other materials in reinforcement because:
options: It is cheapest and good in strength
The coefficient of thermal expansion of steel and concrete is almost same
questions.solution:
**Because the coefficient of thermal expansion of steel and concrete is almost the same.**

**Why this is the decisive property.** All four options are true statements about steel, but **only one identifies a property that no substitute could easily replicate**, and whose absence would make reinforced concrete impossible.

> **Steel: α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C**
> **Concrete: α ≈ 10–12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C**

> **They are close enough that temperature changes do not destroy the bond between them.**

**What would happen if they differed:**

> Every temperature change would cause the two materials to expand by **different amounts**. The bond would be broken by **internal stresses at every daily and seasonal cycle**, and the composite would progressively **delaminate**.

> **Reinforced concrete works as a composite only because the two components move together.** A material stronger and cheaper than steel but with a different thermal coefficient would be useless as reinforcement — which is exactly why this property, and not strength or cost, is the answer.

**The other essential properties**, which the distractors correctly name:

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **High TENSILE strength** | Concrete's tensile strength is only **10–15%** of its compressive — steel supplies what concrete lacks |
| **Good BOND** | **Deformed (ribbed) bars** develop bond mechanically, not just by adhesion |
| **Ductility** | Allows **warning before failure** and permits **moment redistribution** |
| **Alkaline protection** | **Concrete's high pH (~13) PASSIVATES the steel**, protecting it from corrosion |
| Availability and cost | Real, but not distinguishing |

**The alkaline protection point is worth understanding**, because it explains the durability rules:

> Fresh concrete is **strongly alkaline (pH ~13)**, which forms a **passive oxide film** on the steel that prevents corrosion. **Steel in sound concrete does not rust.**

> **CARBONATION** destroys that protection: atmospheric CO₂ penetrates the cover and **reduces the pH to around 9**, depassivating the steel. **CHLORIDES** (from de-icing salts or marine exposure) break down the film locally, causing pitting.

> **Once the steel corrodes, rust occupies 2–4 times the volume of the original steel**, and the expansion **spalls the cover off** — exposing more steel and accelerating the process.

> **That is why COVER is the single most important durability provision**, and why it is specified by **exposure condition** rather than by structural need: **20 mm** mild, **30 mm** moderate, **45 mm** severe, **50 mm** very severe, **75 mm** extreme.

**And why cover and concrete grade are specified together:**

> **A thick cover of permeable concrete protects nothing.** IS 456 therefore pairs each exposure class with **both** a minimum cover **and** a minimum grade and maximum water–cement ratio — because the **permeability of the cover matters as much as its thickness**.

**Deformed bars and bond:**

> **Ribbed bars develop bond MECHANICALLY** — the ribs bear against the concrete — which is far more reliable than the adhesion and friction a plain round bar depends on. That is why **development lengths are shorter for deformed bars**, and why plain bars are effectively obsolete for main reinforcement.

> **Development length L_d = φσ_s/(4τ_bd)**, and it must be available from the section where the bar is fully stressed. **A bar that cannot develop its stress is not carrying the force the calculation assumed** — one of the commonest detailing failures.

examTip.trick: All four options are **true**, so the question asks which is **decisive**. Matching thermal expansion (both ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶/°C) is the one property no substitute could easily replicate — without it the composite would delaminate every temperature cycle.
examTip.trap: Strength and cost are real advantages but **not distinguishing** — plenty of materials are strong and cheap. The thermal match is what makes the composite possible at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Concrete's alkalinity (pH ~13) PASSIVATES the steel** — steel in sound concrete does not rust. **Carbonation** drops the pH to ~9 and depassivates it; rust then occupies **2–4× the volume** and spalls the cover off.

questions.stem: A beam is said to be continuous if it is:
options: Fixed at one end and free at the other end
Supported on more than two supports
questions.solution:
**Supported on more than two supports.**

**The definition.** A **continuous beam** runs **without interruption over three or more supports**, so that it is **statically indeterminate** and its spans interact.

> Each of the other options describes a **different beam type**:

| Option | Beam type |
|---|---|
| Fixed at both ends | **FIXED beam** |
| Fixed at one end, free at the other | **CANTILEVER** |
| Extending beyond the support | **OVERHANGING beam** |

> **All four are real beam types**, which makes this a straightforward test of definitions rather than of reasoning.

**The degree of indeterminacy:**

> For a continuous beam on **n simple supports** with one pin: **D_s = n − 2**.

> A three-span beam on four supports is indeterminate to the **second degree**.

**Why continuity is worth having:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **SMALLER moments** | The support moment relieves the span moment |
| **Smaller deflections** | Continuity stiffens the beam considerably |
| **Less material** | Shallower sections for the same span |
| **REDUNDANCY** | An alternative load path if one section is damaged |

> **Compare a UDL on a single simple span with the same load on a continuous beam:**

| Beam | Maximum span moment |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **wL²/8** |
| **Continuous** (interior span) | About **wL²/12 to wL²/16** |

> **A substantial saving** — which is why continuous construction dominates in concrete, where continuity is achieved simply by running the reinforcement through.

**The costs of continuity:**

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **SETTLEMENT sensitivity** | A support that settles induces **large moments** throughout |
| **Temperature stresses** | The beam cannot expand freely |
| More complex analysis | Indeterminate |
| **HOGGING moments at supports** | Tension in the **TOP** — needs top steel there |

> **The settlement sensitivity is the serious one.** In a determinate structure a settling support causes no stress at all — the beam simply follows it. In a continuous beam it induces bending moments that can be comparable with the load effects.

> **This is why continuous beams need reliable foundations**, and why a continuous structure on compressible soil may need to be articulated with joints instead.

**The detailing consequence, which is where errors occur:**

> **Sagging in the span → tension at the BOTTOM → main steel in the bottom.**
> **HOGGING over the support → tension at the TOP → main steel in the TOP.**

> **A continuous beam therefore needs top steel over its supports**, extending far enough each side to cover the hogging region. **Omitting or curtailing it too early is one of the commonest and most serious detailing failures in reinforced concrete.**

**PATTERN LOADING** is the other essential point:

> The **maximum span moment** and the **maximum support moment** occur under **DIFFERENT arrangements of live load**:

| For maximum | Load |
|---|---|
| **Span moment** | **Alternate spans** loaded |
| **Support moment** | **Both spans ADJACENT to that support** loaded |

> **Analysing only the all-spans-loaded case UNDERESTIMATES both maxima**, and it is a real error — the design must envelope all the patterns, not just the obvious one.

**Moment redistribution** is the compensating advantage: because continuous beams are **ductile and indeterminate**, IS 456 permits up to **30% redistribution** of the elastic moments — allowing the designer to relieve congested support regions by accepting more moment in the span.

examTip.trick: All four options name **real beam types** — fixed, cantilever, overhanging, continuous. This is a definitions question, so match each description to its name rather than reasoning about behaviour.
examTip.trap: **PATTERN LOADING**: maximum span moment needs **alternate** spans loaded; maximum support moment needs **both adjacent** spans loaded. Analysing only the all-loaded case underestimates both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hogging over supports means tension in the TOP** — so a continuous beam needs top steel there, extended far enough. Curtailing it too early is among the commonest serious detailing failures.

questions.stem: The bottom portion of a concrete or masonry gravity dam is usually stepped in order to:
options: increase overturning resistance of the dam
questions.solution:
**To increase the shear strength** at the base and at the joints.

**Why stepping helps.** A flat base offers a **single continuous plane** on which the dam could slide. **Stepping presents a series of horizontal surfaces separated by vertical faces:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Increased shear strength** | Sliding must **shear through concrete or rock**, not merely slip along a plane |
| **Better BOND** with the foundation | More interlocking surface between dam and rock |
| **Interlocking** | The vertical faces bear against the rock, providing mechanical resistance |

> **A flat plane can slip; a stepped one must be sheared or broken.** That is the whole idea, and it is the same principle as a **shear key** — providing mechanical interlock rather than relying on friction alone.

**Where it fits in the sliding checks:**

> **Shear friction factor SFF = (μ(ΣV − U) + c·B)/ΣH ≥ 3 to 5**

> Stepping raises the **c·B** term — the **cohesion/shear strength** contribution — rather than the friction term. That is precisely why the keyed answer is **shear strength** and not **frictional resistance**.

> **Option (d) is the well-made near-miss**: increasing friction would require more weight or a rougher surface, not steps. **Stepping works by forcing shear rather than by raising μ.**

**The full set of measures against sliding:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Stepped base** | **Shear strength and bond** |
| **Shear KEY** in the foundation | A concrete plug in a trench cut in the rock |
| **Anchor bars/cables** into the foundation | Direct shear resistance across the plane |
| Sloping the base upstream | The thrust must push the dam **uphill** |
| Increasing base width | More weight, more friction |
| **DRAINAGE to reduce uplift** | **Raises the effective ΣV directly** |

**The forces on a gravity dam:**

| Force | Note |
|---|---|
| **Self weight W** | The **stabilising** force — a gravity dam resists by weight alone |
| **Water pressure P** | **γH²/2 per metre**, acting at **H/3 above the base** |
| **UPLIFT U** | Acts **upward** on the base — **reduces the effective weight** |
| Silt pressure | Behind the dam |
| **Earthquake** | Inertia **plus hydrodynamic** pressure (Westergaard) |
| Ice, wave, wind | Usually minor |

**UPLIFT is the force that most often decides the section:**

> Water penetrating the foundation and the dam–rock contact exerts an **upward pressure over the base**, reducing the effective weight — **and weight is the only thing holding a gravity dam in place.**

> **Uplift was not understood in early dam engineering, and several nineteenth-century failures are attributed to it.**

**The remedies, and why drainage beats grouting:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **GROUT CURTAIN** near the heel | **Reduces SEEPAGE** by sealing the rock |
| **DRAINAGE GALLERY with relief holes** | **RELIEVES the PRESSURE** by giving water a low-pressure escape |

> **Grouting reduces FLOW; drainage reduces PRESSURE — and it is pressure that threatens the dam.** A well-drained foundation can cut the uplift diagram to a fraction of its undrained value, which is why the drainage gallery is typically the more effective of the two.

**The scale of what uplift costs:**

> The elementary gravity profile has base width **B = H/√(S_c − c)**. With **uplift ignored** (c = 0) and S_c = 2.4, **B ≈ 0.65H**; with **full uplift** (c = 1), **B ≈ 0.85H**.

> **A 30% larger dam** — which is a direct measure of what controlling uplift is worth.

examTip.trick: **A flat plane can SLIP; a stepped one must be SHEARED.** Stepping raises the **cohesion (c·B)** term in the shear friction factor, not the friction term.
examTip.trap: **"Increase frictional resistance" is the near-miss.** Friction depends on weight and μ; stepping works by **forcing shear through material** rather than by raising μ. Both options are about sliding, but by different mechanisms.
examTip.mnemonic: **GROUT cuts FLOW; DRAINAGE cuts PRESSURE — and pressure is what threatens the dam.** Full uplift makes the elementary profile about **30% wider** (0.85H against 0.65H), which measures what the drainage gallery saves.

questions.stem: The daily average traffic calculated based on a 30-day survey in 365 days is:
questions.solution:
**ADT — Average Daily Traffic.**

**The distinction that this question turns on:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **AADT** — Annual Average Daily Traffic | Total volume for a **FULL YEAR ÷ 365** |
| **ADT** — Average Daily Traffic | Average over a period **SHORTER than a year** — a season, a month, a week, or a specified number of days |
| **AAWT** — Annual Average Weekday Traffic | Full year, **weekdays only** ÷ 260 |
| **AWT** — Average Weekday Traffic | A shorter period, weekdays only |

> **The word "ANNUAL" is the discriminator.** A count of only **30 days** cannot be an *annual* average, however it is scaled — so **AADT and AAWT are both excluded** by the survey duration alone.

> That leaves **ADT** and **AWT**, and since the question says nothing about restricting to weekdays, **ADT** is correct.

**Why the distinction matters practically:**

> **Traffic varies systematically** — by hour of day, by day of week, and by season. A 30-day count captures a particular slice of that variation and **cannot by itself represent the year.**

| Variation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Seasonal** | Festival periods, harvest, monsoon; tourist routes vary enormously |
| **Weekly** | Weekday commuting versus weekend leisure |
| **Hourly** | Morning and evening peaks |

> **In Nepal the seasonal effect is very large** — the monsoon suppresses travel on many hill roads, and festival periods produce extreme peaks. A count taken in either window would badly misrepresent the year.

**Converting a short count to AADT:**

> **AADT = ADT × seasonal adjustment factor × day-of-week factor**

> These factors come from **permanent count stations** operating year-round, which is why a road authority maintains a few continuous counters alongside many short-duration ones.

**Why AADT matters:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pavement design** | Traffic loading in **msa** (million standard axles) derives from AADT |
| **Capacity and level of service** | — |
| **Economic appraisal** | Vehicle operating cost savings depend on volume |
| Road classification and priority | — |

**The DESIGN HOURLY VOLUME**, which is what geometric design actually uses:

> Design is **not** based on the average or on the absolute peak. It uses the **30th HIGHEST HOURLY VOLUME** of the year — typically **8–12% of AADT**.

> **Designing for the absolute peak hour would be uneconomic**, since it occurs once a year; **designing for the average would leave the road congested for much of the time.** The 30th highest hour is the conventional compromise — the road is congested on about 29 hours a year, which is accepted.

**Traffic survey methods:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Manual count** | Flexible; classifies vehicles; labour intensive |
| **Pneumatic tube** | Automatic; short duration; counts axles |
| **Inductive loop** | Permanent stations |
| Video / ANPR | Increasingly common |

**And the loading conversion that matters most for pavements:**

> The **FOURTH POWER LAW**: pavement damage is proportional to **(axle load)⁴**.

> **One heavily overloaded truck can do more damage than thousands of cars.** A truck at twice the legal axle load causes **sixteen times** the damage of a legal one.

> **That is why axle load control matters far more than traffic volume control** for pavement life, and why overloading is the single greatest cause of premature pavement failure in Nepal.

examTip.trick: **"ANNUAL" is the discriminator.** A 30-day count cannot be an annual average, so AADT and AAWT are excluded by the survey duration alone — leaving ADT (all days) or AWT (weekdays only).
examTip.trap: The extra **A** for "annual" and the **W** for "weekday" are the only differences between the four acronyms. Read them letter by letter rather than by shape.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design uses the 30th HIGHEST HOURLY VOLUME (8–12% of AADT)** — not the average, not the peak. And the **FOURTH POWER LAW** means one overloaded truck outweighs thousands of cars for pavement damage.

questions.stem: When a jet strikes a vertical stationary plate, the jet after striking moves:
options: Normal to the surface of plate
questions.solution:
**Along the plate.**

**Why.** When a jet strikes a flat plate held perpendicular to it, the jet **cannot pass through** and **does not rebound**. It **spreads radially outward across the face of the plate**, leaving in all directions **parallel to the plate surface**.

> **The jet's momentum in the original direction is destroyed entirely**, and the outgoing flow has **no component normal to the plate**.

**The force follows from momentum:**

> **F = ρ A V²** for a jet striking a **stationary flat plate normally**

> The entire initial momentum flux **ρAV × V** is destroyed, so the force equals it.

**The standard cases** — and the pattern in them:

| Situation | Force |
|---|---|
| **Stationary FLAT plate, normal** | **F = ρAV²** |
| **Stationary plate, inclined at θ** | F = ρAV² sin²θ |
| **Moving flat plate** (velocity u) | **F = ρA(V − u)²** |
| **Stationary CURVED (hemispherical) vane** | **F = 2ρAV²** — **TWICE** |
| **Series of vanes** (as on a wheel) | F = ρAV(V − u) |

> **The curved vane gives DOUBLE the force**, and the reason is momentum: a flat plate destroys the momentum (**ΔV = V**), while a **hemispherical vane REVERSES it** (**ΔV = 2V**).

> **That factor of two is the entire reason turbine buckets are curved rather than flat**, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising — it doubles the power from the same jet.

**Why a Pelton bucket deflects 165° and not 180°:**

> A full 180° reversal would give the theoretical maximum force, but the returning water would **strike the back of the following bucket**. The **15° shortfall** is the price of clearance, and it costs a little efficiency.

> The bucket is also **split by a central ridge (splitter)**, dividing the jet into two halves that leave on either side — which balances the axial thrust on the shaft.

**The maximum efficiency condition:**

> For a **series of vanes**, work done is **ρAV(V − u)u**, which is maximised at **u = V/2**.

> **The bucket travels at HALF the jet speed** — which is exactly what leaves the water with **zero absolute velocity**, transferring all its kinetic energy.

> In practice **u ≈ 0.46V** (a speed ratio of 0.43–0.48), slightly below the theoretical optimum to account for friction and windage.

**Why the material of the plate is irrelevant:**

> Option (d) is the only one that appeals to a property of the plate rather than to mechanics. **The force and the deflection follow from the momentum equation alone** — the material affects wear and durability, not the flow pattern.

> **Momentum arguments do not care what the surface is made of**, only what shape it is and how fast it moves. Recognising that eliminates option (d) immediately.

**Why momentum rather than energy is used here:**

> The impact involves **turbulence and energy loss that cannot be quantified in advance**. But the **forces are directly measurable from the change in momentum**, which requires no assumption about the losses.

> **This is the same reasoning that makes the hydraulic jump a momentum problem rather than an energy one** — and it is the recurring theme wherever a flow changes abruptly.

examTip.trick: The jet cannot pass through and does not bounce — it **spreads radially across the face**, leaving parallel to the plate. Its normal momentum is entirely destroyed, giving **F = ρAV²**.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) appeals to the plate's MATERIAL** — but momentum arguments depend only on shape and speed, never on what the surface is made of. That eliminates it instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **A curved vane gives DOUBLE the force (2ρAV²)** because it REVERSES the momentum rather than merely destroying it. That factor of two is why turbine buckets are curved — and why Pelton buckets deflect **165°, not 180°**, to clear the following bucket.

questions.stem: Which distribution system is used in an irregularly developed old city?
questions.solution:
**The dead end (tree) system.**

**Why it suits an irregular old city.** A dead end system consists of **one main supply line** from which **sub-mains branch**, dividing further into **branches and laterals** — like a tree.

> **It requires no planned street layout.** Pipes simply follow whatever lanes exist, branching wherever they must.

> A **gridiron or ring system requires a regular street pattern** to form loops — and an organically-grown old city has no such pattern. That geometric requirement is what makes the choice.

**The four distribution layouts:**

| System | Layout | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **DEAD END (tree)** | Branching, **no loops** | **Irregular, old, haphazardly developed towns**; hilly terrain |
| **GRIDIRON (grid, reticulation)** | Mains and sub-mains **all interconnected** | **Well-planned cities** with a rectangular street pattern |
| **RING (circular)** | A **closed loop** around each block | **Well-planned towns**; pressures reasonably equal |
| **RADIAL** | Distribution reservoirs at centres, **radiating outward** | Cities with **radial roads**; also called zonal distribution |

**Dead end system — the honest balance sheet:**

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| **Simple to design** — flows are **DETERMINATE** | **STAGNATION at dead ends** |
| **Cheap** — fewer pipes, smaller diameters | A break **cuts off everything downstream** |
| **Easy to extend** | Poor for **fire fighting** — water from one direction only |
| Valves are few | Pressure falls toward the extremities |

> **The determinate flow calculation is a genuine advantage** — no Hardy Cross iteration is needed, because each pipe carries exactly the demand beyond it.

**The stagnation problem is the serious one:**

> At a dead end, water **sits and does not move**. The consequences:

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Chlorine residual DECAYS to zero** | The water is no longer protected |
| **Sediment accumulates** | — |
| **Bacterial regrowth and biofilm** | — |
| **Taste and odour complaints** | The first symptom users notice |

> **Dead ends are where contamination shows up first**, and where water quality complaints cluster.

> **The remedy is a SCOUR VALVE at every dead end and a regular flushing programme.** That is an operational obligation, not an optional refinement — and neglecting it is the commonest cause of water quality failure in a distribution system that is otherwise sound.

**Compare the looped systems:**

> In a **gridiron or ring** system, **water reaches any point by more than one route.** A break can be isolated without cutting off the area beyond, fire flows can be drawn from several directions, and **circulation prevents stagnation**.

> The price is **more pipe, higher cost, and an INDETERMINATE network** requiring **Hardy Cross** or equivalent analysis.

**Distribution system design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Design flow** | **Peak hourly demand** (≈ **2.7 × average**) |
| **Minimum residual pressure** | **7 m** at the consumer for a single storey |
| **Velocity** | 0.6 – 3.0 m/s |
| Minimum main | 100 mm (150 mm where fire demand applies) |

> **The peak factors compound**: maximum daily **1.8 ×** average, maximum hourly **1.5 ×** maximum daily — giving **2.7 × average** for the peak hour, and **that is what sizes the mains.**

> **The distribution system is usually the largest single cost in a water supply scheme** — often more than the source and treatment works combined, which is why the choice of layout matters financially as well as operationally.

examTip.trick: A **gridiron or ring needs loops, and loops need a regular street pattern.** An organically-grown old city has none — so the branching dead-end system is the only one its geometry allows.
examTip.trap: **Dead ends STAGNATE** — chlorine residual decays, sediment settles, bacteria regrow. That is where water quality complaints cluster, and the cure is a **scour valve plus regular flushing**, not a design change.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead end flows are DETERMINATE** (no Hardy Cross needed); looped networks are indeterminate but give **more than one route to every point**. And the peak hour is **2.7 × average** — that is what sizes the mains.

questions.stem: The coefficient of uniformity is:
questions.solution:
**C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀.**

**The two grading coefficients:**

| Coefficient | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Coefficient of UNIFORMITY** | **C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀** |
| **Coefficient of CURVATURE** | **C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀ × D₆₀)** |

> **D₁₀, D₃₀, D₆₀** are the particle sizes at which **10%, 30% and 60%** of the soil by weight is **finer**, read off the particle size distribution curve.

> **D₁₀ is called the EFFECTIVE SIZE**, and it is the single most useful grading parameter — permeability correlates strongly with it (**Hazen: k ≈ C D₁₀²**), because the **fine fraction controls the pore sizes** through which water must pass.

**Note that option (c) is C_c with its denominator incomplete** — a well-made distractor, since D₃₀²/D₆₀ is most of the curvature coefficient but missing the D₁₀.

**Reading the numbers:**

| C_u | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C_u = 1** | **All particles the SAME size** — the theoretical minimum |
| **C_u < 4** (gravel) or **< 6** (sand) | **UNIFORM / POORLY graded** |
| **Larger C_u** | **WELL graded** — a wide spread of sizes |

> **C_u must always be ≥ 1**, since D₆₀ ≥ D₁₀ by definition. **An answer below 1 means the ratio was inverted** — which is exactly what option (a) would give.

**The classification criteria (IS 1498 / USCS):**

| Soil | Well graded requires |
|---|---|
| **GRAVEL (GW)** | **C_u > 4** AND **1 < C_c < 3** |
| **SAND (SW)** | **C_u > 6** AND **1 < C_c < 3** |

> **BOTH conditions must be met.** Failing either makes the soil **poorly graded (GP or SP)**.

> **C_c catches the GAP-GRADED soil**, which is the reason it exists: a soil can have a very wide overall spread (high C_u, looking well graded) while **missing an intermediate size range entirely**. C_c detects that gap, because the missing middle displaces D₃₀.

> **C_u alone would pass a gap-graded soil as well graded**, which is why the two are always quoted together.

**Why grading matters so much:**

| Property | Well graded | Uniform |
|---|---|---|
| **Density achievable** | **HIGH** — small particles fill the voids between large ones | Low |
| **Shear strength** | **Higher** | Lower |
| **Compressibility** | Lower | Higher |
| **Permeability** | **Lower** | Higher |
| Suitability as fill or sub-base | **Excellent** | Poor |

> **A well graded soil compacts to a higher density because the fines pack into the voids between the coarse particles.** That single fact explains why well graded material is specified for **road sub-bases, embankment fill and filter layers**, and why it commands a premium.

**FILTER design** is the application where grading is most critical:

> A filter must **retain the soil it protects** while **passing the water freely**:

> **D₁₅(filter)/D₈₅(soil) < 4 to 5** — the **retention** criterion
> **D₁₅(filter)/D₁₅(soil) > 4 to 5** — the **permeability** criterion

> **The two criteria pull in opposite directions**, and the filter's grading must satisfy both simultaneously. A filter that is too fine clogs and builds pore pressure; one too coarse lets the soil wash through — **PIPING**, which is the mechanism that destroys earth dams.

> **Piping is the leading cause of earth dam failure**, and a properly graded filter is the principal defence against it — which is why these two inequalities are worth carrying.

examTip.trick: **C_u must always be ≥ 1**, since D₆₀ ≥ D₁₀ by definition. Option (a) is the ratio inverted and would give a value below 1 — impossible, so it can be discarded without recall.
examTip.trap: Option (c) is **C_c with its denominator incomplete** — the full curvature coefficient is **D₃₀²/(D₁₀ × D₆₀)**. Missing the D₁₀ is the kind of near-miss that catches a hurried reader.
examTip.mnemonic: **C_c exists to catch GAP-GRADED soils** that C_u alone would pass — a wide spread with a missing middle. Both are needed: **C_u > 4 (gravel) or 6 (sand) AND 1 < C_c < 3** for well graded.

questions.stem: A pitot tube is used to measure:
questions.solution:
**The velocity of flow** at a point.

**How it works.** A pitot tube has an opening facing directly **into the flow**. The fluid is brought to rest there — a **STAGNATION POINT** — and its **kinetic energy is converted into pressure**.

> **Stagnation pressure = static pressure + dynamic pressure**
> **p₀ = p + ρV²/2**

> Measuring the difference gives the velocity:

> **V = C_v √(2gh)**

> where **h** is the difference in head between the stagnation and static readings, and **C_v ≈ 0.98**.

**The pitot-STATIC tube** is the practical instrument:

> It combines **both** measurements in one probe — a **central hole facing the flow** (stagnation) and **side holes parallel to the flow** (static). The difference is read directly on a differential manometer.

> **A plain pitot tube alone measures only the stagnation pressure** and needs a separate static tapping. That is why the pitot-static (Prandtl) tube is the standard form.

**The critical characteristic:**

> **A pitot tube measures the velocity at ONE POINT, not the average velocity or the discharge.**

> To obtain the discharge, the velocity must be measured at **several points across the section** and **integrated** — which is precisely how a river gauging is performed with a current meter.

> **This point-measurement property is both its limitation and its great advantage**: it is the instrument of choice for **surveying a velocity PROFILE**, which no other simple device can do.

**Where the average velocity sits in a profile:**

| Flow | Location of mean velocity |
|---|---|
| **Turbulent pipe flow** | **At about 0.75 R from the axis** |
| **Open channel** | At **0.6 × depth** below the surface — or the **average of 0.2 and 0.8 depth** |

> **The 0.6-depth rule is what makes river gauging practical** — a single reading at 0.6 depth gives the mean velocity in that vertical, and the **two-point method (0.2 and 0.8)** is used where more accuracy is needed.

**Comparison with the other flow meters:**

| Device | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PITOT tube** | **POINT velocity** | Small head loss; needs traversing for discharge |
| **VENTURIMETER** | **DISCHARGE** | **Low permanent head loss (~10%)**; expensive; long |
| **ORIFICE meter** | **DISCHARGE** | **High head loss (~50%)**; cheap; compact |
| Nozzle meter | Discharge | Intermediate |
| Rotameter | Discharge | Variable area, visual |

> **The venturimeter versus orifice choice is a classic trade-off**: the venturi's gradual divergent cone (**5–7°**) **recovers most of the pressure**, so its permanent loss is small — but it is long and costly. The orifice is cheap and short but **dissipates about half the differential permanently**.

> **Over a plant's lifetime, the venturi's lower pumping cost often outweighs its higher capital cost** — the same economic reasoning that governs penstock diameter.

> **The divergent cone is deliberately gentler than the convergent one** (which can be 20–22°), because **a flow accelerating in a contraction will not separate, whereas a decelerating flow in an expansion readily does.** That asymmetry is a general principle in fluid mechanics, not a detail of this instrument.

**A note on C_d values:** venturimeter **0.95–0.98**; orifice meter **0.60–0.65**. The orifice's much lower coefficient reflects the **vena contracta** — the jet contracts to about 62% of the orifice area just downstream, and that contraction is where most of its loss originates.

examTip.trick: The pitot tube brings fluid to rest at a **stagnation point**, converting kinetic energy to pressure: **p₀ = p + ρV²/2**, so **V = C_v√(2gh)**. It reads a velocity, not a pressure.
examTip.trap: **It measures velocity at ONE POINT, not the average or the discharge.** For discharge you must traverse the section and integrate — which is exactly how a river gauging works.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mean velocity sits at 0.6 depth** in an open channel (or average 0.2 and 0.8) — the rule that makes river gauging practical. And **venturi loses ~10%, orifice ~50%** — the venturi's gentle 5–7° cone recovers the pressure.

questions.stem: The removal of oil and grease from sewage is known as:
questions.solution:
**Skimming.**

**Why.** Oil and grease are **LIGHTER than water**, so they **float to the surface**. **Skimming removes them from the surface** — the opposite operation to settling.

**The preliminary and primary treatment units, each with its own target:**

| Unit | Removes | By |
|---|---|---|
| **SCREENING** | **Floating solids** — rags, plastics, sticks | Physical straining on bars |
| **GRIT CHAMBER** | **Grit, sand, gravel** — inorganic, heavy | Settling at **controlled velocity (0.3 m/s)** |
| **SKIMMING TANK** | **OIL and GREASE** | **Floating to the surface** and being skimmed off |
| **SEDIMENTATION** | **Suspended organic solids** — denser than water | Gravity settling |

> **Each unit targets a different physical property**: size (screening), density-heavier-and-inorganic (grit), density-lighter (skimming), density-heavier-and-organic (sedimentation).

> **The order is deliberate and cannot be rearranged**: coarse before fine, and each unit protects the next. Screens protect pumps from rags; grit chambers protect pumps and digesters from abrasive sand.

**The grit chamber's controlled velocity is worth understanding:**

> A grit chamber is designed to hold the flow at about **0.3 m/s** — and that value is a **compromise**, not a maximum:

| If velocity is | Result |
|---|---|
| **Too HIGH** | **Grit is not removed** — it stays in suspension |
| **Too LOW** | **ORGANIC matter settles too**, which is not wanted |

> **The organic matter must go forward to biological treatment**, not into the grit hopper where it would putrefy and smell. So the velocity is deliberately kept high enough to keep organics moving while letting the denser grit fall.

> **A proportional (Sutro) weir at the outlet maintains that velocity constant despite varying flow** — an elegant piece of design, since the velocity criterion would otherwise be met at only one discharge.

**Why grease removal matters:**

| Problem if left in | Note |
|---|---|
| **Clogs pipes and pumps** | Congeals on cool surfaces |
| **Interferes with biological treatment** | Coats the biomass and blocks oxygen transfer |
| **Forms surface scum** on tanks | Impedes settling and looks bad |
| **FATBERGS in sewers** | Grease combined with wipes forms solid masses that block whole sewers |

> **Grease is best intercepted at source** — restaurants, hotels and canteens should have **GREASE TRAPS**, because removing it at the treatment works after it has congealed through kilometres of sewer is far harder.

**How skimming is enhanced:**

> **Compressed air is blown through the tank** in some designs. The rising bubbles **attach to the grease globules and float them faster**, and the agitation prevents heavier solids from settling in the skimming tank where they do not belong.

> That is the same principle as **DISSOLVED AIR FLOTATION (DAF)**, used for sludge thickening and for treating oily industrial wastewater — bubbles carrying particles upward rather than gravity carrying them down.

**The full treatment train:**

| Stage | Units | Removes |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary** | Screens, grit chamber, skimming | Coarse and inert material |
| **PRIMARY** | Primary sedimentation | **~60% SS, ~35% BOD** |
| **SECONDARY** | **Biological** — activated sludge, trickling filter | **~85–95% BOD** |
| **Tertiary** | Filtration, nutrient removal, disinfection | Residual solids, N and P, pathogens |

> **Primary treatment is physical and removes solids; SECONDARY is BIOLOGICAL and removes dissolved organic matter.** That distinction is fundamental — no amount of settling removes dissolved BOD, which is why biological treatment cannot be skipped.

examTip.trick: Sort by physical property: **screening = size; grit = heavy and inorganic; skimming = LIGHTER than water (floats); sedimentation = heavier organic.** Oil floats, so skimming.
examTip.trap: **The grit chamber's 0.3 m/s is a COMPROMISE, not a maximum** — too fast and grit escapes, too slow and organics settle where they would putrefy. A **proportional (Sutro) weir** holds it constant across flows.
examTip.mnemonic: **PRIMARY is physical (settling); SECONDARY is BIOLOGICAL.** No amount of settling removes **dissolved** BOD — which is exactly why biological treatment cannot be skipped.

questions.stem: In a Sarda type fall, the rectangular crest may be used for discharge up to:
questions.solution:
**14 cumecs.**

**The Sarda fall's design rule:**

| Discharge | Crest section |
|---|---|
| **Less than 14 cumecs** | **RECTANGULAR** |
| **More than 14 cumecs** | **TRAPEZOIDAL**, with upstream batter **1 : 3** and downstream batter **1 : 8** |

**What a Sarda fall is:**

> Developed on the **Sarda canal in Uttar Pradesh**, it is a **vertical impact fall with a RAISED CREST**. Energy is dissipated by the **vertical drop of the nappe into a CISTERN** below, **without forming a hydraulic jump**.

**Its design characteristics** (from the source's own list):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Discharge intensity** | **1.6 to 3.5 cumec/m** |
| **Drop** | **0.6 to 2.5 m** |
| **Crest section** | Rectangular below 14 cumecs; trapezoidal above |
| **Depth of cut-off** | **1 to 1.5 m** |

**Why a raised crest?**

> The Sarda command had **sandy strata overlain by sandy clay**, so the **depth of cutting had to be kept to a minimum**. A raised crest achieves the drop **without excavating deep into the erodible sand** — which is the whole reason for the design.

> **It is a design shaped by its geology**, which is why it carries a place name rather than a generic one.

**The types of canal fall, for comparison:**

| Type | Energy dissipation |
|---|---|
| **Ogee fall** | Smooth transition; **minimal dissipation** — suits a small drop |
| **SARDA (vertical drop) fall** | **Vertical impact into a cistern**; no jump |
| **Glacis fall** | Sloping glacis forming a **HYDRAULIC JUMP** |
| **Baffle fall** | Baffle blocks **force** the jump to form at a fixed position |
| Well / cylinder fall | For a large drop in a small channel |

> **The glacis fall is the modern general-purpose choice**, because a hydraulic jump is an efficient and well-understood dissipator — and the **baffle** version fixes the jump's position, removing the risk of sweep-out that a plain glacis carries.

**Why a fall is provided at all:**

> Where the **natural ground slope exceeds the canal's designed bed slope**, the canal would ride further and further above the ground. **A fall steps the bed down**, restoring a workable depth and dissipating the surplus energy.

> **The falls are located on the LONGITUDINAL SECTION, where the ground line and the designed bed line diverge too far** — the whole design method in one sentence.

**And the economic optimisation:**

> **Fewer, larger falls** cost less in structures but more in earthwork; **more, smaller falls** the reverse. The optimum balances the two, and it is settled by trial on the longitudinal section.

**A fall is also a natural place to put other works:**

| Combined with | Why |
|---|---|
| **Metering flume** | The fall provides a **control section** where discharge can be measured |
| **Regulator** | The structure is being built anyway |
| **Bridge** | A crossing point |
| Canal escape | — |

> **Combining a fall with a metering device is standard and economical** — the drop already forces critical flow, which is exactly what a measuring structure needs.

**The cistern** is the element that makes the Sarda fall work: a **depressed floor downstream** of the crest, deep and long enough to contain the falling nappe and dissipate its energy in a confined pool of water rather than on the canal bed. **Its dimensions are set empirically** from the drop and the discharge intensity — one of the many places in irrigation engineering where field experience outran theory.

examTip.trick: **14 cumecs is the crest-shape threshold**: rectangular below, **trapezoidal above (batters 1:3 upstream, 1:8 downstream)**. The number is pure recall, but the batters often come with it.
examTip.trap: A Sarda fall dissipates energy by **VERTICAL IMPACT into a cistern, WITHOUT a hydraulic jump** — unlike a glacis fall, which forms one. Assuming every fall works by a jump is the conceptual error here.
examTip.mnemonic: **The raised crest exists because the Sarda command was SANDY** — deep cutting had to be avoided. It is a design shaped by its geology, which is why it carries a place name.

questions.stem: Precipitation caused by the lifting of an air mass due to pressure difference is called:
questions.solution:
**Cyclonic precipitation.**

**The three mechanisms**, distinguished by **what lifts the air**:

| Type | Lifting mechanism | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **CYCLONIC** | **PRESSURE difference** — air converges into a low-pressure area and is forced upward | Widespread, **long duration**, moderate intensity |
| **CONVECTIVE** | **HEATING** — warm surface air rises because it is less dense | **Localised, short, very intense**; thunderstorms |
| **OROGRAPHIC** | **MOUNTAIN BARRIER** — air is forced up a topographic obstacle | **Heavy on the windward side; RAIN SHADOW to lee** |

> **All precipitation requires air to be LIFTED, cooled, and its moisture condensed.** The three types differ only in what does the lifting — pressure, heat, or terrain. That single organising idea makes them impossible to confuse.

**Cyclonic precipitation subdivides:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **FRONTAL** | At the boundary between warm and cold air masses. A **WARM front** gives gentle, prolonged rain; a **COLD front** gives brief, intense rain |
| **Non-frontal** | Convergence into a low without a distinct front |

**OROGRAPHIC precipitation dominates Nepal**, and it explains the country's whole hydrology:

> Monsoon air from the Bay of Bengal is **forced up the Himalayan front**, cooling as it rises and dropping its moisture on the **windward (southern) slopes**.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very heavy rainfall on southern slopes** | Some of the highest totals in the world — **Lumle and Pokhara receive over 5000 mm** |
| **Severe RAIN SHADOW beyond the range** | **Manang and Mustang are arid**, at a few hundred mm, though only tens of kilometres away |
| **Extreme spatial variability** | Rainfall can vary several-fold over a short horizontal distance |

> **That variability is why rain gauge network density matters so much in Nepal**, and why interpolating rainfall between distant gauges is unreliable in mountainous terrain.

**And the temporal concentration:**

> About **80% of Nepal's annual rainfall falls in the four monsoon months** (June–September). **That distribution, not the annual total, is the country's water problem** — and it is the whole case for storage reservoirs.

**Measuring areal rainfall from point gauges:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Arithmetic mean** | Simple average; suits **uniform** terrain and even gauge spacing |
| **THIESSEN polygon** | Weights each gauge by its **area of influence**; assumes rainfall is uniform near each gauge |
| **ISOHYETAL** | Contours of equal rainfall drawn using judgement — **best for MOUNTAINOUS terrain** |

> **The isohyetal method is the right choice for Nepal**, because it allows the analyst to draw contours reflecting **topography** — which a Thiessen polygon, being purely geometric, cannot do.

> **Thiessen polygons take no account of elevation at all**, so in a mountainous catchment they can assign a valley gauge's low rainfall to a high ridge that actually receives several times as much.

**Rain gauge network density** (WMO guidance): about **1 gauge per 250 km²** in flat regions, but **1 per 100 km² or denser in mountainous areas** — precisely because of the variability orographic effects create.

**And the check on gauge records:** the **DOUBLE MASS CURVE** — plotting a gauge's cumulative rainfall against the cumulative mean of surrounding gauges. **A change in slope reveals an inconsistency** (a gauge moved, a building erected nearby, an instrument changed), and the record can then be corrected.

examTip.trick: All precipitation needs air to be **LIFTED**. The three types differ only in **what lifts it**: **PRESSURE (cyclonic), HEAT (convective), MOUNTAIN (orographic).** One idea, three causes.
examTip.trap: Convective and cyclonic are both driven by atmospheric conditions rather than terrain, so they are easy to swap. **Convective is local, brief and intense; cyclonic is widespread and prolonged.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal is orographic: 5000 mm at Pokhara, a few hundred in Mustang's rain shadow.** With that variability, use the **ISOHYETAL** method — Thiessen polygons are purely geometric and ignore elevation entirely.

questions.stem: Principal planes are subjected to:
options: normal stresses as well as tangential stresses
questions.solution:
**Normal stresses only** — by definition, a principal plane carries **NO shear**.

**The definition:**

> **PRINCIPAL PLANES are the planes on which the SHEAR STRESS IS ZERO.** The normal stresses acting on them are the **PRINCIPAL STRESSES** — the maximum and minimum normal stresses at that point.

> The two statements are equivalent: **the planes of extreme normal stress are exactly the planes of zero shear.** That is not a coincidence but a mathematical consequence — at a maximum, the derivative vanishes, and the derivative of the normal stress with respect to plane orientation is proportional to the shear.

**Seeing it on Mohr's circle** — the clearest way:

> Principal stresses are where the circle **crosses the σ axis**. **On that axis τ = 0 by construction**, so principal planes are shear-free automatically.

| Feature | Location on the circle |
|---|---|
| **Principal stresses** | Where it **crosses the σ axis** — **τ = 0** |
| **Maximum shear** | **Top and bottom** of the circle |
| **Centre** | (σ_x + σ_y)/2 |
| **Radius** | **R = τ_max** |

**The formulae:**

> **σ_{1,2} = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]**
> **tan 2θ_p = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y)**
> **τ_max = √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²] = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2**

**Three results worth carrying:**

> **1. The two principal planes are 90° apart** in reality (180° on the circle).

> **2. The plane of maximum shear is at 45° to the principal planes** — because it is 90° round the circle from the σ axis, and **circle angles are DOUBLE real angles**.

> **3. The plane of maximum shear is NOT free of normal stress.** At the top of the circle σ equals the centre value, **(σ_x + σ_y)/2**, which is generally not zero.

> **Only principal planes are free of shear; no plane is generally free of normal stress.** That asymmetry catches many candidates, who assume the two extremes are symmetrical cases.

**Why principal stresses matter:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Failure theories** | Every one is expressed in terms of principal stresses |
| **BRITTLE materials** | Fail on the plane of **maximum PRINCIPAL (tensile) stress** — Rankine |
| **DUCTILE materials** | Fail on the plane of **maximum SHEAR** — Tresca, von Mises |
| **Crack direction** | Cracks open **perpendicular to the maximum principal tensile stress** |
| Reinforcement direction | Ideally along the principal tensile trajectories |

> **The crack direction result is directly useful in reinforced concrete:** since concrete cracks perpendicular to the principal tension, **diagonal shear cracks in a beam run at about 45°** — and that is exactly why **stirrups are vertical** (crossing those cracks) and why **bent-up bars at 45°** were historically used.

> **Reading the crack pattern tells you the stress state that caused it**, which makes principal stress theory a diagnostic tool on site as well as a design tool on paper.

**The soil mechanics application** is the same circle used differently:

> **Mohr–Coulomb: τ = c + σ tan φ.** A series of circles from triaxial tests at different confining pressures share a **common tangent**, and that envelope gives **c and φ**.

> **For a saturated clay tested undrained, every circle has the SAME diameter** whatever the cell pressure — the extra pressure goes entirely into pore water and σ′ is unchanged. Their common tangent is **horizontal**: **φ_u = 0, τ = c_u**.

examTip.trick: **Principal planes are DEFINED by zero shear** — so the answer follows from the definition alone. On Mohr's circle they are where it crosses the σ axis, where τ = 0 by construction.
examTip.trap: **The plane of maximum SHEAR still carries normal stress** — the centre value (σ_x+σ_y)/2. Only principal planes are shear-free; no plane is generally free of normal stress. The two extremes are not symmetrical.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cracks open perpendicular to the maximum principal TENSION** — which is why diagonal shear cracks run at ~45° and why stirrups are vertical to cross them. The crack pattern reveals the stress state.

questions.stem: When a uniformly distributed load (UDL) of length greater than the length of the girder is moved from left to right, the bending moment is maximum:
options: When the UDL is to the left of the midpoint of the beam
When the UDL is at the middle of the beam
When the UDL crosses the midpoint of the beam
When the UDL covers the entire beam
questions.solution:
**When the UDL covers the entire beam.**

**Why.** Use the influence line rule for a distributed load:

> **Effect of a UDL = w × the AREA under the influence line over the loaded length.**

> The influence line for bending moment at any section of a simply supported beam is a **TRIANGLE, entirely POSITIVE** — it has no negative region at all.

> **Since every ordinate is positive, adding more loaded length can only ADD to the moment.** The maximum is therefore reached when the load covers as much of the span as possible.

> **The load being LONGER than the span is the key phrase**: it means the whole beam can be covered simultaneously, so the maximum occurs in that position.

**The general placement rules for influence lines:**

| Load | Placement for maximum effect |
|---|---|
| **Point load** | At the **maximum ORDINATE** |
| **UDL shorter than the span** | Positioned to cover the **greatest AREA** under the line |
| **UDL longer than the span** | **Covers the WHOLE beam** |
| Any load, for **SHEAR** | **One side of the section only** |

**The contrast with SHEAR is the point worth carrying:**

> A **shear** influence line has a **UNIT STEP at the section** — it is **positive on one side and NEGATIVE on the other**.

> **Loading both sides therefore partly CANCELS.** Maximum shear needs the load on **one side only**, stopping exactly at the section.

> **That is why a UDL covering the whole beam maximises the MOMENT but NOT the SHEAR** — the two require completely different load positions, and it is the clearest illustration of why influence lines are needed at all.

**This is also the origin of PATTERN LOADING** in continuous beams:

| For maximum | Load pattern |
|---|---|
| **Span moment** | **ALTERNATE spans** loaded |
| **Support moment** | **Both spans ADJACENT** to that support loaded |

> **Analysing only the all-spans-loaded case UNDERESTIMATES both maxima**, and the reason is exactly the sign-change argument above: a continuous beam's influence lines have both positive and negative regions.

**Standard influence lines for a simply supported span L**, section at a from the left (b = L − a):

| Quantity | Shape | Peak |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | Linear, 1 → 0 | 1 at A |
| **Moment at the section** | **Triangular, all positive** | **ab/L** |
| **Shear at the section** | Two lines with a **unit step** | +b/L and −a/L |

> **Maximum moment at midspan: ab/L = L/4**, giving **wL²/8** under a full UDL ✓ — which confirms the standard result.

**What an influence line is**, since the concept underlies all of this:

> **One quantity, ONE FIXED section, MOVING load.** The horizontal axis is the **position of the LOAD**, not position along the beam — which is what distinguishes it from a bending moment diagram, even though the two can share a triangular shape.

**For an INDETERMINATE structure** the influence line is a **CURVE** and cannot be obtained by statics — but **MÜLLER-BRESLAU's principle** gives its shape directly: **release the restraint corresponding to the quantity wanted, impose a unit displacement, and the deflected shape IS the influence line.**

> That principle is what makes pattern loading tractable for continuous beams and frames, since the deflected shape immediately shows which spans should be loaded.

examTip.trick: **A UDL's effect = w × AREA under the influence line.** The moment influence line is a triangle that is **entirely positive**, so more loaded length always adds — cover the whole span.
examTip.trap: **The same load position does NOT maximise SHEAR.** A shear influence line changes sign at the section, so loading both sides partly cancels — maximum shear needs **one side loaded only**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load → maximum ORDINATE; UDL → greatest AREA; shear → one side only.** And for indeterminate structures, **MÜLLER-BRESLAU** gives the influence line as the deflected shape after releasing the restraint.

questions.stem: A body is subjected to a direct tensile stress of 300 MPa in one plane accompanied by a simple shear stress of 200 MPa. The maximum normal stress on the plane will be:
questions.solution:
**400 MPa.**

**Working.** With **σ_x = 300 MPa**, **σ_y = 0**, **τ_xy = 200 MPa**:

> **σ_max = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 + √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]**
> **= 300/2 + √[(300/2)² + 200²]**
> **= 150 + √(22 500 + 40 000)**
> **= 150 + √62 500**
> **= 150 + 250 = 400 MPa** ✓

**Notice the arithmetic is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled up:**

> **150, 200, 250** is **50 × (3, 4, 5)**.

> **Examination problems are very often built on Pythagorean triples**, precisely so the square root comes out whole. **Spotting 150 and 200 and expecting 250 saves the entire calculation** — and if your radical does not come out neatly, it is worth re-checking the arithmetic before trusting it.

**The complete stress state at this point:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **σ_max (σ₁)** | **150 + 250 = 400 MPa** |
| **σ_min (σ₂)** | **150 − 250 = −100 MPa** — **COMPRESSIVE** |
| **τ_max** | **= R = 250 MPa** |
| Centre of Mohr's circle | 150 MPa |
| Radius | 250 MPa |

**Two things worth noticing:**

> **1. The minimum principal stress is NEGATIVE (−100 MPa) even though the applied direct stress was purely tensile.** Shear alone has produced compression on one plane. That is not an error — pure shear is equivalent to equal tension and compression at 45°, and adding it to a tension produces a compressive principal stress whenever the shear is large enough.

> **2. τ_max = 250 MPa EXCEEDS the applied shear of 200 MPa.** The combination is more severe in shear than either component alone.

> **Both results show why a stress transformation must be done rather than assumed.** Judging the severity from the applied values alone would understate both the tension and the shear.

**On Mohr's circle:**

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| **Centre** | **((σ_x + σ_y)/2, 0) = (150, 0)** |
| **Radius** | **R = √[((σ_x−σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²] = 250** |
| **Principal stresses** | Centre ± R = **400 and −100** |
| **τ_max** | **= R = 250** |

> **The radius IS the maximum shear stress** — a result worth internalising, because it makes τ_max immediate once the circle is drawn.

**The orientation:**

> **tan 2θ_p = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y) = 400/300 = 1.333**, so **2θ_p = 53.1°** and **θ_p = 26.6°**.

> The plane of **maximum shear** lies at **45° to that**, i.e. **θ = 71.6°** — because **angles on Mohr's circle are DOUBLE the real angles**, and the top of the circle is 90° round from the σ axis.

**Which failure theory applies:**

| Material | Theory | Governing quantity |
|---|---|---|
| **BRITTLE** (cast iron, concrete) | **Rankine** — maximum principal stress | **σ₁ = 400 MPa** |
| **DUCTILE** (steel) | **Tresca** — maximum shear | **(σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = 250 MPa** |
| Ductile | **von Mises** — distortion energy | Best fit to test data |

> **Note that Tresca uses (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = (400 − (−100))/2 = 250 MPa** — the full range including the compressive principal stress. **Omitting the negative σ₂ would give 200 and badly understate the severity**, which is the commonest error in applying Tresca.

examTip.trick: **Spot the Pythagorean triple: 150, 200 → 250** (that is 50 × 3-4-5). Examination stress problems are usually built on triples so the root comes out whole — and 150 + 250 = 400 in one step.
examTip.trap: **σ₂ comes out at −100 MPa — COMPRESSIVE — from a purely tensile applied stress.** Pure shear is equivalent to equal tension and compression at 45°, so large shear drives one principal stress negative.
examTip.mnemonic: **The RADIUS of Mohr's circle IS τ_max.** And Tresca uses **(σ₁ − σ₂)/2** including the negative σ₂ — omitting it here gives 200 instead of 250 and badly understates the severity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
**Pelton is an impulse turbine.**

**The classification, which the source gives as a mnemonic:**

| Class | Turbines |
|---|---|
| **IMPULSE** | **Crossflow, Pelton, Turgo — "CPT"** |
| **REACTION** | **Francis, Kaplan, Propeller — "FrKPr"** |

**The physical distinction:**

| | **IMPULSE** | **REACTION** |
|---|---|---|
| Energy at the runner | **ALL KINETIC** — converted in the nozzle before it arrives | **Kinetic AND pressure** |
| Pressure at the runner | **ATMOSPHERIC throughout** | **Above atmospheric**, falling through the runner |
| Runner environment | **Runs in AIR**; casing not full | **Runs FULL of water** |
| **Draft tube** | **NOT used** | **ESSENTIAL** |
| Flow control | **Spear (needle) valve** in the nozzle | **Guide vanes (wicket gates)** |
| **Cavitation** | **CANNOT occur** — pressure never drops | **Must be checked** (Thoma's σ) |
| Casing | Not pressurised; only prevents splashing | **Pressure-retaining** |

> **The single distinguishing question: does the pressure DROP across the runner?** In a reaction turbine it does — the runner is a pressure-containing device. In an impulse turbine the pressure drop happens entirely in the nozzle, and the runner works at atmospheric pressure.

**Why a reaction turbine NEEDS a draft tube:**

> The **draft tube recovers the kinetic energy** of water leaving the runner and, by creating **suction**, lets the turbine be set **above the tailwater without losing that head**.

> **Without a draft tube, the head between the runner and the tailwater would simply be lost.**

> A **Pelton discharges to atmosphere** into the tailrace — there is no pressure to recover, so a draft tube would achieve nothing. **The head between a Pelton runner and the tailwater IS lost**, which is why the machine is set as close above the tailwater as flooding allows.

**Selection by head:**

| Turbine | Head | Discharge | N_s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pelton** | **High — above ~250 m** | **Low** | **10 – 35** |
| Turgo / Crossflow | Medium | Medium | — |
| **Francis** | **Medium — 30 to 250 m** | Medium | **60 – 300** |
| **Kaplan** | **Low — below ~30 m** | **High** | **300 – 1000** |

> **Specific speed N_s = N√P/H^{5/4} rises as head falls**, and it is the parameter that actually selects the machine.
