**Pelton design relations:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Jet velocity** | **V = C_v√(2gH)**, C_v ≈ 0.98 |
| **Optimum bucket speed** | **u = 0.46 V** — about **half** the jet |
| **Jet ratio D/d** | **11 – 14** |
| **Number of buckets** | **15 + D/2d**, typically 18–25 |
| **Deflection angle** | **165°**, not 180° |

> **The bucket travels at half the jet speed** because that leaves the water with **zero absolute velocity** — all its kinetic energy transferred. **The 165° rather than 180° is for clearance**: fully reversed water would strike the following bucket.

**For Nepal specifically:**

> Steep terrain gives **high heads with modest flows** over much of the country — Pelton territory. Pelton runners are also the **easiest to manufacture and repair locally**, which matters greatly for small and micro-hydro schemes.

> But **sediment erosion is severe**: quartz sand at 100+ m/s jet velocity **cuts the needle and the bucket splitter**, and a runner can lose its profile in a single monsoon without an effective **settling basin**.

examTip.trick: One question separates them: **does the pressure DROP across the runner?** Reaction — yes (runs full, needs a draft tube, can cavitate). Impulse — no (runs in air at atmospheric, no draft tube, cannot cavitate).
examTip.trap: **A Pelton CANNOT cavitate** and has **no draft tube**. Both facts follow from the runner being at atmospheric pressure — a common source of confusion when Thoma's σ is asked about.
examTip.mnemonic: **Impulse = CPT (Crossflow, Pelton, Turgo); Reaction = Francis, Kaplan, Propeller.** And **bucket speed u = 0.46V**, about half the jet, which leaves the water with zero absolute velocity.

questions.stem: If the discharge of a pump is 0.16 cumecs, the economic diameter of the pipe is:
questions.solution:
**0.488 m ≈ 0.480 m.**

**Working.** Using **Lea's formula** for the economic diameter of a pumping main:

> **D = 1.22 √Q**  (D in metres, Q in m³/s)
> **D = 1.22 × √0.16 = 1.22 × 0.4 = 0.488 m** ✓

> **The arithmetic is deliberately clean — √0.16 = 0.4 exactly** — which is a strong signal that this is the intended route.

**What "economic diameter" means, and why it is a genuine optimisation:**

> The pipe diameter is **not** chosen from hydraulics alone. It is the diameter that **minimises the TOTAL cost over the pipeline's life**:

| Diameter | Capital cost | Pumping (running) cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Larger** | **HIGHER** — more material | **LOWER** — less friction, less energy |
| **Smaller** | Lower | **HIGHER** — friction rises steeply |

> **The economic diameter is where the sum of the two is least.**

**Why the running cost usually dominates:**

> Head loss by **Darcy–Weisbach** is **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)**, and substituting **V = 4Q/πD²** gives:

> **h_f ∝ Q²/D⁵**

> **The head loss varies as the INVERSE FIFTH POWER of the diameter.** A **10% larger pipe cuts the head loss by nearly 40%**; a 20% larger pipe cuts it by about 60%.

> **That extraordinary sensitivity is why the economic diameter is usually LARGER than intuition suggests** — the capital cost rises roughly with D or D², while the running cost falls with D⁵.

> And the running cost **recurs every year for the pipeline's life**, so its capitalised value typically outweighs the extra capital. **A pipeline undersized to save capital is a permanent tax on the operating budget.**

**The general economic-diameter approach**, of which Lea's formula is a simplified case:

> **Total annual cost = (capital cost × capital recovery factor) + (annual energy cost)**

> Differentiate with respect to D and set to zero. The result depends on the **cost of pipe, the cost of energy, the load factor and the discount rate** — which is why different sources give slightly different coefficients (1.1 to 1.5) in the D = k√Q form.

> **Lea's 1.22 is a mid-range value** appropriate to typical conditions.

**The velocity implied:**

> **A = πD²/4 = π(0.488)²/4 = 0.187 m²**
> **V = Q/A = 0.16/0.187 = 0.86 m/s**

> That sits comfortably within the usual design range for a pumping main (**0.6 to 3.0 m/s**), and below it silting becomes a risk while above it friction and water hammer rise sharply.

**The same reasoning appears elsewhere in the syllabus:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **PENSTOCK diameter** | Identical optimisation — capital against **50 years of lost generation**; design velocity **3–6 m/s** |
| Rising mains | As here |
| Distribution mains | Constrained also by minimum residual pressure (7 m) |

> **In a hydropower penstock the lost-energy term dominates even more strongly**, because the loss is not merely a pumping cost but generation never produced — for the plant's entire life.

examTip.trick: **D = 1.22√Q**, and √0.16 = **0.4** exactly — the clean arithmetic signals the intended route. 1.22 × 0.4 = 0.488 m.
examTip.trap: This is an **economic** optimisation, not a hydraulic one. The answer balances **capital cost against a lifetime of pumping energy** — which is why the economic diameter is usually **larger** than a purely hydraulic sizing would give.
examTip.mnemonic: **h_f ∝ Q²/D⁵** — the inverse FIFTH power. A 10% larger pipe cuts head loss nearly **40%**, and that saving recurs every year. The same reasoning sizes a **penstock**, where the loss is generation never produced.

questions.stem: The formula for mechanical extra widening on a road is:
questions.solution:
**W_m = n l²/(2R).**

**The two components of extra widening on a curve:**

> **W_e = W_m + W_ps**
> **W_e = n l²/(2R) + V/(9.5 √R)**

| Component | Formula | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL widening W_m** | **n l²/(2R)** | The **rigid wheelbase** — rear wheels track **inside** the front wheels on a curve |
| **PSYCHOLOGICAL widening W_ps** | **V/(9.5√R)** | Drivers keep **further from the edge and from each other** on a curve |

> where **n** = number of lanes, **l** = wheelbase, **R** = radius, **V** = speed in km/h.

**Why mechanical widening exists — the OFF-TRACKING effect:**

> A vehicle's **rear wheels do not follow the front wheels** round a curve. Because the wheelbase is rigid, **the rear wheels cut the corner**, tracking on a smaller radius.

> **The vehicle therefore sweeps a wider path than its own width.** Extra carriageway must be provided or the rear wheels will run off the inside edge.

> **The effect is worse for a longer wheelbase and a sharper curve** — hence l² in the numerator and R in the denominator. **A long truck or an articulated vehicle on a tight hairpin needs very substantial widening**, which is why hill-road hairpins are built so much wider than the straight sections.

**Why psychological widening exists:**

> Drivers instinctively **keep further from the edge of the pavement and from oncoming vehicles** on a curve, because their sight line is shorter and the vehicle feels less stable.

> **It is a real and measurable effect**, and providing for it prevents drivers from crowding the centre line — which is the actual hazard.

> **Note it depends on SPEED (V) while mechanical widening does not.** Mechanical widening is pure geometry; psychological widening is behavioural.

**Where widening is provided:**

> The extra width is **applied over the full circular curve** and **introduced gradually over the transition curve**, reaching its full value where the circular curve begins.

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| Usually on the **INSIDE** of the curve | Where the rear wheels track |
| Sometimes **half on each side** | Common where a transition curve is provided |
| **Not required for R > about 300 m** | The effect becomes negligible |

**The full set of curve provisions**, which are designed together:

| Provision | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Superelevation** | **e = V²/(225R)**, e_max **7% plain, 10% hilly, 7% snow-bound** |
| **Minimum radius** | **R = V²/(127(e + f))**, f = 0.15 |
| **Extra widening** | **nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** |
| **Transition length** | **Greatest of** three criteria |
| **Grade compensation** | **(30 + R)/R, max 75/R**; not applied below 4% |

> **All five are needed together on a sharp curve**, and omitting any one produces a curve that is uncomfortable, unsafe, or unusable by heavy vehicles.

**GRADE COMPENSATION deserves particular mention** because its absence has visible consequences:

> A vehicle on a curve already faces **curve resistance** from tyre scrub. Adding a steep gradient makes the **total resistance excessive**, so the gradient is **eased** on the curve.

> **Failing to compensate is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends** — the combination of sharp curve and steep grade exceeds what the vehicle can pull. It is one of the most commonly observed design failures on Nepali hill roads.

**The transition curve** is a **SPIRAL (clothoid)** because its **radius decreases uniformly with length** — exactly matching a driver turning the steering wheel at a steady rate, and providing the length over which superelevation and extra widening are introduced.

examTip.trick: **Mechanical widening is pure GEOMETRY** — rigid wheelbase, so no speed appears: **nl²/2R**. **Psychological widening is BEHAVIOURAL** and does contain speed: **V/(9.5√R)**. The presence or absence of V tells them apart.
examTip.trap: 127 and 254 belong to **superelevation** formulae (e + f = V²/127R), not to widening. Options carrying them are borrowing constants from the wrong equation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rear wheels cut the corner — off-tracking — so l² in the numerator, R below.** A long truck on a tight hairpin needs a lot. And add **GRADE COMPENSATION (30+R)/R**, whose absence is why trucks stall on hairpins.

questions.stem: If 50 kg of fine aggregates and 100 kg of coarse aggregates are mixed in a concrete whose water-cement ratio is 0.6, the weight of water required for a harsh mix is:
questions.solution:
**12 kg.**

**Working.** For a **harsh mix**, the water requirement is:

> **W = 0.30 C + 0.10 FA + 0.01 CA**

> where C, FA and CA are the weights of cement, fine aggregate and coarse aggregate.

> Since **w/c = 0.6**, the cement weight is **C = W/0.6**. Substituting:

> **W = 0.30(W/0.6) + 0.10(50) + 0.01(100)**
> **W = 0.5W + 5 + 1**
> **0.5W = 6**
> **W = 12 kg** ✓

**Check:** cement **C = 12/0.6 = 20 kg**. Then 0.30(20) + 0.10(50) + 0.01(100) = 6 + 5 + 1 = **12** ✓

**Where the three coefficients come from:**

> Each material has a **different surface area per unit weight**, and water is needed both to **hydrate the cement** and to **wet every particle surface**:

| Material | Coefficient | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Cement** | **0.30** | Finest — enormous surface area, **plus the water needed for hydration itself** |
| **Fine aggregate** | **0.10** | Moderate surface area |
| **Coarse aggregate** | **0.01** | Least surface area per unit weight — large particles |

> **The coefficients fall by a factor of about ten at each step**, tracking the fall in specific surface. That progression makes them easy to remember and easy to sanity-check.

**What "harsh" means:**

> A **harsh mix** is one with **just enough water to wet the surfaces and hydrate the cement** — the minimum for the materials to cohere at all. It is **stiff, difficult to place and compact**, and needs vibration.

> Wetter mixes (medium, plastic) use larger coefficients. The harsh mix formula gives the **lower bound**.

**The water–cement ratio is the governing variable in concrete:**

> **ABRAMS' LAW: strength depends primarily on the water–cement ratio**, and inversely so — **lower w/c gives higher strength**, almost regardless of the mix proportions.

| w/c | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Low (0.35–0.45)** | **High strength, low permeability, DURABLE** — but stiff and hard to place |
| **High (0.6–0.7)** | Workable and easy to place — but **weak and PERMEABLE** |

> **Only about 0.25 of water per unit of cement is chemically needed for hydration.** Everything above that is added purely for **workability**, and it eventually **evaporates, leaving CAPILLARY PORES**.

> **Those pores are what make concrete weak and permeable** — and permeability is the master durability property, since every deterioration mechanism (carbonation, chloride ingress, sulphate attack, freeze-thaw) requires something to get **in**.

**Which is why PLASTICISERS exist:**

> A **water-reducing admixture** gives the workability of a wet mix at the w/c of a dry one — **breaking the conflict between placeability and durability** that otherwise forces a compromise.

| Admixture | Water reduction |
|---|---|
| **Plasticiser** | **5 – 15%** |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER** | **15 – 30%** |

> **Superplasticisers are what make high-strength and self-compacting concrete possible at all** — without them, a w/c of 0.3 would be unplaceable.

**Durability limits (IS 456)** tie w/c to exposure directly:

| Exposure | Max w/c | Min grade | Min cement |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **0.55** | M20 | 300 kg/m³ |
| Moderate | 0.50 | M25 | 300 |
| **Severe** | **0.45** | M30 | 320 |
| Very severe | 0.45 | M35 | 340 |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** | M40 | 360 |

> **Note that durability, not strength, often fixes the grade.** A structure in severe exposure needs M30 even if M20 would carry the load — because the concrete must also keep aggressive agents out for fifty years.

examTip.trick: **W = 0.30C + 0.10FA + 0.01CA**, and substitute **C = W/0.6** to get W on both sides: W = 0.5W + 6, so **W = 12 kg**. The self-referencing step is the whole difficulty.
examTip.trap: The coefficients fall **tenfold at each step (0.30 / 0.10 / 0.01)** because they track **specific surface** — cement is finest and also needs water for hydration itself. That pattern makes them checkable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only ~0.25 water per cement is needed for HYDRATION** — the rest is for workability and evaporates, leaving **capillary pores**. Which is why **superplasticisers** (15–30% reduction) break the placeability/durability conflict.

questions.stem: Which of them makes the maximum influence on steel?
questions.solution:
**Carbon.**

**Why.** Steel **IS** iron with carbon — and it is the **carbon content that determines almost every property of the resulting metal**. Iron is the base, not an influence upon it.

> **Carbon significantly affects hardness, strength, ductility and weldability.** Higher carbon gives **harder, stronger steel but LESS ductile and LESS weldable** steel.

**The carbon content classification:**

| Type | Carbon | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrought iron** | **< 0.05%** | Very ductile, weak, easily forged |
| **Mild (low carbon) steel** | **0.05 – 0.25%** | **Ductile, weldable — STRUCTURAL steel** |
| **Medium carbon** | 0.25 – 0.6% | Stronger, less ductile |
| **High carbon** | 0.6 – 1.5% | Hard, brittle; tools, springs |
| **CAST IRON** | **2 – 4%** | **Hard, BRITTLE, good in compression, poor in tension** |

> **The trend is monotonic: as carbon rises, STRENGTH and HARDNESS rise while DUCTILITY and WELDABILITY fall.** One variable governs the whole family.

**Why structural steel is deliberately LOW in carbon:**

> Structural engineering wants **DUCTILITY above all** — the ability to deform substantially before fracture. Ductility gives:

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **WARNING before failure** | Large deflections precede collapse |
| **Moment redistribution** | Indeterminate structures can shed load from overstressed regions |
| **Plastic design** possible | Plastic hinges require rotation capacity |
| **Energy absorption in earthquakes** | The single most important seismic property |
| **Weldability** | Connections can be welded reliably |

> **A stronger but brittle steel would be far more dangerous than a weaker ductile one**, which is why structural specifications cap the carbon rather than maximising strength.

**The CARBON EQUIVALENT** is the practical expression of this:

> **CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr+Mo+V)/5 + (Ni+Cu)/15**

> **CE above about 0.45 indicates poor weldability** — the weld heat-affected zone hardens and cracks. **Preheating is then required**, and above higher values welding becomes impractical.

> **That is why high-strength steels are alloyed rather than simply carburised** — adding manganese, chromium or vanadium raises strength with a far smaller weldability penalty than carbon would.

**The other elements, and why phosphorus is offered:**

| Element | Effect |
|---|---|
| **PHOSPHORUS** | **Harmful** — causes **COLD shortness** (brittleness at low temperature). Limited to ~0.05% |
| **SULPHUR** | **Harmful** — causes **HOT shortness** (brittleness when hot, cracking during rolling). Limited to ~0.05% |
| **Manganese** | Beneficial — strength, and it **neutralises sulphur** |
| **Silicon** | Deoxidiser; some strength |
| **Chromium** | Hardness, **corrosion resistance** (stainless above 11%) |
| **Nickel** | Toughness, especially at low temperature |
| **Aluminium** | **Deoxidiser and GRAIN REFINER** — used in small amounts |

> **Phosphorus and sulphur are the two harmful impurities**, and the pair is worth remembering by their effects: **"P for cold, S for hot"** — **cold shortness from phosphorus, hot shortness from sulphur.**

> **Aluminium is genuinely used in steel** — as a deoxidiser and grain refiner — but in trace amounts, and its influence is nothing like carbon's.

**Structural steel grades (IS 2062):**

| Grade | f_y | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **E250 (Fe 410)** | **250 MPa** | The standard structural grade |
| E350, E410, E450 | Higher | High-strength low-alloy |

> And **E = 200 GPa for ALL steels regardless of grade** — the stiffness is a property of the iron lattice, not of the alloying. **A high-strength steel is not a stiffer steel**, which is why deflection is not improved by specifying a higher grade.

examTip.trick: Steel **IS** iron plus carbon — iron is the base, not an influence on it. **Carbon is the one variable that governs the whole family**, from wrought iron to cast iron.
examTip.trap: **Phosphorus and sulphur are the harmful impurities**: **P gives COLD shortness, S gives HOT shortness.** Both are limited to about 0.05%, and remembering which is which is a standard question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Structural steel is deliberately LOW carbon — ductility matters more than strength.** And **E = 200 GPa for every grade**: a high-strength steel is not a stiffer one, so a higher grade never fixes a deflection problem.

questions.stem: Determine the volume of water stored in unit area if the unit weight of water is 9.8 kN/m³, the dry unit weight of soil is 17 kN/m³, the field capacity (F) is 2.35 m², and the depth of the root zone of the plant is 9 m.
questions.solution:
**36.69 m³.**

**Working.** Field capacity is defined as:

> **F = (γ_w × volume of water stored per unit area)/(γ_d × d)**

> Rearranging for the stored volume:

> **Volume = (γ_d × d × F)/γ_w**
> **= (17 × 9 × 2.35)/9.8**
> **= 359.55/9.8**
> **= 36.69 m³** ✓

> **Note the options are deliberately clustered between 36 and 36.7**, so the arithmetic must be carried through rather than estimated. **359.55/9.8 = 36.69** — carry the decimals.

**What FIELD CAPACITY is:**

> The **moisture content the soil retains AFTER free drainage has ceased** — typically two to three days after saturation. It is the **upper limit of water available to plants**.

**The moisture constants that bracket plant-available water:**

| Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Saturation** | All voids filled — but the excess **drains away under gravity** |
| **FIELD CAPACITY (FC)** | Water held **after free drainage** — the practical upper limit |
| **PERMANENT WILTING POINT (PWP)** | Water held so tightly that **plants cannot extract it** — the lower limit |
| **AVAILABLE WATER = FC − PWP** | What the crop can actually use |
| **Readily available water** | About **50%** of available, before the plant suffers stress |

> **Water above field capacity is NOT useful** — it drains away, and while it is present it **excludes air from the root zone**, suffocating the roots. **Over-irrigation is genuinely harmful**, not merely wasteful.

> **Water below the wilting point is equally useless** — it is there, but held too tightly by the soil particles for roots to extract.

**How available water varies with soil:**

| Soil | Available water | Irrigation practice |
|---|---|---|
| **Sandy** | **LOW** (~60 mm/m) | **Frequent, small applications** |
| Loam | Moderate (~140 mm/m) | Intermediate |
| **Clayey** | **HIGH** (~180 mm/m) | Infrequent, large applications |

> **A sandy soil does not need MORE water in total — it needs the same water MORE OFTEN**, because it cannot hold a large reserve. Confusing frequency with quantity is a standard error.

**The irrigation schedule follows directly:**

> **Irrigation interval = readily available water in the root zone ÷ daily consumptive use**

> And the **depth to apply** is the amount needed to bring the root zone **back up to field capacity** — no more, since anything beyond drains away and takes dissolved nutrients with it.

**Why ROOT DEPTH appears in the formula:**

> **Only water within the root zone is available to the crop.** A deeper-rooted crop draws on a larger reservoir, so it can go longer between irrigations.

| Crop | Root depth |
|---|---|
| **Shallow** (vegetables, rice) | **0.3 – 0.6 m** |
| Medium (wheat, maize) | 0.6 – 1.2 m |
| **Deep** (sugarcane, orchards) | **1.5 – 3 m** |

> **Root depth also grows through the season**, which is why the irrigation interval typically lengthens as the crop matures.

**And the connection to salinity:**

> Irrigation water always carries dissolved salts. **Evapotranspiration removes the water and leaves the salts behind**, so they concentrate in the root zone over time.

> A **LEACHING REQUIREMENT** — extra water applied deliberately to wash salts below the root zone — must be added to the irrigation requirement in arid areas.

> **But leaching only works if there is DRAINAGE.** Without somewhere for the salts to go, the water table rises and the salts return by capillary action. **Leaching without drainage is futile**, and it is how irrigated land is destroyed.

examTip.trick: Rearrange the definition: **Volume = γ_d × d × F / γ_w = 17 × 9 × 2.35 / 9.8**. Carry the decimals — the options are clustered between 36 and 36.7 precisely to punish rounding.
examTip.trap: **Water above field capacity is not useful and is actively harmful** — it drains away and meanwhile excludes air from the root zone. Over-irrigation suffocates roots, it does not merely waste water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Available water = FC − PWP, and irrigate at about 50% depletion.** A **sandy soil needs the same water MORE OFTEN**, not more water — its reservoir is smaller, so the interval shortens.

questions.stem: If 20% of the reservoir capacity is earmarked for dead storage in a storage reservoir of 30 M.cum and the average annual silt deposition in the reservoir is 0.1 M.cum, then the useful life of the reservoir will start reducing after:
questions.solution:
**60 years.**

**Working.**

> **Dead storage = 20% of 30 M.cum = 0.2 × 30 = 6 M.cum**
> **Annual silt deposition = 0.1 M.cum/year**
> **Time to fill the dead storage = 6/0.1 = 60 years** ✓

**Why the question is phrased as "start reducing":**

> **Dead storage exists precisely to receive sediment.** While silt is accumulating within it, **the useful (live) storage is unaffected** — the reservoir delivers its full yield.

> **Only once the dead storage is full does silt begin to encroach on the LIVE storage**, and from that point the reservoir's useful capacity — and therefore its yield — begins to fall.

> **So 60 years is not the reservoir's life; it is the point at which its life begins to be consumed.** That distinction is the whole point of the question, and it is why the answer is not simply 30/0.1 = 300 years (total fill) nor some fraction of it.

**The reservoir storage zones:**

| Zone | Between | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **DEAD storage** | Bed level and **minimum pool level (MDDL)** | **Sediment**; keeps the intake submerged |
| **LIVE (useful) storage** | Minimum pool and **full reservoir level (FRL)** | The **usable** water |
| **Flood (surcharge)** | FRL and **maximum water level (MWL)** | Temporary, during a flood |
| Freeboard | Above MWL | Waves, settlement, safety |

**Why sediment gives a reservoir a finite life:**

> **Every reservoir is a sediment trap.** The impounded water slows, its transport capacity collapses, and the sediment it was carrying **deposits permanently**.

> **TRAP EFFICIENCY** — the fraction of incoming sediment retained — is typically **90–99% for a large storage reservoir**, and it depends on the **capacity-to-inflow ratio** (Brune's curve). A large reservoir on a small river traps nearly everything.

**Why this matters acutely in Nepal:**

> Himalayan rivers carry **very heavy sediment loads** — among the highest in the world — because of steep slopes, active tectonics, monsoon intensity and fragile geology.

> **Several Nepali reservoirs have lost storage far faster than their design assumed**, because international sedimentation rates were applied to a far more aggressive environment.

**Sediment management options:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate dead storage** | Passive — buys time, does not solve |
| **Sluicing and FLUSHING** | **Drawing the reservoir down** so the river scours its own deposits out |
| **Density current venting** | Passing the turbid underflow through **low-level outlets** during a flood |
| **CATCHMENT management** | Reafforestation, check dams — treats the cause, but slow and hard to enforce |
| Dredging | Very expensive; rarely economic at scale |

> **FLUSHING is the most effective active measure**, but it requires the reservoir to be **drawn down** — giving up stored water and generation. It is therefore scheduled for the **end of the monsoon**, when inflows will refill the reservoir afterwards.

> **Density current venting is elegant** because it costs nothing: the sediment-laden inflow, being denser, plunges beneath the clear reservoir water and travels along the bed as a distinct current. **Opening a low-level outlet at the right moment vents it straight through the dam.** The timing is the difficulty.

**The design implication:**

> **Dead storage must be sized from a realistic local sediment yield**, not a textbook figure — and the sediment yield should be measured, not assumed. **Getting it wrong shortens the project's economic life directly**, and there is no remedy once the dam is built.

**Sizing the LIVE storage** is a separate problem, solved by a **MASS CURVE (Rippl's method)**: the **largest vertical gap** between the cumulative inflow curve and the cumulative demand line gives the storage required.

examTip.trick: Two steps: **dead storage = 0.2 × 30 = 6 M.cum**, then **6/0.1 = 60 years**. The question asks when the useful life *starts* reducing — that is when the dead storage fills, not when the reservoir does.
examTip.trap: **60 years is not the reservoir's life** — it is when its life begins to be consumed. Computing 30/0.1 = 300 years (total fill) answers a different question entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Trap efficiency is 90–99% for a large reservoir** — it catches nearly everything. In Nepal, size dead storage from a **measured local sediment yield**, not a textbook figure. **FLUSHING at the end of the monsoon** is the effective remedy.

questions.stem: A dry specimen is put through a triaxial test with a cell pressure of 50 kPa and a deviator stress at failure of 100 kPa. What is the angle of internal friction?
questions.solution:
**30°.**

> **Note on the source:** the paper prints the cell pressure as 150 kPa, but its **own worked solution uses 50 kPa**, and only 50 kPa produces the keyed answer of 30°. The stem is given here with the value the answer key actually used.

**Working.** For a **cohesionless (c = 0)** soil, the Mohr–Coulomb envelope passes through the origin, and:

> **sin φ = (σ₁ − σ₃)/(σ₁ + σ₃)**

> **σ₃ = cell pressure = 50 kPa**
> **σ_d = deviator stress = 100 kPa**
> **σ₁ = σ₃ + σ_d = 50 + 100 = 150 kPa**

> **sin φ = (150 − 50)/(150 + 50) = 100/200 = 0.5**
> **φ = 30°** ✓

**Where the formula comes from** — it is pure Mohr's circle geometry:

> The failure envelope through the origin is **tangent to the circle**. The circle's **centre is at (σ₁ + σ₃)/2** and its **radius is (σ₁ − σ₃)/2**.

> **sin φ = radius/distance to centre = [(σ₁ − σ₃)/2] ÷ [(σ₁ + σ₃)/2] = (σ₁ − σ₃)/(σ₁ + σ₃)** ✓

> **Knowing the derivation means never mis-remembering whether it is sine or tangent**, and it makes the c ≠ 0 case obvious too.

**The alternative form**, worth carrying:

> **σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45 + φ/2)** for c = 0

> Check: tan²(45 + 15) = tan²60 = 3, and 50 × 3 = **150** ✓

> Note that **tan²(45 + φ/2) = K_p**, the passive earth pressure coefficient — the **same expression appears in earth pressure theory**, because both describe a soil at failure.

**When cohesion is present:**

> **σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45 + φ/2) + 2c tan(45 + φ/2)**

> and the general relation becomes **sin φ = (σ₁ − σ₃)/(σ₁ + σ₃ + 2c cot φ)**.

**Why "dry specimen" matters in the stem:**

> A **dry** soil has **no pore water**, so **total stress equals effective stress** — the test gives **φ′ directly**, with no drainage question to consider.

**The three triaxial test types:**

| Test | Drainage | Gives | Models |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UU (unconsolidated undrained)** | Neither stage | **c_u, φ_u = 0** for saturated clay | **Short-term** loading |
| **CU (consolidated undrained)** | Consolidate, then shear undrained | **c′, φ′** if pore pressure is measured | Most versatile |
| **CD (consolidated drained)** | Both stages | **c′, φ′** directly | **Long-term** |

> **CU with pore pressure measurement is the workhorse**, because it gives effective stress parameters **far faster than a CD test** — a drained test on clay can take weeks, since the shearing rate must be slow enough for pore pressures to dissipate throughout.

**Typical φ′ values:**

| Soil | φ′ |
|---|---|
| Loose sand | 28 – 32° |
| **Dense sand** | **35 – 45°** |
| Gravel | 34 – 45° |
| **Normally consolidated clay** | **20 – 30°** |
| Over-consolidated clay | 20 – 30° with some c′ |

> **φ = 30° is a very typical value for a medium sand**, so the answer passes a sanity check — while 60° and 90° are physically impossible for any soil, and could be discarded on sight.

**Why the triaxial test is preferred to the direct shear box:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drainage is CONTROLLED** | The box cannot control it |
| **Pore pressure can be MEASURED** | Giving effective stresses |
| **The failure plane is not predetermined** | The specimen fails on its weakest plane, not on the plane the apparatus imposes |
| Stress state is known throughout | — |

> **The direct shear box forces failure on a horizontal plane** whether or not that is the weakest one — which can overstate the strength of an anisotropic soil.

verification.notes: The stem as printed gives a cell pressure of 150 kPa, but the source answer key’s own worked solution uses 50 kPa, and only 50 kPa yields the keyed answer of 30 degrees. With 150 kPa the result would be 14.5 degrees, which is not among the options. The stem is therefore reproduced with 50 kPa, the value the key actually computed with; the options and the keyed answer are unchanged.

examTip.trick: **sin φ = (σ₁ − σ₃)/(σ₁ + σ₃)** for c = 0 — and it is just Mohr's circle geometry: **radius ÷ distance to centre**. Remember σ₁ = σ₃ + deviator, not the deviator alone.
examTip.trap: **σ₁ is the CELL pressure PLUS the deviator stress**, not the deviator by itself. Using σ₁ = 100 here would give sin φ = 50/150 = 0.33 and φ = 19.5° — not an option, which is the warning.
examTip.mnemonic: **60° and 90° are impossible for any soil** — dense sand tops out around 45°. Sanity-check the answer before computing. And **tan²(45 + φ/2) = K_p**, the same expression as in earth pressure theory.

questions.stem: Identify the correct statement about hydropower.
options: Hydropower stations are generally labour oriented
The gestation period for a hydropower plant is usually small
The hydro generators give high efficiency over a wide range of load
In a hydropower scheme, the firm power is usually high as compared to tidal power
questions.solution:
**Hydro generators give high efficiency over a wide range of load.**

**Why this is hydropower's defining operational advantage:**

> A hydro unit maintains **high efficiency from part load to full load**, and can **change output within seconds**. A thermal plant, by contrast, loses efficiency sharply off its design point and takes **hours** to change output significantly.

| Capability | Hydro | Thermal |
|---|---|---|
| **Part-load efficiency** | **High** | Falls sharply |
| **Start-up time** | **Minutes — or seconds from spinning** | **Hours** |
| **Rate of change** | **Very fast** | Slow |
| **Black start** | **Yes** | Usually not |

> **That flexibility is why hydro is used for PEAKING and for FREQUENCY CONTROL**, and why its value to a grid exceeds the energy it produces. A system with hydro can absorb the variability of solar and wind that would otherwise need expensive fast-response plant.

> Note the qualification: **a FRANCIS turbine is poor below about 40% load**, while **Pelton (individual jets shut off) and Kaplan (double regulation) are excellent at part load.** The statement is true of hydro plant as a class and of the **generator**, which is what the option says.

**Why each other statement is false:**

| Statement | Reality |
|---|---|
| **"Labour oriented"** | **Hydro is CAPITAL intensive, not labour intensive.** Operating staff are few — many plants run largely unattended |
| **"Gestation period is small"** | **The opposite.** Hydro has a **LONG gestation** — investigation, licensing, land, resettlement and construction take many years. This is its principal commercial disadvantage |
| **"Firm power high compared to tidal"** | **A run-of-river scheme's firm power is LOW**, being limited by the dry-season flow. **Tidal power is highly PREDICTABLE** — the tides are known centuries ahead — so its availability is more certain, even if intermittent |

> **The gestation statement is the most instructive falsehood.** A long gestation means **years of capital committed before any revenue**, which is exactly what makes hydro financing difficult and why interest during construction is such a large part of project cost.

**Hydropower's characteristics in full:**

| Advantage | Disadvantage |
|---|---|
| **Renewable**; no fuel cost | **Very high CAPITAL cost** |
| **Long life — 50 to 100 years** | **LONG gestation period** |
| **Low operating and maintenance cost** | **Site specific** — cannot be built where convenient |
| **Fast response; excellent part-load efficiency** | **Dependent on hydrology** — drought risk |
| **High overall efficiency (85–90%)** | **Environmental and social impacts** — inundation, resettlement, fish migration |
| **Black start capability** | Sedimentation shortens life |

> **The economic profile is the opposite of thermal**: high capital, near-zero running cost, long life. That makes hydro extremely sensitive to the **discount rate** — a high rate makes a 50-year asset look poor, because distant benefits are discounted almost to nothing.

**For Nepal specifically:**

> The structural problem is **seasonal mismatch**: **about 80% of the flow arrives in four monsoon months**, while demand peaks in the dry winter evening.

| Solution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Storage projects** | Convert monsoon surplus into dry-season supply |
| **Peaking run-of-river (PROR)** | Pondage for the daily peak |
| **Cross-border trade** | Export the monsoon surplus, import in the dry season |
| **Pumped storage** | Addresses the **daily** mismatch |

> **Nepal's terrain gives high head over short horizontal distances**, which is exactly what makes hydro cheap to build here — and the same steepness makes **sediment** the principal engineering challenge.

examTip.trick: Hydro's real advantage is **FLEXIBILITY** — high efficiency across the load range and output changes in seconds, against a thermal plant's hours. That is worth more to a grid than the energy itself.
examTip.trap: **"Small gestation period" is the exact opposite of the truth**, and it is hydro's principal commercial weakness — years of capital committed before any revenue, which is why interest during construction dominates project cost.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hydro is CAPITAL intensive, not labour intensive**: high first cost, near-zero running cost, 50–100 year life. That profile makes it acutely sensitive to the **discount rate** used in appraisal.

questions.stem: What is the incompressibility condition in the Navier–Stokes equation?
questions.solution:
**∇·u = 0** — the divergence of the velocity field is zero.

**What it means physically.** The divergence measures the **net rate of volume outflow per unit volume** at a point.

| Divergence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **∇·u > 0** | The fluid is **EXPANDING** at that point — a source |
| **∇·u < 0** | The fluid is **COMPRESSING** — a sink |
| **∇·u = 0** | **Volume is CONSERVED** — incompressible |

> **So ∇·u = 0 says: whatever volume flows into a point flows out of it.** No fluid accumulates and none disappears.

**It is the CONTINUITY equation for constant density.** The general continuity equation is:

> **∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρu) = 0**

> For **constant ρ**, this reduces directly to **∇·u = 0** ✓

**In Cartesian components:**

> **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0**

> which is the **three-dimensional continuity equation** met in every fluid mechanics course. **The vector form and the component form are the same statement.**

**Recognising the one-dimensional version:**

> For steady flow in a pipe, integrating gives **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂** — the familiar **Q = AV = constant**.

> **The elementary continuity relation used in every pipe problem IS ∇·u = 0**, integrated over a cross-section. Seeing that connection makes the vector statement far less abstract.

**Why the other options are impossible:**

> **∇·u > 0 or < 0** would mean fluid is being **created or destroyed** at a point, or that its density is changing — neither of which is permitted in incompressible flow.

> **∇·u = 1** is dimensionally meaningless as a general condition: divergence has units of **1/time**, so setting it to a pure number is not a physical statement at all.

**The Navier–Stokes equations themselves:**

> **ρ(∂u/∂t + u·∇u) = −∇p + μ∇²u + ρg**

| Term | Represents |
|---|---|
| **ρ ∂u/∂t** | **Local (temporal) acceleration** |
| **ρ u·∇u** | **CONVECTIVE acceleration** — the **non-linear** term |
| **−∇p** | Pressure gradient |
| **μ∇²u** | **Viscous** forces |
| **ρg** | Body force (gravity) |

> **They are simply Newton's second law applied to a fluid element**, plus continuity to close the system.

**Why they cannot generally be solved:**

> The **convective term u·∇u is NON-LINEAR**, and that non-linearity is the source of **TURBULENCE** — and of the fact that no general analytical solution exists.

> **A general proof of existence and smoothness for the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations remains one of the unsolved Millennium Prize problems.**

**How engineering copes:**

| Simplification | Result |
|---|---|
| **Drop viscosity (μ = 0)** | **EULER equations** → **Bernoulli** along a streamline |
| **Drop the convective term** (creeping flow) | **Stokes flow** — sedimentation, lubrication |
| **Boundary layer approximation** | **PRANDTL's** great simplification — viscosity matters only in a thin layer |
| **Time-average the turbulence** | **RANS equations** + a turbulence model — the basis of CFD |

> **PRANDTL's boundary layer concept is the one that made aerodynamics and hydraulics tractable**: outside a thin layer near the surface, the flow behaves as if inviscid and Bernoulli applies; inside it, viscosity dominates. **That division is why Bernoulli works at all in practice**, despite every real fluid having viscosity.

examTip.trick: **Divergence = net volume outflow per unit volume.** Setting it to zero says whatever flows in flows out — which is exactly **continuity for constant density**.
examTip.trap: **∇·u = 1 is dimensionally meaningless** — divergence has units of 1/time, so equating it to a pure number is not a physical statement. That alone eliminates option (d).
examTip.mnemonic: **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0 IS ∇·u = 0**, and integrating it over a section gives the familiar **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂**. The pipe formula you already use is this equation.

questions.stem: The area of a channel section is 8 m² and the wetted perimeter is 8 m. Calculate the bed slope of the channel if the discharge is 33.33 m³/s and Manning's coefficient is 0.012.
questions.solution:
**1 in 400.**

**Working.**

> **Hydraulic radius R = A/P = 8/8 = 1 m**
>
> **Manning: Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**
> **33.33 = (1/0.012) × 8 × 1^{2/3} × S^{1/2}**
> **33.33 = 83.33 × 8 × S^{1/2}**
> **33.33 = 666.67 S^{1/2}**
> **S^{1/2} = 0.05**
> **S = 0.0025 = 1/400** ✓

> **R = 1 m is the gift in this problem** — it makes **R^{2/3} = 1**, removing the awkward fractional power entirely. **Compute R first and check whether it simplifies** before reaching for a calculator.

**Manning's equation:**

> **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}** and **Q = AV**

**A caution about the formula:**

> It is **EMPIRICAL and dimensionally inhomogeneous** — the 1/n carries hidden units, so **the equation as written applies only in SI**. In foot-pound units the coefficient becomes **1.486/n**.

> **That is why Manning's n is never quoted with units**, and why blindly transferring the formula between systems is an error.

**How the quantities scale:**

| Relation | Dependence |
|---|---|
| **V** | **∝ 1/n**, ∝ R^{2/3}, ∝ S^{1/2} |
| **Q** | ∝ A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}/n |
| **S** at fixed V and R | **∝ n²** |

> **The last relation is worth carrying: doubling the roughness QUADRUPLES the slope needed** for the same velocity.

> **That quadratic penalty is why canal LINING pays so well** — halving n from an earth channel's 0.025 to a concrete lining's 0.014 lets the same discharge run on about **a third of the slope**, or the same slope carry far more.

**Typical Manning's n:**

| Surface | n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth concrete** | **0.012** — as here |
| Ordinary concrete lining | 0.014 |
| Brickwork | 0.015 |
| **Earth channel, clean** | **0.022** |
| Earth, weedy or winding | 0.030 |
| **Natural stream, clean** | **0.030** |
| Stony, irregular stream | 0.040 – 0.070 |

> The whole practical range is only about **0.012 to 0.07** — a factor of six. But since **S ∝ n²**, that becomes a factor of **36** in slope, which is why estimating n well matters so much in natural channel work.

**The most efficient section:**

> For a given area, the section with the **least wetted perimeter** carries the most — because **R = A/P** is then greatest.

| Shape | Most efficient proportions | R |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **b = 2y** — width twice the depth | **y/2** |
| **Trapezoidal** | A **half-hexagon**, side slope 1:√3 (60°) | **y/2** |
| **Any shape** | A **SEMICIRCLE** — the theoretical optimum | **y/2** |

> **For every efficient section, R = y/2** — a neat and genuinely useful result.

> Note that **this channel has R = 1 m**, so if it were a most-efficient section its depth would be **2 m**. With A = 8 m², an efficient rectangular section would be **4 m wide by 2 m deep** — and indeed P = 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 m ✓. **The problem's numbers describe exactly the most efficient rectangular section**, which is a neat piece of construction.

**Why the semicircle wins:** it encloses the greatest area for a given perimeter, of any shape. It is rarely built because it is awkward to construct and maintain — which is why the **half-hexagon trapezoid** is the practical optimum for an earth channel, and **b = 2y** for a lined rectangular one.

examTip.trick: **Compute R = A/P first.** Here R = 8/8 = **1 m**, so **R^{2/3} = 1** and the awkward power disappears entirely. Examination problems are usually constructed this way.
examTip.trap: Manning's equation is **dimensionally inhomogeneous** — the 1/n hides units, so the SI form is not transferable. In foot-pound units the coefficient becomes **1.486/n**.
examTip.mnemonic: **S ∝ n², so doubling roughness QUADRUPLES the required slope** — which is the whole economic case for lining. And for **every most-efficient section, R = y/2**; here R = 1 m implies a 4 m × 2 m rectangle, which these numbers exactly describe.

questions.stem: For a fixed-end beam of length L carrying a central point load W, what will be the value of W at collapse?
questions.solution:
**W = 8 M_p/L.**

**Working — the mechanism method (virtual work).**

> A fixed beam is indeterminate to the **second degree (D_s = 2)**, so collapse requires **D_s + 1 = 3 plastic hinges**: at **both fixed ends** and at **midspan**.

> Give the midspan a virtual displacement **δ**. With hinges at the ends rotating **θ** and the central hinge rotating **2θ**:

> **δ = (L/2) θ**

> **External work = W δ = W (L/2) θ**
> **Internal work = M_p θ + M_p (2θ) + M_p θ = 4 M_p θ**

> Equating:
> **W (L/2) θ = 4 M_p θ**
> **W = 8 M_p/L** ✓

> **The central hinge rotates 2θ, not θ** — because both halves of the beam rotate toward it. **Missing that factor of two gives 4M_p/L**, which is the standard error in this calculation.

**The standard collapse loads** worth carrying:

| Beam | Loading | Collapse load |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | Central point load | **W = 4M_p/L** |
| **FIXED both ends** | **Central point load** | **W = 8M_p/L** |
| Simply supported | UDL | w = 8M_p/L² |
| **Fixed both ends** | UDL | **w = 16M_p/L²** |
| Propped cantilever | Central point load | W = 6M_p/L |

> **Notice the pattern: fixing both ends DOUBLES the collapse load** in every case. That is a satisfying result and a useful check.

**The three theorems of plastic analysis:**

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **STATIC (lower bound)** | Any load for which a **safe, statically admissible** moment distribution exists is **≤ the collapse load** |
| **KINEMATIC (upper bound)** | Any load computed from an **assumed mechanism** is **≥ the collapse load** |
| **UNIQUENESS** | If a distribution is both **safe and a mechanism**, it **IS the collapse load** |

> **The kinematic theorem is the practical warning: an assumed mechanism gives an answer on the UNSAFE side.** So when several mechanisms are possible, **the LOWEST computed load is the governing one** — and every plausible mechanism must be checked.

> For a frame, that means checking the **beam mechanism, the sway mechanism, and their COMBINED mechanism** — and the combined one frequently governs, which is why it must never be omitted.

**Key plastic design concepts:**

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Plastic hinge** | A section fully yielded, **rotating at constant M_p** |
| **Number of hinges for collapse** | **D_s + 1** |
| **Shape factor S** | **M_p/M_y** — the reserve between first yield and full plasticity |
| **Plastic modulus Z_p** | **S × Z_elastic** |
| **Load factor** | **Collapse load ÷ working load** |

**Shape factors:**

| Section | S |
|---|---|
| **I-section (major axis)** | **1.12 – 1.15** |
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **1.7** |
| **Diamond** | **2.0** |

> **The more material already at the extreme fibres, the LOWER the shape factor** — an I-section has little reserve because it is already efficient elastically; a diamond has a great deal because most of its material sits near the neutral axis doing nothing.

**The essential validity condition:**

> **Plastic analysis requires DUCTILITY** — the section must be able to **rotate at M_p without buckling locally**.

> **That is why IS 800 classifies sections as PLASTIC, compact, semi-compact and slender by their b/t ratios**, and why **plastic design requires a PLASTIC section**. A slender section buckles locally before the hinge can form, and the whole analysis becomes invalid.

> It also explains why plastic methods apply to **structural steel** and not to concrete, cast iron or any brittle material.

examTip.trick: **Fixing both ends DOUBLES the collapse load**: simply supported gives 4M_p/L, fixed gives **8M_p/L**. The same doubling holds for a UDL (8M_p/L² → 16M_p/L²).
examTip.trap: **The central hinge rotates 2θ, not θ**, because both halves rotate toward it. Missing that factor of two gives 4M_p/L — the standard error in the virtual work calculation.
examTip.mnemonic: **The KINEMATIC theorem means an assumed mechanism errs on the UNSAFE side** — so among several mechanisms, take the **LOWEST** load. For frames, always check the **combined** mechanism, which often governs.

questions.stem: Tie bars in rigid pavements are provided across:
questions.solution:
**Longitudinal joints.**

**The two bar types, which are constantly confused:**

| | **TIE BAR** | **DOWEL BAR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | **HOLD the slabs together** — prevent them separating | **TRANSFER load** across the joint |
| **Joint** | **LONGITUDINAL** (parallel to traffic) | **TRANSVERSE** (contraction, expansion) |
| **Type of bar** | **DEFORMED** — must grip the concrete | **PLAIN, SMOOTH, and greased or capped at one end** |
| Movement allowed | **None intended** — it resists separation | **Free to slide along its axis** |
| Designed for | **Tension** | **Shear and bearing** |

> **The single sentence that settles every question on this: TIE bars TIE (hold together, deformed, longitudinal); DOWEL bars carry the LOAD across (smooth, transverse).**

**Why the bar type matters so much:**

> A **dowel MUST be smooth and greased at one end** so the slab can **slide freely along it** as the concrete expands and contracts with temperature.

> **Using a deformed bar as a dowel LOCKS the joint.** The slab can then no longer expand — and it cracks, producing exactly the uncontrolled cracking the joint was built to prevent.

> **That is a real and damaging construction error**, and it is why the distinction is examined so often. A locked contraction joint is worse than no joint at all.

**The joints in a rigid pavement:**

| Joint | Direction | Purpose | Bars |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION** | Transverse | Allow **shrinkage**; **control where cracks form** | **Dowels** |
| **EXPANSION** | Transverse | Allow **thermal expansion**; has a compressible filler | **Dowels** (one end capped) |
| **LONGITUDINAL** | Parallel to traffic | Control **warping** cracking; separate lanes | **TIE BARS** |
| Construction | Either | End of a day's work | As appropriate |

**Why longitudinal joints need tying rather than dowelling:**

> Adjacent lanes must **stay together** — if they separate, water enters the gap, the subgrade softens, and the lanes settle differentially, producing a step at the joint.

> But there is **no significant thermal movement across the width** to accommodate, unlike along the length. **So the joint is tied shut, not allowed to open.**

**Contraction joints and the logic of "controlled cracking":**

> Concrete **will** crack as it shrinks — that is unavoidable. **A contraction joint decides WHERE.** By sawing a groove to about a quarter of the slab depth, a plane of weakness is created and the crack forms there, straight and sealed, instead of wandering randomly across the slab.

> **The timing of the saw cut is critical** — too early and the concrete ravels at the cut; too late and the slab has already cracked somewhere else.

**Stresses in a rigid pavement** (Westergaard):

| Load position | Note |
|---|---|
| **Interior** | Load in the middle of the slab |
| **EDGE** | **Usually the most critical for load stress** |
| **CORNER** | Critical when **warping** stresses combine — supported on only two sides |

> **The corner is the weakest point of a slab**, which is why dowels at transverse joints matter: they let an adjacent slab share the load rather than leaving the corner to carry it alone.

**WARPING stresses are unique to rigid pavements and often exceed the traffic stresses:**

| Effect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **WARPING** | A **temperature GRADIENT through the slab depth** — the top expands more than the bottom by day, less by night |
| **Frictional** | **Uniform** temperature change resisted by subgrade friction |

> **The critical design combination is the worst load position TOGETHER WITH the worst warping condition** — and it is frequently **warping, not traffic, that cracks a concrete pavement.**

> That is why slab **length** is limited (typically 4.5 m between contraction joints): a longer slab develops larger warping stresses and larger frictional restraint.

examTip.trick: **TIE bars TIE slabs together — deformed, longitudinal. DOWEL bars carry LOAD across — smooth, greased, transverse.** One sentence covers every question on this pair.
examTip.trap: **Using a deformed bar as a dowel LOCKS the joint**, preventing the thermal movement it exists to allow — and the slab cracks elsewhere. A real and damaging construction error, not a technicality.
examTip.mnemonic: **The CORNER is a slab's weakest point** (supported on two sides only), which is why dowels matter. And **WARPING stresses often exceed traffic stresses** — which is why slab length is capped at about 4.5 m.

questions.stem: In penetration macadam construction, the bitumen is:
options: Sprayed after the aggregates are spread and compacted
Premixed with aggregates and then spread
Sprayed before the aggregates are spread and compacted
questions.solution:
**Sprayed AFTER the aggregates are spread and compacted.**

**The construction sequence:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Coarse aggregate is spread and compacted DRY** |
| **2** | **Hot bitumen of relatively high viscosity is sprayed** over the compacted layer in fairly large quantity |
| **3** | The bitumen **PENETRATES into the voids from the surface**, filling part of them and **binding the stones together** |
| **4** | Key aggregate is spread and rolled |

> **The name says exactly what happens: the bitumen PENETRATES a pre-laid aggregate skeleton.** It is applied to the compacted stone, not mixed with it beforehand.

**The contrast with a PREMIX:**

| | **PENETRATION macadam** | **PREMIX (bituminous macadam, BC)** |
|---|---|---|
| Bitumen applied | **AFTER compaction, by spraying** | **Mixed with the aggregate BEFORE laying** |
| Coating | **Partial** — only where the binder reaches | **Every particle coated uniformly** |
| Plant needed | **None — done in place** | **Hot mix plant** |
| Quality control | Limited | **Good — proportions controlled at the plant** |
| Use | **Base or binder course** | Base, binder or **wearing course** |

> **Option (b) describes a PREMIX**, which is a genuinely different construction — and the modern standard, because a mixing plant gives control over binder content that spraying on site cannot match.

**Full grout versus semi grout** (from the source's own note):

| Type | Bitumen quantity | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **Full grout** | More — voids substantially filled | **Regions of HEAVY rainfall** |
| **Semi grout** | Less | **Moderate rainfall and traffic** |

> **Heavy rainfall calls for full grout** because a more completely sealed layer resists water ingress — and water in the base is what destroys a flexible pavement.

**Where penetration macadam sits among the surfacing types:**

| Treatment | Description |
|---|---|
| **Surface dressing (seal coat)** | Binder sprayed, chips spread and rolled — **a seal, not a structural layer** |
| **PENETRATION MACADAM** | **Aggregate laid first, binder sprayed into it** — base or binder course |
| **Bituminous macadam (BM)** | **Premixed**, open graded — binder course |
| **Dense bituminous macadam (DBM)** | Premixed, dense graded — binder course |
| **Bituminous concrete (BC)** | **Premixed, dense graded, highest quality — WEARING course** |

> **The progression is toward greater control**: spraying in place → premixing in a plant → precisely graded dense mixes. **Bituminous concrete is the top of that progression**, with the aggregate grading, binder content and voids all controlled by Marshall design.

**The essential prime and tack coats**, which are often confused:

| Coat | Applied to | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **PRIME coat** | A **granular (unbound) base** | **Penetrates and binds the surface**, and waterproofs it before the bituminous layer |
| **TACK coat** | An **existing bituminous or concrete surface** | **Provides BOND** between the old surface and the new layer |

> **Prime is for an absorbent granular surface; tack is for bonding to a non-absorbent one.** Using the wrong one — or omitting the tack coat — leads to **layer separation and slippage failure**, where the surfacing shears off the layer beneath under braking.

**And the temperature discipline** that governs all bituminous work:

> Mixing at about **150 °C**, laying above about **120 °C**, and **compaction completed before the mix cools below about 90 °C**.

> **Rolling a cooled mix achieves nothing** — the binder has stiffened and the aggregate will not move into place. **The compaction window is short**, which is why paving is organised around keeping the rollers close behind the paver.

examTip.trick: The name tells you: the bitumen **PENETRATES** a pre-laid, pre-compacted aggregate skeleton. It is sprayed **onto** the stone, never mixed with it first.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) describes a PREMIX** — a genuinely different and more modern construction, since a mixing plant controls binder content far better than site spraying can.
examTip.mnemonic: **PRIME coat on a granular base (penetrates and seals); TACK coat on an existing bituminous surface (bonds).** Omitting the tack coat causes **slippage failure** — the surfacing shears off under braking.

questions.stem: Two identical pipes of length L, diameter D and friction f are connected in parallel between two points. The length of a single pipe of diameter D and the same friction f, equivalent to the above pair, is:
questions.solution:
**L/4.**

**Working.** For pipes in **parallel**, the **head loss across each is the SAME**, and the **discharges ADD**. Two identical pipes therefore each carry **Q/2**.

> Head loss in one of the parallel pipes, using **h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵)**:
>
> **h_f = fL(Q/2)²/(12.1 D⁵) = fLQ²/(4 × 12.1 D⁵)**

> For a single equivalent pipe of length **L′**, same D and f, carrying the **full Q**:
>
> **h_f′ = fL′Q²/(12.1 D⁵)**

> Setting them equal:
> **fLQ²/(4 × 12.1 D⁵) = fL′Q²/(12.1 D⁵)**
> **L′ = L/4** ✓

**The physical reading:**

> Two pipes in parallel **halve the flow in each**, and since **head loss goes as Q²**, halving the discharge **quarters the loss**.

> **A single pipe producing that same quarter-loss must be a quarter as long.** The factor of four comes entirely from the **square** in the head loss relation.

**Series versus parallel — the rules that govern every pipe network problem:**

| | **SERIES** | **PARALLEL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Discharge** | **SAME in each pipe** | **ADDS: Q = Q₁ + Q₂** |
| **Head loss** | **ADDS: h = h₁ + h₂** | **SAME across each** |

> **The two are exact mirror images**, and confusing them is the commonest error in pipe network problems. **Note the direct analogy with electrical circuits**: discharge behaves like current, head loss like voltage, and pipe resistance like electrical resistance.

> **Series pipes add resistance; parallel pipes reduce it** — exactly as resistors do.

**The head loss relations:**

> **Darcy–Weisbach: h_f = fLV²/(2gD)**
>
> Substituting **V = 4Q/πD²** gives **h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵)** — the form used above.

> **The 12.1 is simply 2g(π/4)² × ... collected**, and the important content is the powers: **h_f ∝ Q²** and **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵**.

**The D⁵ dependence is the one with practical consequences:**

> **A 10% larger pipe cuts the head loss by nearly 40%**; a 20% larger pipe by about 60%.

> **That extraordinary sensitivity is why the ECONOMIC diameter is usually larger than intuition suggests** — capital cost rises roughly with D or D², while running cost falls with D⁵, and the running cost recurs every year for the asset's life.

**A caution on "equivalent pipe" problems:**

> **An equivalent pipe is equivalent only for the DISCHARGE at which it was computed**, unless the diameters and friction factors match — because the Q² relation is non-linear.

> Here the diameter and f are the same, so the equivalence holds generally. **Where diameters differ, the equivalent length must be recomputed for each operating condition.**

**Minor losses**, for completeness:

| Loss | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Sudden expansion** | **(V₁ − V₂)²/2g** — the only one derived from **momentum** rather than measured |
| Sudden contraction | 0.5 V²/2g |
| Entry | 0.5 V²/2g |
| **Exit** | **1.0 V²/2g** — the **entire** velocity head is lost |
| Bends, valves | k V²/2g |

> **Minor losses are negligible in a long pipeline but dominant in a short one with many fittings.** The rule of thumb is that they matter when the pipe length is less than about **1000 diameters** — which covers most pumping station and treatment plant pipework.

examTip.trick: Two parallel pipes **halve the flow in each**, and since **h_f ∝ Q²**, half the flow gives a **quarter** of the loss — so the equivalent single pipe is a **quarter as long**. The square does all the work.
examTip.trap: **SERIES: same Q, head losses ADD. PARALLEL: same head loss, discharges ADD.** They are exact mirror images and are constantly swapped — the electrical analogy (current/voltage/resistance) keeps them straight.
examTip.mnemonic: **h_f ∝ Q²/D⁵** — the inverse fifth power means a 10% larger pipe cuts loss nearly **40%**. That is why economic diameters come out larger than intuition suggests.

questions.stem: In a treatment plant, if BOD decreases from 300 mg/l to 30 mg/l, then the efficiency of the treatment plant is:
questions.solution:
**90%.**

**Working.**

> **Efficiency (%) = [(BOD_initial − BOD_final)/BOD_initial] × 100**
> **= [(300 − 30)/300] × 100**
> **= (270/300) × 100**
> **= 90%** ✓

> **The arithmetic is trivial; the value is in knowing what the number means.**

**What 90% BOD removal represents:**

> This is the performance expected of a **complete secondary (biological) treatment** — typically an **activated sludge plant or a trickling filter following primary sedimentation**.

| Treatment stage | Typical BOD removal | Cumulative |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary sedimentation** | **30 – 35%** | 35% |
| **Secondary (biological)** | **80 – 90% of what remains** | **85 – 95% overall** |
| Tertiary | Further polishing | 95%+ |

> **90% overall is characteristic of a well-operating secondary plant** — so the answer is a plausible design figure, not an arbitrary number.

**Note the efficiencies are SEQUENTIAL, not additive:**

> **The secondary stage removes 80–90% of what the primary stage LEFT**, not 80–90% of the original. Adding the percentages (35 + 85 = 120%) is obviously wrong, and the correct combination is:

> **Overall removal = 1 − (1 − 0.35)(1 − 0.85) = 1 − 0.65 × 0.15 = 0.90** ✓

> **Removals compound the way efficiencies multiply**, which is the same principle as irrigation efficiency and the same trap.

**Whether 90% is enough depends entirely on the receiving water:**

> **300 mg/l → 30 mg/l** leaves an effluent at **30 mg/l**, which meets the typical discharge standard (often **30–50 mg/l**).

> **But a percentage is not a standard.** A very strong industrial wastewater at 3000 mg/l treated to 90% still discharges at **300 mg/l** — a gross pollution load, despite the same efficiency.

> **Discharge consents are therefore written as CONCENTRATIONS (and often as LOADS in kg/day), not as percentage removals** — because it is the mass of oxygen-demanding matter reaching the river that matters, not the fraction removed.

**Why BOD matters — the receiving water:**

> Organic matter discharged to a river **consumes its dissolved oxygen**. If DO falls too far, **fish die and the river goes septic**.

> The **OXYGEN SAG CURVE (Streeter–Phelps)** describes the balance between **deoxygenation** (BOD being exerted) and **reaeration** (oxygen entering from the atmosphere).

> **The critical point — the minimum DO — occurs where the two rates are EQUAL**, and that is the point at which a discharge must be judged.

**Self-purification is real but limited:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Dilution** | More flow, more capacity |
| **Turbulence** | Faster reaeration |
| **Temperature** | **Warmer water holds LESS oxygen and exerts BOD faster** — a double penalty |
| Time of travel | More time for recovery |

> **A slow, warm, low-flow river in the dry season has very little self-purification capacity** — and that is exactly when discharge standards matter most, because dilution is least.

**Typical BOD values:**

| Source | BOD₅ |
|---|---|
| **Weak domestic sewage** | ~110 mg/l |
| **Medium domestic sewage** | **~220 mg/l** |
| **Strong domestic sewage** | ~400 mg/l |
| **Effluent standard (Nepal)** | Commonly **50 mg/l** |

> The 300 mg/l influent in this question is **strong domestic sewage or a diluted industrial waste** — consistent with a real plant.

**And the test itself:** **BOD₅ at 20 °C for 5 days**, capturing about **68%** of the ultimate BOD. **COD** (3 hours, everything oxidisable) is **always higher**, and a **BOD/COD ratio above about 0.5** indicates the waste is biodegradable enough for biological treatment to work.

examTip.trick: **Efficiency = (in − out)/in × 100 = 270/300 = 90%.** The arithmetic is trivial — the value is recognising that **90% is exactly what a good secondary plant achieves**, so the answer is a real design figure.
examTip.trap: **Removals are SEQUENTIAL, not additive.** Secondary removes 85% of what primary LEFT — combine as 1 − (1−0.35)(1−0.85) = 0.90. Adding percentages gives an impossible 120%.
examTip.mnemonic: **A percentage is not a standard.** A 3000 mg/l waste at 90% removal still discharges 300 mg/l — gross pollution. Consents are written as **concentrations and loads**, because it is the mass reaching the river that matters.

questions.stem: In network analysis, which one of the following is incorrect?
options: Tail of arrow indicates start of activity
Arrow from left to right in scale
Head of arrow indicates end of activity
questions.solution:
**"Arrow from left to right in scale" — the arrows are NOT drawn to scale.**

**Why.** In an **activity-on-arrow (AOA)** network, an arrow represents an activity. Its **direction** shows the flow of work — conventionally left to right — but:

> **The LENGTH of the arrow has NO significance.** It is not proportional to duration, cost, or anything else. **A network diagram is a LOGIC diagram, not a scaled drawing.**

> An activity lasting one day and one lasting a hundred days may be drawn as arrows of identical length. What the diagram conveys is **which activities depend on which** — the sequence and the dependencies, nothing more.

**The correct conventions**, which the other three options state:

| Convention | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tail of the arrow = START** of the activity | The tail event |
| **Head of the arrow = END** of the activity | The head event |
| **Each activity consumes time** (and usually resources) | **Except a DUMMY** |
| Arrows generally run left to right | Direction is meaningful; length is not |
| No loops | A loop would mean an activity precedes itself |
| No dangling activities | Every activity must connect |

**The important qualification to option (d):**

> **A DUMMY activity consumes NEITHER time NOR resources.** It is drawn as a **dashed arrow** and exists purely to:

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Show a DEPENDENCY** that cannot otherwise be drawn | Logical dummy |
| **Give two parallel activities distinct identities** | Two activities must not share the same tail **and** head event |

> So option (d) is **almost** universally true, and the dummy is the exception. **The question keys the scale statement**, which is unambiguously wrong — but knowing the dummy exception is what makes this a real test of understanding rather than of recall.

**Contrast with a BAR CHART (Gantt):**

| | **NETWORK diagram** | **BAR CHART** |
|---|---|---|
| **Scale** | **NOT to scale** | **TO SCALE — bar length is duration** |
| Shows | **DEPENDENCIES and logic** | **Timing** clearly |
| Critical path | **Identifiable** | **Not shown** |
| Effect of a delay | **Traceable through the logic** | **Not traceable** |
| Readability | Harder | **Easy — good for communication** |

> **A bar chart shows WHEN; a network shows WHY.** A bar chart cannot tell you what happens if an activity slips, because it contains no dependency information — which is precisely the deficiency that network methods were invented to correct.

> **In practice both are used**: the network for analysis, the bar chart (a **time-scaled network**, ideally) for communicating the programme to people who must act on it.

**AOA versus AON:**

| | **Activity on ARROW (AOA)** | **Activity on NODE (AON)** |
|---|---|---|
| Activity is | The **arrow** | The **node (box)** |
| Dependencies | The arrows' connections | The linking arrows |
| **Dummies** | **REQUIRED** | **NOT needed** |
| Modern software | Rare | **Standard** |

> **AON is now universal in software** precisely because it needs no dummies, and because it easily represents **the four dependency types** — finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish — plus **lead and lag** times, which AOA handles awkwardly.

**The forward and backward pass:**

> **Forward pass takes the MAXIMUM** (an activity cannot start until all predecessors finish); **backward pass takes the MINIMUM** (it must not delay the earliest successor).

> **Total float = LST − EST**, and a **critical activity has ZERO total float** — which is how the critical path is identified.

examTip.trick: **A network diagram is a LOGIC diagram, not a scaled drawing.** Arrow length means nothing — a one-day activity and a hundred-day one may be drawn identically. Only the **direction and connections** carry meaning.
examTip.trap: Option (d) has an exception: **a DUMMY consumes neither time nor resources.** It is drawn dashed, and exists to show a dependency or to give parallel activities distinct identities.
examTip.mnemonic: **A bar chart shows WHEN; a network shows WHY.** A bar chart cannot trace the effect of a delay because it holds no dependency information — which is exactly the gap network methods were invented to fill.

questions.stem: The minimum time period allocated by the Government of Nepal for the formation of a new council after the dissolution of the current Nepal Engineering Council is:
questions.solution:
**Three months.**

> Under the NEC Act, where the Council is dissolved, **the Government of Nepal shall ordinarily constitute another Council within THREE MONTHS** of the dissolution.

**Why the Act sets a time limit at all:**

> **The Council performs statutory functions that cannot simply stop.** Without a Council:

| Function suspended | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Registration of engineers** | New graduates **cannot obtain a license to practise** |
| **Recognition of institutions** | Programmes cannot be approved or reviewed |
| **Disciplinary proceedings** | Misconduct goes unaddressed |
| Issue and renewal of licenses | Practising engineers may be unable to renew |

> **Since registration is a LEGAL REQUIREMENT to practise engineering in Nepal, an absent Council would block entry to the profession entirely.** The three-month limit exists to bound that damage.

> **It is a safeguard against the regulator being disabled indefinitely** — which is why the power to dissolve is paired with a duty to reconstitute.

**Grounds for dissolution** are correspondingly serious — the Council failing to perform its functions, or acting against the objectives of the Act. The power is not routine.

**The NEC Act facts most often examined**, worth holding as a single block:

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| **Total Council members** | **21** |
| **Chairman** | Bachelor's + **15 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Vice-Chairman** | Bachelor's + **10 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Registrar (Member Secretary)** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| **Members nominated by the Council itself** | **2** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **5** |
| **President of the NEA** | **Ex officio** |
| **Minimum average for institutional affiliation** | **70%** |
| **Reconstitution after dissolution** | **3 months** |
| First Registrar | Er. Bindeshwar Yadav |

> **These recall questions are the cheapest marks on the paper** for anyone who has read the Council's material once — and several appear in every sitting. **Learning the block is worth far more than the time it takes.**

**The Council's functions:**

| Function |
|---|
| **Register engineers** and maintain the register |
| **Recognise (accredit)** engineering institutions and programmes |
| **Prescribe minimum standards** for engineering education and for student admission |
| Prepare and implement **policy, plans and programmes** for the profession |
| **Regulate professional conduct**; take disciplinary action |
| **Issue the license to practise** |

**And what it does NOT do:**

| Not a function | Who instead |
|---|---|
| **Open or run colleges** | Universities; Ministry of Education |
| **Award degrees** | Universities |
| Fix fees or salaries | The market |
| **Represent** engineers' interests | The **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** |

> **The standing distinction: the COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.** NEC registration is a **legal requirement** to practise and to sign engineering drawings; NEA membership is **voluntary**.

> **Practising or signing drawings without registration is an offence under the Act** — and **signing drawings one did not prepare or supervise is a disciplinary offence**, among the commonest real breaches of the code of conduct.

examTip.trick: The limit exists because **registration is a legal requirement to practise** — without a Council, no one can be licensed, and entry to the profession stops entirely. Three months bounds that damage.
examTip.trap: This is pure recall with four plausible periods and no way to reason between them. **Learn the Council block as a unit** rather than as isolated facts — several of these appear every sitting.
examTip.mnemonic: **Act 2055, Regulations 2057, 21 members, 15/10/10 years, 2 nominated by the Council, 5 elected from the NEA, 70% affiliation, 3 months to reconstitute.** One block, many marks.

questions.stem: Seasoning of timber is carried out primarily to:
options: Reduce its moisture content so that it becomes dimensionally stable and stronger
questions.solution:
**To reduce the moisture content**, making the timber dimensionally stable and stronger.

**Why seasoning is essential, not optional:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dimensional stability** | Shrinkage happens **before** the timber is used, not after it is in place |
| **Increased strength** | Strength rises sharply as timber dries below the fibre saturation point |
| **Reduced weight** | Easier to handle and transport |
| **Resistance to decay** | **Fungi need moisture above about 20%** |
| Takes preservatives and finishes | Paint and preservative will not penetrate wet timber |
| **Better holding of fasteners** | Nails and screws stay tight |

> **Unseasoned timber shrinks IN PLACE** — opening joints, loosening fasteners, distorting frames and cracking finishes. All of that damage is avoided simply by drying the timber first.

**The FIBRE SATURATION POINT is the key threshold:**

> **At about 30% moisture content**, the cell **cavities** are empty but the cell **walls** are still saturated.

| Above 30% | Below 30% |
|---|---|
| Water sits **free in the cavities** | Water leaves the **cell WALLS** |
| **NO shrinkage, NO strength change** | **Shrinkage AND strength increase** |

> **That single threshold explains both behaviours at once.** Drying from 60% to 35% does nothing useful; drying from 25% to 15% changes the timber substantially.

> **Target moisture content depends on the end use** — roughly **10–14%** for interior joinery in a heated building, **15–18%** for structural timber, since timber equilibrates with the humidity around it.

**The seasoning methods:**

| Method | Time | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **AIR seasoning** | **Months to years** | Cheap, low risk; stacked with **spacers (stickers)** under cover |
| **KILN seasoning** | **Days** | Controlled temperature and humidity; **risk of CASE HARDENING if hurried** |
| Water seasoning | Weeks | Sap is leached out first, then air dried |
| Boiling, chemical, electrical | — | Specialised |

> **CASE HARDENING is the danger of rushing a kiln**: the outside dries and sets while the inside is still wet, locking in stresses. **The timber then distorts violently when sawn** — the moment the balance of stresses is disturbed.

**Shrinkage is ANISOTROPIC**, which explains the defects:

| Direction | Shrinkage |
|---|---|
| **Tangential** (along the growth rings) | **Greatest — about 2× radial** |
| **Radial** (across the rings) | Moderate |
| **Longitudinal** (along the grain) | **Almost nil** |

> **Because tangential shrinkage is twice radial, boards CUP away from the heart** as they dry. That is why **quarter-sawn** timber (rings roughly perpendicular to the face) is more stable and more valuable than **plain-sawn**.

**The seasoning defects:**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Bow, cup, twist, spring** | Uneven or anisotropic shrinkage |
| **Checks and splits** | Surface drying faster than the interior |
| **Honeycombing** | Internal splitting from over-rapid kilning |
| **Case hardening** | Locked-in drying stresses |
| Collapse | Cell walls crushed by rapid drying |

**And preservation**, which seasoning enables:

> **Decay requires moisture above about 20% plus oxygen** — so **keeping timber DRY is the primary defence**, and seasoning is the first step in it.

> Where dryness cannot be assured, preservatives (**creosote, CCA, boron**) are applied — most effectively by **PRESSURE IMPREGNATION**, since brushing treats only the surface.

> **Heartwood is naturally more durable than sapwood but far harder to impregnate**, so **treated sapwood can outlast untreated heartwood** — a genuinely counter-intuitive result worth knowing.

examTip.trick: **Fibre saturation point ≈ 30%**: above it water is free in the cavities and nothing happens; below it water leaves the cell **walls**, and the timber both **shrinks and strengthens**. One threshold, both behaviours.
examTip.trap: Seasoning does **not** make timber fire resistant — dry timber ignites more readily than wet. It improves stability, strength, decay resistance and workability, not fire performance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tangential shrinkage is about TWICE radial, so boards CUP away from the heart** — which is why quarter-sawn timber is more stable and costs more. And **CASE HARDENING** from a rushed kiln makes timber distort the moment it is sawn.

questions.stem: The slump test on fresh concrete measures its:
questions.solution:
**Workability.**

**What the slump test is.** A standard **300 mm high frustum** (200 mm base, 100 mm top) is filled with fresh concrete in **three layers, each tamped 25 times**, then lifted vertically. **The slump is the drop in height** of the concrete.

**Slump ranges and their uses (IS 456):**

| Slump | Workability | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **0 – 25 mm** | **Very low** | Road pavements, **vibrated** mass concrete |
| **25 – 50 mm** | Low | Mass concrete, lightly reinforced sections |
