| **50 – 100 mm** | **Medium** | **Normal reinforced concrete — beams, slabs, columns** |
| **100 – 150 mm** | High | **Heavily reinforced or congested** sections |
| > 150 mm | Very high | Requires a superplasticiser; risk of segregation |

**The three types of slump**, which the test's interpretation depends on:

| Type | Appearance | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **TRUE slump** | Even, uniform subsidence | **A valid result** |
| **SHEAR slump** | Top half **slides off** at an angle | Mix is **harsh or lacks cohesion** — **RETEST** |
| **COLLAPSE slump** | Concrete collapses completely | **Too wet** — the test is **not applicable** |

> **Only a TRUE slump gives a meaningful number.** Reporting a shear or collapse slump as though it were a measurement is an error — and both are diagnostic in themselves, telling you the mix is wrong.

**What "workability" actually means:**

> The **ease with which concrete can be MIXED, TRANSPORTED, PLACED and COMPACTED without segregation.**

> **It is not simply wetness.** A very wet mix is easy to place but **segregates** — the coarse aggregate settles and the water rises as **BLEEDING** — producing a weak, porous, non-uniform result.

**The other workability tests, and when each is used:**

| Test | Suits |
|---|---|
| **SLUMP** | **Medium to high workability** — the everyday site test |
| **COMPACTING FACTOR** | **LOW workability** mixes, where slump is insensitive |
| **VEE-BEE consistometer** | **VERY LOW workability** — very dry mixes |
| Flow table | Very high workability, self-compacting |

> **The slump test is insensitive at low workability** — a dry mix gives zero slump whether it is merely stiff or completely unworkable. **That is exactly where the compacting factor and Vee-Bee tests take over**, and why three tests exist rather than one.

**Why the slump test survives despite its crudeness:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Simple, cheap, quick** | No power, no laboratory |
| **Requires no skill** to perform | Done by anyone on site |
| **Excellent for CONSISTENCY checking** | Detects a change between batches immediately |

> **Its greatest value is comparative, not absolute.** A sudden change in slump between loads signals that **something has changed** — usually the water content, or the aggregate moisture — and that is precisely the warning a site needs.

**Factors affecting workability:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Water content** | The dominant factor — but raising it **destroys strength** |
| **Aggregate SHAPE** | **Rounded aggregate is far more workable than angular or FLAKY** |
| Aggregate grading | Well graded is more workable |
| Maximum aggregate size | Larger is more workable for a given water content |
| **Cement content** | More paste, more workable |
| **ADMIXTURES** | **Plasticisers give workability without water** |

> **The right way to increase workability is a PLASTICISER, not water.** Adding water on site — the commonest of all concrete malpractices — raises the w/c ratio and **destroys strength and durability together**, since strength depends on w/c by **Abrams' law** and permeability rises with it.

examTip.trick: The slump test is done on **FRESH** concrete, so it can only measure a fresh property. Strength, durability and air content are all tested by other means — three of the options are about hardened concrete.
examTip.trap: **Only a TRUE slump is a valid measurement.** A **shear** slump means a harsh mix (retest); a **collapse** slump means the concrete is too wet and the test does not apply.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slump for medium workability, COMPACTING FACTOR for low, VEE-BEE for very low** — three tests because slump goes insensitive at the dry end. And increase workability with a **PLASTICISER, never with water**.

questions.stem: A damp proof course (DPC) in a building is provided mainly to prevent:
options: Rising of moisture from the ground into the walls
Loss of heat through the walls
questions.solution:
**To prevent moisture rising from the ground into the walls** — rising damp.

**The mechanism it blocks:**

> Ground moisture is drawn **UPWARD through the pores of masonry by CAPILLARY ACTION** — the same physics that lifts water in a fine tube or a fine-grained soil.

> **h ∝ 1/r**, so the **fine pores of brick and mortar produce a substantial rise** — often a metre or more if unchecked.

> **A DPC is an impermeable horizontal barrier** placed in the wall to break that capillary path.

**Where DPC is placed:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **At PLINTH level**, above ground | The main horizontal DPC in every wall |
| Under the ground floor slab | Prevents damp rising through the floor |
| **Over openings and under sills** | Sheds water clear |
| **Vertically at retaining walls and basements** | Against lateral penetration |
| At parapet junctions and roof abutments | — |

**DPC materials:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous felt** | Common, cheap, flexible |
| **Mastic asphalt** | Durable, jointless |
| **Polythene / PVC sheet** | Cheap, effective; must not be punctured |
| **Cement concrete (1:2:4) with waterproofing compound** | Common in Nepali practice, ~75 mm thick |
| Metal sheet (lead, copper) | Durable, expensive |
| Engineering brick / slate courses | Traditional |

**The requirements a DPC must satisfy:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Impervious** | Obviously |
| **Durable** — as long as the building | It cannot be replaced |
| **Flexible enough** not to crack under settlement | A rigid DPC that cracks has failed |
| **Strong enough** to carry the wall above without extruding | — |
| **CONTINUOUS and unbridged** | The critical requirement |

**Why rising damp is worth preventing:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | Salts carried up by the water crystallise on the surface as the water evaporates |
| **Salt crystallisation damage** | The crystals expand in the pores and **spall the plaster and brick** |
| **Decay of timber** in contact | Skirtings, joists, door frames |
| Failure of plaster and paint | Repeatedly, however often redecorated |
| **Unhealthy interior** — mould, damp | — |
| Reduced thermal insulation | Wet masonry conducts heat far better than dry |

> **The salt damage is the serious one structurally.** Ground water carries dissolved salts; the water evaporates at the wall surface and **leaves the salts behind, where they crystallise and expand**, progressively destroying the plaster and eventually the brick itself.

**The failure that makes a DPC useless — BRIDGING:**

> **A DPC works only if the moisture path is completely broken.** It is defeated by anything that carries water **around** it:

| Bridge | Note |
|---|---|
| **External ground or paving raised ABOVE the DPC level** | The commonest fault of all |
| **Plaster or render carried down across the DPC** | Provides a continuous capillary path |
| Debris in a cavity wall | Mortar droppings bridging the cavity |
| A discontinuity at a junction | The DPC not lapped or turned up properly |

> **A correctly installed DPC that is later bridged by raising the path or garden outside performs no better than none at all** — and this is by far the most frequent cause of rising damp in buildings that were built correctly.

> **The DPC must be at least 150 mm above the finished external ground level**, and that clearance must be maintained for the building's life.

**Note the other options describe real building problems with different remedies:** settlement is a foundation matter; heat loss is addressed by **insulation**; temperature cracking by **movement joints**. **None of them is what a DPC does.**

examTip.trick: The mechanism is **capillary rise in masonry pores** — the same physics as capillary rise in soil, where **h ∝ 1/r**. Fine pores lift water a long way, and the DPC simply breaks the path.
examTip.trap: **BRIDGING is what defeats most DPCs** — external ground or paving raised above DPC level, or render carried down across it. A correctly built DPC later bridged works no better than none.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the DPC at least 150 mm above finished external ground, for the building's life.** And the real damage is **SALT crystallisation** — the water evaporates, the salts stay and expand, spalling plaster and brick.

questions.stem: In the analysis of rates, the percentage usually added to cover the contractor's profit is about:
questions.solution:
**About 10%.**

**What analysis of rates is.** The build-up of the **rate for one unit of an item of work** — one cubic metre of concrete, one square metre of plaster — from its actual constituent costs.

**The build-up:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Materials** | Quantities per unit of work, at market rates, **including wastage** |
| **Labour** | Number and type of workers per unit, at prevailing wages |
| **Plant and equipment** | Hire or ownership cost |
| **Transport / carriage** | To the site |
| **Water, sundries, tools** | Usually a small percentage |
| **OVERHEADS** | **About 15%** — establishment, supervision, insurance, temporary works |
| **CONTRACTOR'S PROFIT** | **About 10%** |

> **The two percentages are worth learning together: overheads ≈ 15%, profit ≈ 10%.** They are added to the direct cost, and together they typically raise the direct cost by about a quarter.

**Why profit is only about 10%:**

> Construction is a **high-turnover, low-margin** business. A contractor's profit is a modest percentage of a very large sum, and it must also **absorb the risk** of the work costing more than estimated.

> **25–30% would be exceptional**, and 1–2% would not cover the risk of a single bad job. **10% is the conventional and realistic figure**, and it is what the standard schedules assume.

**Contingencies** are a separate provision and often confused with profit:

> **Contingencies of 3–5%** are added to the **total estimate** — not to individual rates — to cover **unforeseen items and minor variations**. They belong to the **employer**, not the contractor, and are released only as needed.

> **Work-charged establishment** of about **1.5–2%** covers site supervision staff paid from the works budget.

**Why analysis of rates matters:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Justifies the rate** to the sanctioning authority | Not merely asserted |
| **Allows fair comparison** of tendered rates | An unbalanced rate is visible |
| **Basis for VARIATIONS** | New items are rated by analogy |
| Reveals the cost drivers | Shows where savings are possible |

> **When a variation introduces an item not in the contract, its rate is derived by analysis** — which is why the method matters long after the tender is awarded, and why a properly documented analysis prevents disputes.

**The estimate types and their accuracy:**

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary / rough cost** | Feasibility; **administrative approval** | ±15–20% |
| Plinth area / cube rate | Approximate | — |
| **DETAILED** | Item by item from drawings; **technical sanction** | **±5%** |
| **REVISED** | When the sanctioned amount is exceeded by **more than 5%** | — |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY** | For **ADDITIONAL work** not originally included | — |

> **REVISED = same work costing more; SUPPLEMENTARY = additional work.** The two are constantly swapped, and the discriminator is whether the **scope** changed or only the **cost**.

**The measurement conventions that cause most disputes:**

| Item | Convention |
|---|---|
| **Earthwork** | **Mean area or PRISMOIDAL formula** — the two give different answers |
| Brickwork, concrete | Cubic metres, with **deduction rules for openings** above a stated size |
| Plastering | Square metres, with specific rules for jambs and soffits |
| Reinforcement | Weight, from the bar bending schedule |

> **The deduction rules for openings differ between items and between codes**, and an unstated convention is where money is lost. **The prismoidal formula gives a more accurate earthwork volume than the mean area method**, and which is specified must be agreed before measurement, not after.

examTip.trick: Learn the pair together: **overheads ≈ 15%, profit ≈ 10%** — added to the direct cost. Construction is a high-turnover, low-margin business, so 25–30% would be exceptional.
examTip.trap: **Contingencies (3–5%) are NOT profit.** They are added to the **total estimate**, belong to the **employer**, and are released only as unforeseen items arise.
examTip.mnemonic: **Analysis of rates outlives the tender** — when a variation introduces a new item, its rate is derived by analysis. A documented build-up is what prevents the dispute.

questions.stem: Quick sand condition occurs in a soil when:
options: The soil is a particular variety of fine sand
The upward seepage force makes the effective stress zero
The soil is fully saturated but not seeping
questions.solution:
**When upward seepage reduces the effective stress to zero.**

**The mechanism:**

> Water seeping **UPWARD** exerts a **drag (seepage force) on the soil grains**. When that upward force **equals the submerged weight** of the soil, the grains are no longer pressed together:

> **σ′ = 0**

> And since **shear strength τ = c + σ′ tan φ**, a cohesionless soil with **σ′ = 0 has ZERO shear strength**. It behaves as a **dense liquid**, unable to support anything.

**The critical hydraulic gradient:**

> **i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) = γ′/γ_w**

> For typical values (**G = 2.65, e = 0.65**): **i_c = 1.65/1.65 = 1.0**

> **The critical gradient is very close to UNITY for most soils** — a memorable and genuinely useful result. **It means a head loss roughly equal to the thickness of the soil layer is enough to fluidise it.**

**The most important correction to the popular idea:**

> **"QUICK SAND" IS NOT A TYPE OF SOIL — IT IS A CONDITION.**

> **Any cohesionless soil** can become quick if the upward gradient is high enough. There is no special variety of sand involved, which is exactly what option (a) wrongly suggests.

> **The name is misleading** and it misleads consistently — which is why the question is worth asking.

**And note that the TOTAL stress is not zero:**

> **σ′ = σ − u = 0 means u = σ**, not σ = 0. The **pore pressure has risen to equal the total stress**, and the soil is still there with all its weight. Option (d) confuses the two.

**Where it matters in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excavation below the water table** | The base **BOILS** — the classic failure |
| **Downstream of a dam or sheet pile wall** | Upward exit gradient at the toe |
| **Deep excavations in sand** | Dewatering is essential |
| Artesian pressure beneath an excavation | **Base heave** — the whole base lifts |

**PIPING is the progressive form and the dangerous one:**

> Once a boil starts, **soil is washed out**, forming a channel. The channel **shortens the seepage path**, which **raises the gradient**, which **erodes faster** — a **self-accelerating** process working **backwards toward the reservoir**.

> **Piping is the leading cause of earth dam failure**, and it gives very little warning before breach.

**The defences:**

| Measure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Graded FILTER** at the exit | **Retains the soil while passing the water** — the principal defence |
| **Lengthen the seepage path** | Cut-off walls, sheet piles, upstream blankets — **reduces i** |
| **Loaded (inverted) filter** at the toe | Adds weight where the gradient is highest |
| **Relief wells** | Relieve the pressure directly |
| Dewatering | Reverses the gradient |

**The filter criteria** are the two inequalities worth carrying:

> **D₁₅(filter)/D₈₅(soil) < 4 to 5** — the **RETENTION** criterion
> **D₁₅(filter)/D₁₅(soil) > 4 to 5** — the **PERMEABILITY** criterion

> **The two pull in opposite directions**, and a filter must satisfy both at once. **Too fine and it clogs, building pore pressure; too coarse and the soil washes through** — which is the very failure it was built to prevent.

**The factor of safety** against piping is taken on the **exit gradient**: **FoS = i_c/i_exit ≥ 4 to 5** — a large factor, appropriate to a failure mode that is sudden, progressive and catastrophic.

> **Khosla's theory** is what made this calculable for barrage floors: it solved the actual potential flow and showed that safety depends on the **EXIT GRADIENT** and on a **downstream cut-off**, not on total creep length as Bligh had assumed.

examTip.trap: **"Quick sand" is a CONDITION, not a type of soil.** Any cohesionless soil becomes quick under a high enough upward gradient — the name misleads consistently, which is why option (a) is offered.
examTip.trick: **i_c = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1.0** for most soils — so a head loss roughly equal to the layer thickness fluidises it. And σ′ = 0 means **u has risen to equal σ**, not that σ is zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **PIPING is self-accelerating** — erosion shortens the path, raising the gradient, eroding faster, working backwards toward the reservoir. It is the leading cause of earth dam failure, and a **graded filter** is the main defence.

questions.stem: In the standard penetration test (SPT), the N value is the number of blows required for a penetration of:
options: The last 300 mm of a 450 mm drive
questions.solution:
**The last 300 mm of a 450 mm drive.**

**The procedure.** A **split spoon sampler** is driven into the base of a borehole by a **63.5 kg hammer falling 750 mm**, and the blows are counted in **three 150 mm increments**:

| Increment | Counted? |
|---|---|
| **First 150 mm** | **NO — the "seating drive"** |
| **Second 150 mm** | **YES** |
| **Third 150 mm** | **YES** |

> **N = blows for the second plus third increments = the last 300 mm.**

**Why the first 150 mm is discarded** — and this is the whole point of the question:

> The **bottom of a borehole is DISTURBED** — loosened by the drilling, and possibly softened by water or by stress relief. **Blows in that disturbed zone say nothing about the undisturbed soil.**

> The seating drive pushes the sampler **through the disturbance** so that the counted blows are driven into **material representative of the ground**.

> **Counting all 450 mm would include the disturbed zone and UNDERSTATE the soil's density** — which is why option (b) is wrong, and why option (c) (the first 300 mm) is wrong for the same reason but worse.

**Refusal:** if **50 blows** are reached without completing an increment, the test is stopped and recorded as refusal.

**The corrections applied to the field value N:**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **OVERBURDEN pressure (C_N)** | The same soil gives a **higher N at greater depth** simply from confinement |
| **Energy / hammer efficiency** | Standardised to **N₆₀** — 60% of theoretical free-fall energy |
| **Dilatancy correction** | For **fine saturated sand/silt below the water table**: **N′ = 15 + 0.5(N − 15)** when N > 15 |
| Rod length, borehole diameter, liner | Minor |

> **The dilatancy correction is the one most often forgotten**, and it matters because it **REDUCES** N. Fine saturated silty sand **dilates** during driving, generating **negative pore pressure** that temporarily stiffens it, giving a falsely high blow count.

> **The overburden and energy corrections are applied FIRST, and the dilatancy correction LAST.** Order matters, and getting it wrong changes the answer.

**Correlations from N:**

| N | Sand density | φ |
|---|---|---|
| **0 – 4** | **Very loose** | < 28° |
| 4 – 10 | Loose | 28 – 30° |
| **10 – 30** | **Medium** | 30 – 36° |
| 30 – 50 | Dense | 36 – 41° |
| **> 50** | **Very dense** | > 41° |

> For clay, **c_u ≈ 6N kN/m²** as a rough guide — but **SPT is unreliable in clay** and should not be relied upon where an undisturbed sample or a vane test is possible.

**Why SPT survives despite being crude:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Simple and cheap** | Minimal equipment |
| **Works in most soils** | Including gravelly soils that defeat other tests |
| **Enormous body of correlations** | Decades of accumulated experience |
| **Gives a SAMPLE** as well as a number | Disturbed, but allows identification |

> **Its great weakness is variability** — results depend on the hammer, the operator, the rod length and the borehole condition. **Energy correction to N₆₀ exists precisely because the raw number is not comparable between rigs.**

**The alternative** is the **CONE PENETRATION TEST (CPT)**, which is **continuous, repeatable and operator-independent** — a far better test where the ground permits, though it gives no sample and cannot penetrate gravel.

> **SPT is used for LIQUEFACTION assessment** too, through **(N₁)₆₀** — which matters greatly in Kathmandu valley, where saturated loose sand and silt lenses are exactly the material at risk.

examTip.trick: The **first 150 mm is a SEATING DRIVE, discarded** — the borehole base is disturbed by drilling, so blows there say nothing about the real soil. N is the **last 300 mm of 450 mm**.
examTip.trap: **The dilatancy correction REDUCES N** for fine saturated sand or silt: **N′ = 15 + 0.5(N − 15)**. Dilation generates negative pore pressure that stiffens the soil temporarily and inflates the count.
examTip.mnemonic: **63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm drop, three 150 mm increments, count the last two.** And apply corrections in order: **overburden and energy first, dilatancy LAST**.

questions.stem: A cantilever retaining wall derives most of its stability from:
options: The self weight of the stem alone
The weight of the backfill resting on the heel slab
The passive resistance in front of the toe alone
The tensile strength of the concrete stem
questions.solution:
**The weight of the backfill resting on the heel slab.**

**Why.** A **cantilever retaining wall** is a slender reinforced concrete structure — its own weight is far too small to resist the earth pressure by itself.

> **Its stability comes from the SOIL sitting on its heel slab.** That soil is engaged by the base projecting back under the fill, and its weight acts as though it were part of the wall.

> **The wall borrows the backfill's own weight to resist the backfill's own thrust** — which is the elegant idea that makes a cantilever wall possible at a fraction of a gravity wall's concrete.

**The comparison:**

| Wall type | Stability from | Economical height |
|---|---|---|
| **GRAVITY** | Its **own massive weight** alone | **Up to about 3 m** |
| **CANTILEVER** | **Weight of backfill on the heel** + base friction | **3 to 6 m** |
| **COUNTERFORT** | The same, with **counterforts** in TENSION on the **backfill side** tying the stem to the base | **Above 6 m** |
| Buttressed | Buttresses in **compression** on the **exposed** side | Above 6 m |

> **Counterfort versus buttressed** is the pair most often confused: **counterforts are hidden in the fill and work in TENSION; buttresses are exposed and work in COMPRESSION.** The counterfort is preferred because the fill hides it, even though concrete is better in compression.

**The four stability checks:**

| Check | Factor of safety |
|---|---|
| **Overturning** | **2.0** |
| **Sliding** | **1.5** |
| **Bearing pressure** | **3.0** |
| **OVERALL (deep-seated) slope stability** | **1.5** |

> **The fourth is the one most often skipped**, and on a Nepali hillside it frequently governs — **a wall can pass every internal check and still ride down the slope on a deeper failure surface passing beneath it.** No amount of internal strengthening prevents that; only a stability analysis of the whole slope will find it.

**Why passive resistance is discounted** — the reason option (c) is wrong:

> Passive resistance in front of the toe is real, but:

| Reason to discount it | Note |
|---|---|
| **It needs LARGE movement** — 0.02 to 0.05 H | Far more than the wall may tolerate before being unserviceable |
| **The soil may be REMOVED** | Excavation for services, erosion, scour |
| It is shallow and easily disturbed | — |

> **Passive resistance is therefore usually ignored, or taken at a heavily reduced value** — and never relied upon as the primary mechanism.

> Note the contrast: the **ACTIVE state needs only about 0.001 H of movement**, so it always develops fully. **Active always acts; passive may never be mobilised.**

**But the commonest cause of actual failure is none of the four checks:**

> **INADEQUATE DRAINAGE behind the wall.**

> Water adds a **full hydrostatic thrust** (γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³) on top of an effective soil thrust often around 6 kN/m³ — **and it reduces the soil's own strength at the same time.** The design load can easily **double**.

> **Weep holes and a granular filter drain are not a detail — they are the design.** Blocked weep holes have brought down more retaining walls than any calculation error.

**And the tension crack in cohesive backfill:**

> Active pressure is negative over a depth **z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a)**, and that block is ignored — but **the crack FILLS WITH WATER**, and the resulting thrust often **exceeds the earth pressure it replaced**.

> **Which is why a cohesive backfill is a poor choice**, and why free-draining granular fill is specified wherever possible.

**The structural detailing** follows from the mechanism: the **stem is a vertical cantilever** with tension on the **earth face**; the **heel slab carries the fill above it downward**, so its tension is in the **TOP**; the **toe slab is pushed up by bearing pressure**, so its tension is in the **BOTTOM**. **The three elements have their steel in three different faces**, and getting any of them wrong is a serious detailing error.

examTip.trick: **The wall borrows the backfill's own weight to resist the backfill's thrust** — soil on the heel acts as part of the wall. That is why a cantilever wall needs a fraction of a gravity wall's concrete.
examTip.trap: **Passive resistance is usually discounted** — it needs 0.02–0.05H of movement and the soil may be excavated away. Active needs only 0.001H, so it always acts; passive may never be mobilised.
examTip.mnemonic: **Four checks — overturning 2.0, sliding 1.5, bearing 3.0, OVERALL SLOPE 1.5** — and the last is most often skipped though it often governs on a hillside. But **blocked drainage fells more walls than any calculation error.**

questions.stem: Negative skin friction on a pile occurs when:
options: The pile is loaded beyond its capacity
The pile is driven into dense sand
The pile carries only a lateral load
The surrounding soil settles more than the pile, dragging it downward
questions.solution:
**When the surrounding soil settles MORE than the pile and drags it down.**

**The mechanism.** Normally, soil resists a pile's downward movement, and **skin friction acts UPWARD, helping to carry the load.**

> **Negative skin friction reverses that.** If the **soil settles more than the pile**, it moves **downward relative to the pile**, and the friction now acts **DOWNWARD — adding load instead of carrying it.**

> **The soil hangs on the pile.** It becomes an additional load the pile must carry down to its bearing stratum, on top of the structural load.

**What causes the surrounding soil to settle:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **Newly placed FILL** over a compressible layer | The commonest case |
| **Consolidation of a soft clay** under any surcharge | — |
| **LOWERING of the groundwater table** | Raises effective stress throughout, causing widespread settlement |
| Vibration-induced settlement of loose sand | — |
| Consolidation of the soil disturbed by pile driving itself | — |

> **A pile driven through a recent fill into firm ground beneath is the classic situation** — the fill consolidates for years afterward, hanging on every pile through it.

**Why it matters so much:**

> **The pile capacity is reduced TWICE over:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1. Skin friction is LOST** | The shaft no longer contributes capacity |
| **2. Downdrag is ADDED as load** | The pile must carry it in addition |

> **So the safe capacity can be reduced dramatically** — and a pile designed on positive skin friction that instead experiences negative skin friction can be overloaded by a very large margin.

> **The design equation becomes:**
> **Q_safe = (Q_end bearing + Q_skin below the settling layer)/F − Q_negative friction**

> **Note the negative friction is subtracted UNFACTORED**, because it is a load, not a resistance.

**The remedies:**

| Remedy | How it works |
|---|---|
| **BITUMEN (slip) coating** on the shaft | **Reduces the friction that can be transmitted** — the standard solution, and highly effective |
| **Sleeve or casing** through the settling layer | Isolates the shaft |
| **Preloading the ground** before piling | Lets the settlement happen first |
| Increasing pile capacity | Accepts the load rather than avoiding it |
| Reducing pile spacing effects | In a group, only the perimeter piles may be affected fully |

> **A bitumen slip coat is remarkably effective** — it reduces the transferable shear stress to a small fraction, at trivial cost compared with lengthening every pile.

**Pile capacity generally:**

> **Q_ultimate = Q_end bearing + Q_skin friction**

| Pile type | Resistance mainly from |
|---|---|
| **END BEARING** | The **tip**, resting on rock or dense stratum |
| **FRICTION (floating)** | The **shaft**, in soil with no firm stratum within reach |
| Combined | Both |

**GROUP action** is the other essential concept:

> **Group efficiency = capacity of the group ÷ (n × capacity of a single pile)**

> **For piles in CLAY the efficiency is LESS than 1** — the group's stress bulbs overlap and it tends to fail as a **block**. **Spacing of 2.5 to 3.5 diameters** is used to limit the loss.

> **In dense SAND, driving can actually DENSIFY the soil**, and group efficiency can **exceed 1** — a genuinely counter-intuitive result.

> **And group SETTLEMENT is always greater than a single pile's**, because the group stresses a much deeper zone of soil. **A group of piles each individually satisfactory can settle unacceptably as a group** — which is why settlement is checked for the group, not the pile.

examTip.trick: Ask **which moves down more**. Normally the pile moves relative to the soil, so friction acts **up**. If the **soil** moves down more, the friction reverses and **hangs on the pile**.
examTip.trap: **The capacity is hit TWICE**: skin friction is lost **and** downdrag is added as load — and the downdrag is subtracted **unfactored**, because it is a load, not a resistance.
examTip.mnemonic: **A BITUMEN slip coat is the standard cure** — trivial cost against lengthening every pile. And in **clay, group efficiency is LESS than 1** (overlapping bulbs, block failure); in **dense sand driving densifies** and it can exceed 1.

questions.stem: In seismic design, the base shear of a building is directly proportional to:
options: The height of the building only
The seismic weight of the building
questions.solution:
**The seismic weight of the building.**

**Why.** An earthquake does not apply a force to a building — **it moves the ground beneath it.** The building's own **INERTIA** resists that movement, and the resulting force is:

> **F = m a**

> **Force is proportional to MASS.** That is the entire foundation of seismic design.

**The design base shear (IS 1893 / NBC 105):**

> **V_B = A_h × W**

> where **A_h** is the design horizontal acceleration coefficient and **W** the **seismic weight**:

> **A_h = (Z/2) × (I/R) × (S_a/g)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Z** | **Zone factor** — seismicity of the region |
| **I** | **Importance factor** — hospitals, schools higher |
| **R** | **Response reduction factor** — credit for **DUCTILITY** |
| **S_a/g** | **Spectral acceleration**, from the **natural period T** |
| **W** | **SEISMIC WEIGHT** |

**What seismic weight includes:**

> **Full DEAD load + a fraction (25–50%) of the IMPOSED load.**

> Only part of the live load is counted because **only part is likely to be present**, and because loose contents do not move rigidly with the structure. **Roof live load is usually excluded entirely.**

**The single most important consequence:**

> **REDUCING MASS REDUCES EARTHQUAKE FORCE, directly and proportionally.**

> **This is unique among load types.** A heavier structure is *safer* against wind uplift and overturning — but in an earthquake **the weight IS the load**. Every extra tonne attracts extra force.

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Lighter roofing** (CGI instead of heavy tile) | Directly reduces V_B |
| **Lighter partitions** | — |
| **Avoiding heavy water tanks high up** | Mass at height is worst — it has the largest lever arm |
| Removing unnecessary finishes and fill | — |

> **Mass high in the building is doubly damaging**: it contributes to base shear **and** it acts at a large lever arm, so it dominates the **overturning moment**. A heavy tank on a roof is among the worst things a designer can permit.

**Why concrete strength is nearly irrelevant** — the reason option (d) is wrong:

> **Increasing the concrete grade does NOT reduce earthquake force.** It may slightly stiffen the building, which **shortens the period T** and can actually **INCREASE S_a/g** — making the force **larger**.

> **Seismic design is about DUCTILITY and mass, not strength.** A stronger but brittle structure performs worse than a weaker ductile one, which is exactly what **R**, the response reduction factor, encodes: **a ductile detailed frame is permitted to be designed for a fraction of the elastic force**, because it can absorb energy by yielding.

**The design philosophy that follows:**

| Earthquake | Expected performance |
|---|---|
| **Minor** | **No damage** |
| **Moderate** | **Repairable non-structural damage** |
| **SEVERE** | **STRUCTURAL DAMAGE PERMITTED — but NO COLLAPSE** |

> **Buildings are deliberately NOT designed to remain elastic in a severe earthquake** — that would be prohibitively expensive. **They are designed to be damaged in a controlled, ductile way while protecting life.**

**And the detailing rules that deliver ductility:**

| Rule | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **STRONG COLUMN – WEAK BEAM** | Hinges form in **beams**, not columns — a beam hinge is local, a **column hinge collapses the storey** |
| **Closely spaced ties in the plastic hinge zone** | **Confine** the concrete and prevent bar buckling |
| **135° hooks with adequate extension** | 90° hooks **open out** and the tie is useless when the cover spalls |
| Adequate development and anchorage | — |

> **The 135° hook is the smallest detail with the largest consequence** in seismic construction — and the one most often ignored on site.

**The configuration faults that cause most damage:**

> **SOFT STOREY** (an open ground floor for parking or shops, with infill walls above) and **SHORT COLUMN** (a column restrained over part of its height by a partial-height wall, attracting large shear over a short length).

> **Both were prominent in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake damage**, and both are configuration problems that no amount of member strengthening fully corrects — they must be avoided in the layout.

examTip.trick: **F = ma** — an earthquake moves the ground, and the building's own **inertia** creates the force. So the force is proportional to **MASS**, which is why seismic weight appears directly in V_B = A_h × W.
examTip.trap: **A higher concrete grade does NOT reduce seismic force** — it stiffens the building, shortening T, which can **increase** S_a/g. Seismic design is about **ductility and mass**, not strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reducing mass reduces earthquake force directly — unique among load types.** Mass high up is worst (base shear **and** overturning). And **STRONG COLUMN–WEAK BEAM** with **135° hooks**: a column hinge collapses the storey.

questions.stem: In a two-way slab simply supported on all four sides and carrying a uniform load, the load is transferred:
options: Equally along both spans regardless of their lengths
Only to the two supports parallel to the longer side
questions.solution:
**Predominantly along the SHORTER span.**

**Why.** The slab spans in both directions, and the two directions **share the load in proportion to their STIFFNESS**. Since deflection **δ ∝ L⁴**, the **stiffer (shorter) direction attracts far more of the load**.

> Equating deflections at the centre for the two strips:
>
> **w_x L_x⁴ = w_y L_y⁴**, so **w_x/w_y = (L_y/L_x)⁴**

> **The load share goes as the FOURTH POWER of the span ratio** — an extremely strong effect.

**Working an example:**

> For **L_y/L_x = 1.5**: **w_x/w_y = 1.5⁴ = 5.06**

> **The short span carries about 83% of the load** and the long span only 17% — from a span ratio of just 1.5.

> **That fourth-power sensitivity is why the two-way / one-way boundary is drawn where it is.**

**The classification (IS 456):**

| Ratio L_y/L_x | Behaviour | Design as |
|---|---|---|
| **≤ 2** | Both directions contribute meaningfully | **TWO-WAY slab** |
| **> 2** | The **short span carries over 94%** | **ONE-WAY slab** |

> At a ratio of exactly 2, **2⁴ = 16**, so the short span takes **16/17 ≈ 94%** of the load. **Beyond that, treating it as one-way costs almost nothing in accuracy** — which is precisely why the code draws the line at 2.

> **The apparently arbitrary limit of 2 is a direct consequence of the fourth power law.** Knowing that makes it memorable and makes the reasoning transferable.

**Design consequences:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Main steel** | In the **SHORT span direction**, placed in the **outer (lower) layer** — where the effective depth is greatest |
| Secondary steel | Long span direction, above the main steel |
| **CORNER (torsion) reinforcement** | Required at corners **held down** — the slab tries to lift there |
| Deflection control | By the **span/effective depth** ratio |

> **Placing the main bars in the outer layer of the short-span direction matters** — it gives them the largest effective depth, and reversing the layers loses capacity for no reason.

**The corner effect is worth understanding:**

> A two-way slab **tries to LIFT at its corners**. If the corners are **held down** (by a wall or a monolithic beam), **torsional moments develop** there and **corner reinforcement in both faces and both directions** is required.

> **Omitting corner steel produces diagonal cracking at the corners** — a common and easily avoided defect.

**For a one-way slab:**

| Steel | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Main steel** | Across the **short span** — carries the load |
| **DISTRIBUTION steel** | Along the long span — **0.12% of gross area for Fe 415** |

> **Distribution steel is not structural in the load-carrying sense.** It distributes concentrated loads, resists **shrinkage and temperature** stresses, and holds the main bars in position. **It is essential even though the calculation does not require it.**

**Deflection control by span/depth ratio** — the check that usually governs slab thickness:

| Support | Basic L/d |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **7** |
| **Simply supported** | **20** |
| **Continuous** | **26** |

> Modified by **modification factors** for tension steel (**up to 2.0**), compression steel (up to 1.5) and flanged sections.

> **For slabs, deflection almost always governs the depth rather than strength** — which is why the span/depth ratio is the first thing computed, not the last.

examTip.trick: **Deflection ∝ L⁴, so the load share goes as the FOURTH power of the span ratio.** A ratio of 1.5 sends **83%** down the short span; a ratio of 2 sends **94%**.
examTip.trap: **The code's L_y/L_x = 2 limit is not arbitrary** — at that ratio 2⁴ = 16, so the short span takes 16/17 ≈ 94% and one-way design costs almost nothing. Knowing why makes it memorable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Main steel in the SHORT span, in the OUTER layer** (greatest effective depth). And a two-way slab **lifts at its corners** — held-down corners need torsion steel, or they crack diagonally.

questions.stem: In an environmental impact assessment, the "no project" alternative is included in order to:
options: Satisfy a formality with no analytical purpose
Reduce the cost of the assessment
Provide the baseline against which the project's impacts are measured
questions.solution:
**To provide the baseline against which every impact is measured.**

**Why it is analytically essential.** An "impact" is a **CHANGE**, and a change can only be stated **relative to something**.

> **The "no project" alternative describes what would happen if the project were NOT built** — and every predicted impact is the difference between that future and the with-project future.

> **Without it, there is nothing to compare against**, and impact statements become assertions rather than measurements.

**The subtlety that makes it more than a formality:**

> **The "no project" case is NOT the same as the present condition.** The environment would continue to change anyway — through population growth, land use change, deforestation, climate change, or other developments already committed.

> **The correct baseline is the FUTURE WITHOUT the project, not the present.**

> **Getting this wrong systematically misattributes impacts.** A river whose water quality is deteriorating anyway would be recorded as degraded *by the project*, when much of the change would have occurred regardless — and conversely, a project's genuine contribution can be hidden inside a trend.

**Where the alternatives analysis sits in the EIA:**

| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| Project description | — |
| **Baseline environment** | Physical, biological, **socio-economic** — the pre-project state and its trends |
| **ALTERNATIVES** | Site, technology, design, timing — **and "no project"** |
| **Impact prediction** | Magnitude, extent, duration, **REVERSIBILITY** |
| **Mitigation measures** | Avoid → minimise → mitigate → compensate |
| **Environmental Management Plan (EMP)** | Who does what, when, at what cost |
| **Monitoring programme** | — |

**The EIA process in order:**

> **SCREENING → SCOPING → EIA study → PUBLIC HEARING → review and CLEARANCE → MONITORING**

| Step | Decides |
|---|---|
| **Screening** | **WHETHER** an assessment is needed, and at what level (IEE or EIA) |
| **Scoping** | **WHAT** the study must cover — produces the **Terms of Reference** |
| Study | The assessment |
| **Public hearing** | Affected people comment on the **findings** |
| Clearance | Approval, with conditions |
| **MONITORING** | Verifies the mitigation is actually implemented |

> **The order is forced by logic**: you cannot scope a study you have not decided to do, and the public cannot comment on findings that do not exist.

**The MITIGATION HIERARCHY** is the other principle worth carrying:

> **AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE → COMPENSATE**, in that order of preference.

> **Avoidance is always better than compensation.** Rerouting an alignment away from a forest costs less and achieves more than replanting elsewhere afterwards — and **compensation is the last resort, not the default**.

> **A great deal of poor practice consists of jumping straight to compensation** because it is easy to quantify and easy to promise.

**The step most often neglected:**

> **MONITORING.** An EIA not followed by monitoring and enforcement is **a document, not a safeguard**. The mitigation measures it promises must be built, operated and verified.

> **That is where environmental assessment most often fails in practice** — not in the prediction, but in the implementation.

**IEE versus EIA:**

| | **IEE** | **EIA** |
|---|---|---|
| For | **Smaller** projects | **Large or sensitive** projects |
| **Scoping required?** | **No** | **YES** |
| Public hearing | Usually not | **Required** |

> **A project in a protected area requires an EIA regardless of size** — the sensitivity of the location overrides the scale threshold.

examTip.trick: An **impact is a CHANGE**, and change needs something to measure from. The "no project" case supplies it — without a baseline, impact statements are assertions rather than measurements.
examTip.trap: **The baseline is the FUTURE without the project, not the PRESENT.** The environment changes anyway, and confusing the two systematically misattributes impacts to the project.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mitigation hierarchy: AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE → COMPENSATE.** Avoidance beats compensation every time — and jumping straight to compensation is the commonest failure of practice, after neglecting **MONITORING**.

questions.stem: According to Khosla's theory, the safety of a barrage floor against piping is judged primarily by the:
options: Exit gradient at the downstream end
Length of the upstream cut-off only
questions.solution:
**The exit gradient at the downstream end.**

**Khosla's contribution.** He solved the **actual potential flow** beneath the floor (using the theory of complex variables) rather than relying on an empirical creep path, and showed two things that overturned earlier practice:

> **1. Safety against PIPING depends on the EXIT GRADIENT**, not on total creep length.
> **2. A DOWNSTREAM cut-off (vertical sheet pile at the toe) is the effective control** on that gradient.

**The exit gradient:**

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ)**

> where **H** is the head, **d** the depth of the downstream cut-off, and **λ** a function of the floor length to cut-off depth ratio.

> **The exit gradient is compared with the CRITICAL gradient i_c ≈ 1.0**, and a factor of safety of **4 to 5** is required — a large factor, appropriate to a failure mode that is sudden, progressive and catastrophic.

**Safe exit gradients by soil:**

| Soil | Safe G_E |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1/5 to 1/6** |
| **Fine sand** | **1/6 to 1/7** |

> **Finer soil, lower permissible gradient** — because fine particles are more easily carried away once movement begins.

**The progression of theories** is the substance of this topic:

| Theory | Assumption | Defect |
|---|---|---|
| **BLIGH's creep** | Water creeps along the profile; **vertical and horizontal creep weighted EQUALLY** | **Wrong** — vertical creep is far more effective |
| **LANE's weighted creep** | **Vertical creep counted THREE times** horizontal | Empirical correction, still not a solution |
| **KHOSLA's theory** | **Solves the actual potential flow** | The correct approach |

> **Bligh's error was treating a horizontal metre of creep as equal to a vertical metre.** In reality a vertical cut-off is far more effective at reducing the exit gradient, because it forces the flow deep and lengthens the path where it matters most.

> **Lane's weighting of 3:1 was an empirical patch on that error; Khosla removed the need for a patch by solving the problem properly.**

**The practical consequences of Khosla's theory:**

| Finding | Consequence for design |
|---|---|
| **The DOWNSTREAM cut-off controls the exit gradient** | It is essential; the upstream one is not, for piping |
| **Intermediate cut-offs are of little value** | They were formerly provided under Bligh's theory and are largely useless |
| **The UPSTREAM cut-off reduces UPLIFT** on the floor | A different function entirely |
| Uplift pressures follow from the flow net | Floor thickness computed rationally |

> **So the two cut-offs do different jobs: UPSTREAM controls UPLIFT; DOWNSTREAM controls the EXIT GRADIENT.** That division is the practical heart of Khosla's method, and it is why option (d) — naming only the upstream cut-off — is wrong.

**The two failure modes of a barrage floor**, which must both be checked:

| Failure | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **PIPING** (undermining) | **Exit gradient too high** — soil washed out downstream | **Deeper DOWNSTREAM cut-off**; longer floor |
| **UPLIFT** (floor rupture) | Seepage pressure beneath exceeds the floor's weight | **Thicker floor**; **upstream cut-off** to reduce the pressure |

> **A floor can be perfectly safe against uplift and still fail by piping**, and the reverse. **Both checks are independent and both are necessary.**

**Why piping is so dangerous:**

> Once erosion begins at the exit, the **channel formed shortens the seepage path**, which **raises the gradient**, which **erodes faster** — working **backwards toward the upstream water**.

> **The process is self-accelerating and gives very little warning** before the structure is undermined. **That is why the factor of safety is 4 to 5** rather than the 1.5 to 3 used for most geotechnical checks.

**Khosla's correction factors** are applied to the theoretical pressures for **floor thickness, slope of the cut-off, and interference between cut-offs** — refinements that make the ideal solution applicable to a real structure.

examTip.trick: **Khosla replaced creep length with the EXIT GRADIENT** — the physical quantity that actually moves soil particles. Compare it against **i_c ≈ 1.0** with a factor of safety of **4 to 5**.
examTip.trap: **Bligh weighted vertical and horizontal creep EQUALLY — his central error.** Lane patched it by counting vertical creep **three times**; Khosla removed the need for a patch by solving the flow properly.
examTip.mnemonic: **UPSTREAM cut-off controls UPLIFT; DOWNSTREAM cut-off controls the EXIT GRADIENT.** Two cut-offs, two different jobs — and intermediate ones, provided under Bligh's theory, are largely useless.

questions.stem: A canal escape is provided in an irrigation system to:
options: Raise the water level for an offtake
Carry the canal across a natural drain
Lower the canal bed where the ground falls steeply
Dispose of surplus water from the canal
questions.solution:
**To dispose of surplus water out of the canal.**

**Why an escape is needed.** A canal is fed at its head, but its **demand can fall suddenly and without warning**:

| Cause of surplus | Note |
|---|---|
| **RAINFALL** in the command | Irrigation demand collapses; outlets are closed |
| **Sudden closure of outlets** | Downstream demand stops |
| Breach or blockage downstream | Flow cannot continue |
| **Excess supply at the head** | Regulation error, or a flood |
| Canal being emptied for maintenance | Deliberate |

> **The water already in the canal has nowhere to go.** Without an escape, the level rises and **the banks overtop or breach** — and a canal breach floods the surrounding land and destroys a length of embankment.

> **An escape is a SAFETY VALVE**, and it is what lets a canal be operated at all.

**Types of escape:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weir / surplus escape** | An automatic side weir at bank level; spills whenever the level rises |
| **Scouring (sluice) escape** | Gated, at bed level; **also flushes accumulated silt** |
| **Tail escape** | At the end of the canal, keeping the tail reach in supply |

> **A scouring escape performs two jobs at once** — relieving surplus water and **flushing silt from the canal bed**, which is why it is placed at low points where silt accumulates.

**Where escapes discharge to:** a natural drain, a river, or a depression — and the discharge point must be able to take the flow without causing damage, which is itself a design consideration.

**The distinction from the other canal structures** — which is exactly what the distractors test:

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **ESCAPE** | **Dispose of SURPLUS water OUT** of the canal |
| **CROSS REGULATOR** | **RAISE the water level** so an offtake can draw |
| **HEAD REGULATOR** | Control flow **INTO the distributary** |
| **FALL** | Take the **BED down a step** where the ground falls faster than the canal |
| **CROSS-DRAINAGE works** | **Carry the canal past a natural drain** |
| **OUTLET** | Deliver water from a minor to a watercourse |

> **Each distractor names a real structure with a completely different function**, so this is a test of whether the family is understood as a set.

**The four cross-drainage works**, named by **which one goes over**:

| Structure | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **Canal over drain**; drain flows free |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | Canal over drain; **drain under PRESSURE** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **Drain over canal**; canal free |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | Drain over canal; **canal under PRESSURE** |

> **"Aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top. Add "syphon" when the thing underneath runs under pressure.** That one rule generates all four.

> A **LEVEL CROSSING** (both at the same level, with regulators) is the fifth arrangement, used where the drain is large and the canal small — but it **mixes drainage water with irrigation supply** and is avoided where possible.

**The cross regulator and head regulator work as a PAIR:**

> Built together at every major offtake — **the cross regulator provides the head; the head regulator controls how much is taken.**

**And the canal alignment decision** that determines how many of these structures are needed at all:

| Alignment | Cross-drainage works |
|---|---|
| **WATERSHED (ridge)** | **NONE** — streams flow away on both sides; **commands land on BOTH sides** |
| **Side slope** | **None** — runs parallel to the drainage |
| **CONTOUR** | **MANY** — crosses every natural drain; commands one side only |

> **The ridge alignment is preferred wherever the topography allows**, because it eliminates cross-drainage works entirely — the largest single saving available in canal design. Its cost is a **long lead** from the headworks to the ridge, commanding nothing.

examTip.trick: An escape is a **SAFETY VALVE**. Demand can vanish suddenly — rain in the command closes every outlet at once — and the water already in the canal must go somewhere or the banks breach.
examTip.trap: **Each distractor names a real structure with a different job**: cross regulator (raise level), fall (lower bed), cross-drainage (cross a drain). The family must be known as a set.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Aqueduct" means the CANAL is on top; add "syphon" when what is underneath runs under pressure.** And a **SCOURING escape** does two jobs — relieves surplus water and flushes silt.

questions.stem: The main purpose of providing a leaching requirement in an irrigation schedule is to:
options: Wash accumulated salts below the root zone
questions.solution:
**To wash accumulated salts below the root zone.**

**Why salts accumulate.** **All irrigation water carries dissolved salts** — even good quality water. The crop takes up the **water** and leaves most of the **salts** behind, and **evapotranspiration removes water while the salts remain.**

> **Over seasons, salts concentrate in the root zone**, and the process is cumulative and inexorable unless something removes them.

**Why salinity harms crops:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **OSMOTIC stress** | Saline soil water is harder for roots to extract — the plant experiences **drought even in wet soil** |
| **Specific ion toxicity** | Sodium, chloride and boron are directly toxic in excess |
| **Nutrient imbalance** | Sodium displaces calcium and potassium |
| **Structural damage (sodic soils)** | Sodium **disperses clay particles**, destroying soil structure and permeability |

> **The osmotic effect is the one that surprises**: a plant in saline soil wilts although the soil is moist, because it cannot extract water against the osmotic gradient. **Salinity mimics drought.**

**The leaching requirement:**

> **LR = EC_iw/(5 EC_e − EC_iw)** approximately

> where EC_iw is the electrical conductivity of the irrigation water and EC_e that permitted in the soil saturation extract.

> **It is expressed as a FRACTION of the irrigation requirement**, and it is **added to** the crop's needs — the water must be applied **in excess of** what the crop consumes, so that the surplus carries salts downward.

> **That is why option (b) is exactly wrong: leaching INCREASES the water requirement, it does not reduce it.**

**The absolute prerequisite:**

> **LEACHING ONLY WORKS IF THERE IS DRAINAGE.**

> The salts must have **somewhere to go**. Without adequate drainage:

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Excess water applied | **Water table RISES** |
| Water table reaches the root zone | **WATERLOGGING** |
| **Capillary rise** brings water back up | Carrying the salts with it |
| Evaporation at the surface | **Salts concentrate at the surface — worse than before** |

> **Leaching without drainage is not merely futile — it is actively harmful**, because it raises the water table and accelerates the very salinisation it was meant to cure.

> **That combination has destroyed vast areas of irrigated land worldwide**, and it is the central lesson of irrigation history: **drainage is not optional infrastructure that can be added later.**

**Waterlogging and salinity are therefore a single problem:**

| Cause of waterlogging | Note |
|---|---|
| **Over-irrigation** | The commonest |
| **CANAL SEEPAGE** | Which is why lining pays twice — water saved **and** waterlogging prevented |
| Poor natural drainage | — |
| Impervious subsoil | — |
| Flat topography | — |

> **Both are WATER TABLE problems, so both require SUBSURFACE drainage** — tile drains or open ditches deep enough to lower the water table. **Surface drainage removes standing water and does nothing to the water table beneath.**

**And for a SODIC (alkali) soil the order matters:**

> **Apply GYPSUM FIRST, then leach.**

> Gypsum (CaSO₄) supplies **calcium, which displaces the sodium** from the clay's exchange sites so it can be washed out.

> **Leaching a sodic soil WITHOUT gypsum makes it worse** — it removes the remaining soluble calcium and leaves the sodium in place, further **dispersing the clay** and destroying what permeability remains. **The soil then becomes impermeable and cannot be reclaimed at all.**

> That is a genuine and irreversible mistake, and it is why the distinction between **saline** and **sodic** soils must be established before any reclamation is attempted.

**Tile drain placement**, for completeness: **within a pervious stratum, below the root zone (1–2 m), and ABOVE any impervious layer** — never below one, or the water cannot reach the drain. **Spacing is proportional to permeability**, from Hooghoudt's equation.

examTip.trick: Every irrigation water carries salts; the crop takes the **water** and leaves the **salts**. Leaching applies water **in excess** of the crop's need to carry them down — so it **increases**, never reduces, the requirement.
examTip.trap: **Leaching without DRAINAGE is actively harmful**, not merely useless — it raises the water table, causes waterlogging, and capillary rise returns the salts to the surface. Drainage is a prerequisite, not an add-on.
examTip.mnemonic: **Salinity mimics DROUGHT** — the plant wilts in moist soil because it cannot extract water osmotically. And for a **SODIC** soil: **gypsum FIRST, then leach** — leaching alone disperses the clay and can ruin it permanently.

questions.stem: The firm (dependable) power of a hydropower plant is:
options: The maximum power the plant can generate at any time
The power available for at least 95% of the time
The average power generated over a year
The installed capacity of the plant
questions.solution:
**The power available for at least 95% of the time** — the power the plant can be relied upon to deliver almost always.

**The definitions:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (dependable / primary) power** | Power available **essentially at all times** — typically taken at **Q95** or the minimum flow |
| **SECONDARY power** | Power available **only part of the time**, in excess of firm power |
| **Installed capacity** | The **rated** output of the machines |
| **Average power** | Annual energy ÷ hours in the year |

> **Firm power is limited by the DRY SEASON flow**, because that is the flow that is exceeded almost always.

**Why firm power matters commercially:**

> **Firm power commands a much higher price than secondary power**, because a utility can **plan around it**. Secondary power arrives when the river happens to be high — often when everyone else's plants are also generating, and when it is least needed.

> **Two plants with the same annual energy can have very different values** if one has high firm power and the other does not. **The distribution of generation matters as much as its total.**

**Reading it from the flow duration curve:**

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Q10** | A **high** flow, available only 10% of the time |
| **Q40** | The typical **design discharge** for a run-of-river plant |
| **Q95** | **Firm / dependable flow** — available almost always |
| Q100 | The absolute minimum |

> **A HIGHER percentage means a LOWER flow**, because it is exceeded a greater proportion of the time. **Reading the curve backwards is the standard error in this topic.**

**Why a run-of-river plant has LOW firm power:**

> Its output follows the river. In the **dry season the flow may be a small fraction of the monsoon flow**, so the power it can guarantee is correspondingly small — even though its annual energy may be large.

> **In Nepal about 80% of the flow arrives in four monsoon months**, so a run-of-river plant's firm power can be a **small fraction of its installed capacity** — and dry-season firm power is exactly what the system needs most, since demand peaks in the winter evening.

**How firm power is increased:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **STORAGE reservoir** | **Converts monsoon surplus into dry-season supply** — the fundamental solution |
| **Pondage (PROR)** | Addresses the **daily** peak, not the seasonal deficit |
| **Interconnection** with other plants | Diversity between catchments |
| **Cross-border trade** | Import in the dry season, export in the monsoon |
| Pumped storage | Time-shifts within the day |

> **Only STORAGE addresses the seasonal problem.** Pondage and pumped storage shift energy within a day; they cannot move monsoon water into January.

**The power equation:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η**, with **η ≈ 0.85–0.90** overall.

> **Q comes from the flow duration curve** — at **Q95 for firm power**, at **Q40 for the design discharge**. **H comes from the topography.**

**And the related plant factors, which are constantly confused:**

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PLANT LOAD FACTOR (capacity factor)** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED capacity** |
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND** |
| **Utilisation factor** | Maximum demand ÷ rated capacity |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | Σ individual maxima ÷ system maximum — **always > 1** |

> **The denominator is the discriminator**: plant load factor divides by **installed capacity**; load factor by **maximum demand**.

> **A low plant load factor is not necessarily bad** — a peaking plant is meant to run rarely, and its value lies in being **available**, not in the energy it produces.

examTip.trick: **Firm power is what the plant can be RELIED on to deliver** — set by the **dry season** flow, read at **Q95**. It is not the maximum, the average, or the installed capacity.
examTip.trap: **A HIGHER percentage on the flow duration curve means a LOWER flow.** Q95 is a small dependable discharge; Q10 a large rare one. Reading the curve backwards is the standard error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only STORAGE raises seasonal firm power** — pondage and pumped storage shift energy within a day but cannot move monsoon water into January. And firm power **sells for far more** than secondary power.

questions.stem: The California Bearing Ratio (CBR) test is used mainly for:
options: Determining the compressive strength of concrete
Measuring the workability of a bituminous mix
Finding the water content of a soil
Evaluating the strength of subgrade and pavement layers for flexible pavement design
questions.solution:
**To evaluate the strength of the subgrade and pavement layers for flexible pavement design.**

**What the test measures.** A **plunger of 50 mm diameter** is pushed into a compacted soil specimen at **1.25 mm/min**, and the load is recorded:

> **CBR (%) = (test load ÷ standard load on crushed stone) × 100**

| Penetration | Standard load |
|---|---|
| **2.5 mm** | **1370 kg (13.44 kN)** |
| **5.0 mm** | 2055 kg (20.55 kN) |

> **The CBR is normally taken at 2.5 mm penetration.** If the 5 mm value comes out **higher**, the test is **repeated**; if it is again higher, **the 5 mm value is adopted** — a check on specimen preparation.

**Why it is an empirical index, not a fundamental property:**

> **CBR is a RATIO — a comparison against a standard crushed stone.** It has no direct physical meaning as a strength; it is a **relative measure**, calibrated by decades of pavement performance.

> **That empirical basis is both its weakness and the reason it survives.** It correlates well with pavement behaviour because it was derived from pavement behaviour.

**The test conditions matter greatly:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **SOAKED for 4 days** before testing | Simulates the **worst (monsoon) condition** |
| **Surcharge weights** applied | Represent the weight of pavement layers above |
| Compacted to field density | Usually at OMC |

> **The 4-day soak is the essential feature.** A subgrade tested dry gives a flattering result that the monsoon will not honour. **Design must be for the weakest condition the pavement will experience**, and in Nepal that is unambiguously the saturated monsoon state.

**Typical values:**

| Material | CBR |
|---|---|
| **Very poor subgrade (soft clay)** | **< 3%** |
| Poor to fair subgrade | 3 – 7% |
| **Good subgrade** | **7 – 20%** |
| **Sub-base** | **20 – 30%** |
| **Base course** | **> 80%** |

> **A subgrade below about 2% CBR usually requires treatment** — replacement, stabilisation, or a capping layer — because the pavement thickness needed would otherwise be uneconomic.

**How it is used (IRC 37):**

> **Pavement thickness is read from design charts as a function of the subgrade CBR and the traffic in msa** (million standard axles of 8160 kg).

> **The relationship is steeply non-linear**: halving the CBR increases the required thickness substantially, which is why **improving a weak subgrade is often cheaper than building a thicker pavement over it.**

**The traffic side of the design:**

> **The FOURTH POWER LAW: pavement damage ∝ (axle load)⁴.**

> **A truck at twice the legal axle load does SIXTEEN times the damage.** One overloaded vehicle can outweigh thousands of cars.

> **That is why axle load control matters far more than traffic volume for pavement life**, and why overloading is the single greatest cause of premature pavement failure in Nepal.

**Flexible versus rigid pavement design:**

| Pavement | Design parameter |
|---|---|
| **FLEXIBLE** | **CBR of the subgrade** (IRC 37) |
| **RIGID** | **Modulus of subgrade reaction k**, and the concrete's **flexural strength f_cr** (Westergaard) |

> **A flexible pavement transmits load by GRAIN-TO-GRAIN contact**, so stress reduces with depth and the **subgrade ultimately carries everything** — which is exactly why its strength is the design parameter.

> **A rigid pavement spreads load by SLAB ACTION**, bridging over weak spots, so the subgrade matters much less.

**And the practical point about drainage:**

> Since CBR is measured **soaked**, and since a wet subgrade is a weak one, **keeping water out of the pavement is worth as much as building it thicker.** Side drains, camber, and a sealed surface are all pavement structure in effect, not merely accessories.

examTip.trick: **CBR is a RATIO against standard crushed stone**, taken at **2.5 mm penetration (1370 kg)** — an empirical index calibrated from real pavement performance, not a fundamental strength.
examTip.trap: **The 4-day SOAK is the essential condition.** A subgrade tested dry gives a flattering result the monsoon will not honour — design must use the weakest state the pavement will meet.
examTip.mnemonic: **FOURTH POWER LAW: damage ∝ (axle load)⁴** — a truck at twice the legal load does **sixteen times** the damage. Axle load control matters far more than traffic volume for pavement life.

questions.stem: The flakiness index of aggregate is limited in road construction because flaky particles:
options: Break under compaction and traffic and pack poorly
Increase the specific gravity of the mix
questions.solution:
**Because flaky particles break under compaction and traffic, and pack poorly.**

**Why shape matters as much as strength.** A **flaky** particle is one whose **least dimension is less than 0.6 times its mean dimension** — a thin, plate-like fragment.

> When compacted or loaded, such a particle is **stressed across its thinnest dimension**, which is its **weakest direction**. **It snaps** — however strong the parent rock.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **BREAKS under the roller and under traffic** | Changing the grading after laying, which was designed on the original particles |
| **Packs poorly** | Bridges across voids instead of interlocking |
| **Higher voids** | More binder needed; less dense mix |
| **Reduced stability** | Poor interlock means poor shear resistance |
| Larger surface area | More binder for the same volume |

> **The grading change is the insidious part.** A mix designed as dense-graded becomes something else once its flaky particles break, and the pavement no longer behaves as designed.

**The two shape indices:**

| Index | Definition | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **FLAKINESS** | Least dimension **< 0.6 ×** mean dimension | **≤ 15%** (wearing course) |
| **ELONGATION** | Greatest dimension **> 1.8 ×** mean dimension | ≤ 15% |
| **Combined** | Both together | **≤ 30%** |

> **Flakiness is measured with a THICKNESS gauge (slotted plate); elongation with a LENGTH gauge.** Flaky is thin; elongated is long — and a particle can be both.

> **CUBICAL particles are what is wanted**, since they interlock in every direction and have no weak dimension.

**Why an otherwise excellent rock can be rejected:**

> **Particle shape depends on the CRUSHER, not only on the rock.** An **impact crusher** produces more cubical particles than a **jaw crusher**, which tends to produce flaky ones from laminated rock.

> **A quarry with strong rock but the wrong crusher can fail the flakiness test**, and the remedy is a change of plant or an extra crushing stage — not a change of source.

> **Laminated and foliated rocks (shale, slate, some schists) naturally break into flakes** and are poor aggregate sources whatever the crusher.

**The full set of aggregate tests**, all following "lower is better":

| Test | Measures | Limit (wearing course) |
|---|---|---|
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to **gradual** load | **30%** |
| **Impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | **30%** |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | **Abrasion, impact and grinding combined** | **30 – 40%** |
| **Soundness** (sulphate) | Weathering resistance | 12% / 18% |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | **< 2%** |
| **Flakiness / elongation** | **SHAPE** | **15% / 30% combined** |
| **Stripping value** | Binder adhesion | Retention > 95% |
| Polished stone value | Skid resistance retained | — |

> **The Los Angeles test is the most comprehensive single test**, because it combines three mechanisms in one procedure — which is why it is the international preference.

**Why aggregate quality matters so much:**

> **Aggregate is 90–95% of a bituminous mix by weight.** The binder is a thin film holding it together; **the aggregate skeleton carries the load.**

> **A pavement is only as good as its aggregate** — and no amount of good binder, good design or good compaction compensates for aggregate that breaks down.

**And the property that governs long-term safety:**

> **POLISHED STONE VALUE** — the skid resistance the aggregate retains after years of trafficking. **Some aggregates polish smooth under traffic and become dangerously slippery when wet**, even though they pass every strength test.

> That is a durability property invisible in the initial testing, and it is why wearing course aggregate is specified differently from base course aggregate.

examTip.trick: A flaky particle is loaded **across its thinnest dimension — its weakest direction — so it snaps**, however strong the parent rock. Shape matters as much as strength.
examTip.trap: **Flakiness is measured with a THICKNESS gauge, elongation with a LENGTH gauge.** Flaky is thin (< 0.6 × mean); elongated is long (> 1.8 × mean); a particle can be both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Particle shape depends on the CRUSHER, not only the rock** — impact crushers give cubical particles, jaw crushers give flaky ones. And **aggregate is 90–95% of the mix by weight**: a pavement is only as good as its stone.

questions.stem: The capacity of a traffic signal intersection is increased most effectively by:
options: Reducing the total lost time per cycle
questions.solution:
**By reducing the total lost time per cycle.**

**What lost time is.** In every signal cycle, some time is **unusable** — no vehicle moves productively during it:

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Start-up lost time** | Drivers **react and accelerate** at the start of green — the first few seconds carry less than saturation flow |
| **Clearance lost time** | The end of amber and the **all-red** interval |
| **Inter-green period** | Between conflicting phases |

> **Lost time is typically 3–4 seconds per phase.** It is pure overhead — capacity that exists in principle but is never used.

**Why reducing it is the most effective lever:**

> **Total lost time L = n × l + R**, where **n** is the number of phases.

> **Every additional PHASE adds its own lost time.** A four-phase signal wastes roughly twice the time of a two-phase one — which is precisely why **option (d) is wrong: more phases REDUCE capacity**, even though each phase individually looks safer.

> **Fewer phases and shorter inter-greens directly convert wasted time into usable green.**

**Webster's optimum cycle time:**

> **C₀ = (1.5 L + 5)/(1 − Y)**

> where **L** is the total lost time per cycle and **Y** the sum of the critical flow ratios.

> **Note L appears in the numerator** — **reducing lost time shortens the optimum cycle AND increases capacity simultaneously.**

**Why increasing the cycle length indefinitely fails** — the reason option (a) is wrong:

> A longer cycle **does** reduce the proportion of time lost, so capacity rises at first. **But delay increases**, because every vehicle waits longer for its turn.

> **Webster's curve is flat near the optimum but rises steeply on either side.** Beyond about **120 seconds** delay grows sharply, queues lengthen, and drivers begin to violate the signal.

> **Practical cycle lengths are 40 to 120 seconds**, and doubling the cycle roughly doubles the average delay for a modest capacity gain — a poor exchange.

**Why a longer amber does not help** — option (c):

> The **amber period is a SAFETY provision**, sized from **stopping distance and reaction time** — typically **3 to 5 seconds**. It is largely **lost time**.

> **Lengthening it adds lost time and reduces capacity**, and it also encourages drivers to enter on amber, defeating its safety purpose.

**The capacity relation:**

> **Capacity of an approach = saturation flow × (effective green ÷ cycle time)**

> **Effective green = green + amber − lost time**

> **Saturation flow** is about **1800–1900 passenger car units per hour per lane** for ideal conditions, reduced for lane width, gradient, turning movements and parking.

**The green split:**

> **Green time is allocated in PROPORTION TO THE CRITICAL FLOW RATIOS**, not equally between approaches. A heavily loaded approach gets proportionally more.

**When signals are warranted at all:**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| Traffic volume | Both major and minor approaches |
| **Pedestrian volume** | — |
| **Accident record** | A recurring right-angle collision pattern |
| Coordination with adjacent signals | — |

> **Signals are not always an improvement.** At low volumes they cause **unnecessary delay** and can increase **rear-end collisions**. A **roundabout** may serve better at moderate volumes, converting crossing conflicts into weaving without stopping anyone.

> **Signals separate conflicts in TIME; a roundabout converts them; grade separation ELIMINATES them.** Three answers to the same problem at three very different costs — and the right choice depends on volume and on land availability, not on which is technically most complete.

examTip.trick: **Lost time is pure overhead** — 3–4 seconds per phase during which nothing moves productively. Converting it into usable green is the only change that raises capacity without a penalty elsewhere.
examTip.trap: **MORE PHASES REDUCE capacity**, because each phase adds its own lost time. A four-phase signal wastes roughly twice what a two-phase one does — even though each phase looks individually safer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Webster: C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y)**, with L in the numerator — cut lost time and the cycle shortens *and* capacity rises. Practical cycles are **40–120 s**; beyond that delay grows steeply.

questions.stem: In construction contracts, a "retention money" clause is included primarily to:
options: Cover the cost of variations ordered by the employer
Pay for the contractor's insurance premiums
Secure the correction of defects appearing after completion
questions.solution:
**To secure the correction of defects appearing after completion.**

**How retention works:**

> A **percentage of each interim payment — commonly 5 to 10% — is withheld** by the employer, up to a stated limit.

| Stage | Release |
|---|---|
| **At substantial completion / handover** | **HALF** the retention is released |
| **At the end of the DEFECTS LIABILITY PERIOD** | The **remaining half** is released, provided defects have been made good |

> **The defects liability period is typically 12 months**, during which the contractor must return and rectify defects that appear.

**Why it exists:**

> **A contractor paid in full at handover has no financial incentive to return.** Retention keeps a sum at stake until the work has demonstrated itself in service.

> **It converts a promise into security.** Defects often do not appear until a building has been through a full cycle of use and weather — which is exactly what the twelve-month period is designed to cover, and why a **monsoon** must fall within it for any Nepali project to be meaningfully tested.

**The distinction from the other contractual instruments** — which is exactly what the distractors test:

| Instrument | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **RETENTION money** | **Security for DEFECTS** — withheld from payments |
| **LIQUIDATED DAMAGES** | **Pre-agreed sum for DELAY** — per day or week of overrun |
| **PERFORMANCE bond / bank guarantee** | Security for **performance generally**, including contractor default |
| **Advance payment guarantee** | Secures the mobilisation advance |
| **Variation order** | A written instruction **altering the scope** — leads to payment, not deduction |
| **Contingency** | The employer's provision (3–5%) for **unforeseen items** |

> **Each option in this question names a real contractual concept applied to the wrong instrument**, so it is a clean test of whether the family is understood.

**LIQUIDATED DAMAGES deserve a note** because they are the most misunderstood:

> They are a **genuine pre-estimate of the employer's loss from delay**, agreed in advance — **NOT a penalty.**

> **A sum that is a penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate may be unenforceable**, which is why the amount must be justifiable by reference to real anticipated loss (lost revenue, extended supervision, alternative accommodation) rather than set punitively.

> Their advantage to **both** parties: the employer need not **prove** its loss, and the contractor knows its **maximum exposure** in advance.

**VARIATIONS** are the commonest source of dispute:
