> A **variation is a written instruction by the employer or engineer altering the scope** — additions, omissions, or changes in quality or sequence.

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Must be in WRITING** | Verbal instructions are the root of most claims |
| **Rate derived from contract rates** where possible | By analogy, or by **analysis of rates** for a new item |
| May carry **time** as well as cost | An extension of time may be due |

> **The single most valuable discipline on a construction site is confirming instructions in writing** — because the dispute is almost never about whether the work was done, but about whether it was instructed.

**The contract types**, for completeness:

| Type | Risk on |
|---|---|
| **Item rate (unit price)** | **Employer** carries quantity risk; contractor carries rate risk. **The commonest for civil works** |
| **Lump sum** | **Contractor** carries most risk; needs complete drawings |
| **Cost plus** | **Employer** carries almost all risk; for urgent or undefined work |
| Percentage rate | Contractor quotes above/below a schedule |

> **Item rate suits civil engineering because quantities genuinely cannot be known exactly in advance** — earthwork, foundations and rock excavation all depend on ground conditions discovered as work proceeds.

examTip.trick: Retention answers one question: **what makes a contractor come back?** A contractor paid in full at handover has no incentive to return — retention keeps money at stake through the defects liability period.
examTip.trap: **Each distractor names a real instrument applied to the wrong purpose**: delay is covered by **liquidated damages**, variations by a **variation order**, insurance by the contractor's own cost. Know the family as a set.
examTip.mnemonic: **Half released at completion, half at the end of the 12-month defects liability period** — long enough for a full monsoon to test the work. And **liquidated damages are a pre-estimate of LOSS, not a penalty** — a true penalty may be unenforceable.

questions.stem: For two mutually exclusive projects of very different sizes, the correct basis for choosing between them is:
options: The higher internal rate of return
questions.solution:
**The higher net present value.**

**Why NPV is the correct criterion:**

> **NPV measures the ABSOLUTE value added, in today's money.** It answers the question that actually matters: **how much richer does this decision make us?**

> **IRR measures a RATE, and a rate says nothing about scale.**

**The illustration that settles it:**

| Project | Investment | Return | IRR | NPV at 10% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Rs 1 lakh | 50% | **50%** | Small |
| **B** | Rs 1 crore | 20% | 20% | **Large** |

> **Project A has the higher IRR; Project B adds far more value.** A 50% return on a small sum is worth less than a 20% return on a large one.

> **When NPV and IRR disagree on MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE projects, NPV is right.** You cannot spend a percentage.

**IRR's two well-known failures:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCALE (size) problem** | Ranks a small high-rate project above a large value-adding one |
| **MULTIPLE IRRs** | If the cash flow **changes sign more than once** — a project with a large end-of-life cost such as **mine closure or decommissioning** — several rates give NPV = 0, and none is meaningful |

> A third, related issue is the **reinvestment assumption**: IRR implicitly assumes intermediate cash flows are reinvested **at the IRR itself**, which is usually unrealistic. **NPV assumes reinvestment at the discount rate**, which is the correct opportunity cost.

**Where IRR remains useful:**

> **For INDEPENDENT projects (accept or reject, not choose between), IRR and NPV give the SAME answer** — accept if IRR > MARR, which is equivalent to NPV > 0.

> **IRR's advantage is communicative**: it is a single percentage that can be compared against the cost of capital without knowing the discount rate in advance. That is why it survives despite its defects.

**Why payback is not a decision criterion:**

> **Payback answers a LIQUIDITY question — "how soon do I get my money back?" — not a profitability one.**

> **It ignores EVERYTHING that happens after the payback point**, so it systematically penalises **long-lived infrastructure** — exactly the kind of project it is most often applied to.

> It also (in its simple form) **ignores the time value of money** entirely. It survives because it is simple and because it does measure real exposure to risk over time — but it should inform a decision, never make one.

**The appraisal methods compared:**

| Method | Discounted? | Decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| **NPV** | **Yes** | Accept if **≥ 0**; choose the **highest** |
| **IRR** | Yes | Accept if **> MARR** |
| **B/C ratio** | Yes | Accept if **≥ 1** — **standard for PUBLIC projects** |
| **Payback** | **No** | Shorter is better — a supplementary measure only |
| ARR | No | Uses accounting profit, not cash flow |

**A caution about the benefit-cost ratio:**

> **B/C ratio has the SAME scale problem as IRR** — it is a ratio, so it favours small efficient projects over large valuable ones. **For choosing between mutually exclusive public projects, INCREMENTAL analysis is required**: compare the extra benefit against the extra cost of the larger option.

**And the assumption that dominates every public appraisal:**

> **The DISCOUNT RATE.** A high rate discounts distant benefits almost to nothing, making **long-lived infrastructure look poor** — a dam delivering benefits for eighty years is judged mainly on its first fifteen.

> **That single assumption often determines the answer more than any engineering input does**, which is why sensitivity analysis on the discount rate is essential and why the choice of rate for public projects is genuinely contested.

examTip.trick: **You cannot spend a percentage.** IRR is a rate and says nothing about scale — a 50% return on Rs 1 lakh adds less value than 20% on Rs 1 crore. NPV measures **absolute value added**.
examTip.trap: **For INDEPENDENT projects IRR and NPV agree.** The conflict arises only for **mutually exclusive** ones — and IRR also breaks down entirely when cash flows change sign twice (multiple IRRs).
examTip.mnemonic: **Payback answers a LIQUIDITY question, not a profitability one** — it ignores everything after payback, penalising long-lived infrastructure. And **B/C ratio shares IRR's scale problem**: use incremental analysis for public choices.
